In addition, removal of the pier would also generate demolition debris in the form of the concrete

Pier 96 in San Francisco for sorting), followed via truck for disposal include the following:
    2,000 cubic yards of concrete demolition debris
    1,000 cubic yards of timber demolition debris

Dredging and Debris Disposal
Dredging is the process of removing sediment from the bottom of waterbodies to make waterways
deeper for boats. The following specifications represent the maximum extent of potential dredging;
however, further design may decrease the proposed dredging footprint and/or volume.
Nonetheless, for the purposes of environmental analysis, this Environmental Impact Report uses
these conservative assumptions.
As part of the proposed project, dredging would be conducted north of the closed pier. Dredging
would be needed along the existing 100-foot wide United States Army Corps of Engineers (USACE)-
designated federal navigation channel that parallels the closed pier and which future ferry vessels
would use to travel to and from the pier. Refer to Figure 2-2 for the location of dredging. In addition,
dredging would be needed for the turning basin, which would allow for ferry vessels to turn and
dock at the two ferry boarding floats. Dredging would be done to a maximum depth of minus 12.51
feet City of Berkeley mean lower low water (MLLW) 22, which is equal to -12 feet National Oceanic
and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) MLLW. A maximum total of 400,000 cubic yards of dredged
materials would be generated and would require disposal.
Dredged materials and demolition debris would all be transported via barge that have a capacity of
between 3,000 and 6,000 cubic yards. The location for disposal of dredged materials would depend
on the sampling results of the dredged materials, as well as permitting requirements. However,
based on the recently completed Berkeley Marina Dredging Project of 2024 to 2025, it is expected
that disposal would occur at Montezuma Wetland Restoration Project (Beneficial Reuse), Alcatraz
Disposal Site, or another disposal site in the San Francisco Bay.

2.6.2         Construction Schedule
Construction for the proposed project would primarily occur during the day; however, nighttime
work may be required for pile driving. Based on the number of piles per day that are proposed, the
number of nights for nighttime work is not expected to exceed 50 nights. When work occurs during
the day, construction would be limited to 7:00 A.M and 7:00 P.M. on weekdays and 9:00 A.M. and
8:00 P.M. on weekends and holidays, in compliance with the City of Berkeley’s Municipal Code.

2.7              Operational Details
2.7.1            Operational Scenario and Ridership 23
A conceptual plan for ferry service has been provided in the 2022 San Francisco Bay Area Water
Emergency Transportation Authority (WETA) Berkeley Ferry Service Business Plan, Version 1.0. 24
This is a living document and updates to the Business Plan and contemplated ferry service will be
captured in future updates. The following ferry operation is proposed in the current Berkeley Ferry
Service Business Plan, Version 1.0:
      WETA would operate two 250-passenger electric zero-emission vessels on the weekday route
       between Berkeley and San Francisco.
      Weekend service would operate a single 250-passenger vessel to Larkspur and a single 250-
       passenger vessel to San Francisco.
      At least three round-trip services would be completed during peak hours for the Berkeley/San
       Francisco weekday service, pursuant to WETA Board-adopted standards.
      The Berkeley-San Francisco service would travel 6.7 miles between the Berkeley Ferry Terminal
       and the San Francisco Ferry Terminal. The total one-way travel time would be 25 minutes, door-
       to-door. Weekday peak-direction headways 25 would be approximately 35 minutes. Weekend
       headways would be 70 to 110 minutes, depending on the time of day.
      The Berkeley-Larkspur service would travel 11.8 miles between the terminal at the Berkeley
       Marina and the Larkspur Ferry Terminal. The one-way travel time would be 35 minutes, door-to-
       door. Weekend headways would be 90 to 150 minutes, depending on the time of day.
      Special event service may operate between Berkeley and San Francisco or Mission Bay (e.g., for
       events at the Chase Center or Oracle Park or future events at the Berkeley Marina), as well as
       between Larkspur and Berkeley.

2.7.2              Energy Source and Consumption
The project site receives electricity from a community-governed power supplier, Ava Community
Energy (Ava), formerly East Bay Community Energy, delivered by PG&E. Ava’s service area covers
approximately 849 square miles, serving all of Alameda County and the cities of Tracy, Stockton, and
Lathrop. 28 As of 2023, Ava’s power mix is comprised of 54.8 percent eligible renewable energy and is
on track to be 100 percent carbon free by 2030. 29
Power would be delivered by PG&E, which acquires energy from power plants owned by Ava
Community Energy. Electricity would be delivered via PG&E electrical conduits from the nearest
PG&E substation, El Cerrito G, located approximately 5 miles northeast of the project site in Contra
Costa. It is anticipated that the project would require approximately 4 megawatts of electricity to
support operational electricity needs. The project could be served from existing capacity at El
Cerrito G. To the extent that trenching and placement of new conduits for power or other
infrastructure upgrades are required at the project site; those improvements are assessed herein.
PG&E has its own process for evaluating service changes as part of its programming and planning for
the service area. 30 Except as specifically included herein (see Section 2.5.4), PG&E upgrades would
be subject to their own environmental review process as they arise.

2.7.3          Infrastructure and Ferry Vessels Maintenance
The City and WETA would divide the operation and maintenance responsibilities in a separate future
agreement for the leasing and operation phase of the project for the following elements:
    Restroom, trash, landscaping, fish cleaning station, public pier entrance gate, lighting, and
     recreation pier maintenance (City)
    Ferry berth gates, floats, gangways, electrical, and all other ferry-related infrastructure, as
     necessary (WETA)
    Roads, Bay Trail, plaza, landscaping, resurfacing, and other maintenance (City)

In addition, ferry vessels would occasionally layover at the ferry landing. However, any maintenance
on ferry vessels would occur at WETA’s Central Bay Operations and Maintenance Facility at 670
West Hornet Avenue in Alameda, where WETA currently maintains its vessels. 31 Implementation of
this project would not change the maintenance practices currently in place at WETA’s Central Bay
Operations and Maintenance Facility.

2.7.4          Programming and Plaza Operation
Future programming at the public plaza has not yet been determined and would depend on input
from the public, as well as any regulatory agencies that have jurisdiction over the project site, such
as the San Francisco Bay Conservation and Development Commission (BCDC). For the purposes of
environmental analysis in this Environmental Impact Report, the City has identified potential
programming options that could occur in the public plaza. Programming may include small mobile
vendors, such as coffee carts or food trucks. The City may also plan special events, such as small
concerts, fishing derbies, and semi-regular pop-up style events such as a Farmer’s or Craft Market.
Amplified sound would only occur in the public plaza for special events. The City estimates that
special events would be limited to approximately 12 days per year, between the hours of 10:00 A.M.
and 8:00 P.M. The public plaza can also serve as a meeting place for formal or informal group
recreation activities like running, biking, walking, or nature viewing groups.

3          Environmental Impact Analysis

In compliance with California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) and CEQA Guidelines Section 15125
and 15126, this chapter sets forth the physical and regulatory environmental setting and addresses
environmental impacts of the proposed project with respect to the environmental topics listed
below. The discussions of the environmental setting in each subsequent section of this
Environmental Impact Report (EIR) describe the existing physical environmental conditions, or
baseline conditions, at the project site and vicinity. The baseline used for the analysis of
environmental impacts under CEQA reflects the conditions present at the time the EIR Notice of
Preparation (NOP) was published on April 18, 2025. The potential impacts of the proposed project
are compared against the existing baseline conditions for each environmental topic.

Environmental Topics Addressed in this EIR
The following environmental topics are assessed in this chapter in accordance with CEQA and CEQA
Guidelines, including CEQA Guidelines Appendix G:
   Aesthetics                                         Hydrology and Water Quality
   Air Quality                                        Land Use and Planning
   Biological Resources                               Noise
   Cultural Resources                                 Recreation
   Geology and Soils                                  Transportation
   Greenhouse Gas Emissions and Energy                Tribal Cultural Resources
   Hazards and Hazardous Materials                    Utilities and Service Systems

CEQA Guidelines Section 15128 requires that an EIR “contain a statement briefly indicating the
reasons that various possible significant effects of a project were determined not to be significant
and therefore were not discussed in detail in the EIR.” The following environmental topics from
CEQA Guidelines Appendix G are not discussed in detail in this EIR, because no significant impacts
would occur as a result of construction or operation of the proposed project. Therefore, these topics
are addressed in Section 3.15, Effects Found Not to Be Significant, following the aforementioned
topical sections.

   Agriculture and Forestry Resources                 Public Services
   Mineral Resources                                  Wildfire
   Population and Housing

EIR Baseline
Under CEQA, the impacts of a proposed project must be evaluated by comparing expected
environmental impacts as a result of the project to conditions at a point in time referred to as
baseline conditions. State CEQA Guidelines Section 15125 states that the existing physical conditions
in the vicinity of the project will normally constitute the baseline physical conditions by which the
lead agency determines whether an impact is significant. Accordingly, an EIR should describe
physical environmental conditions of the project site and vicinity as they exist at the time that the
EIR NOP is published, or if no NOP is published, then at the time environmental analysis is


Draft Environmental Impact Report                                                                   3-1
City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project

commenced, from both a local and regional perspective. This environmental setting constitutes the
baseline physical environmental conditions against which a lead agency determines whether a
proposed project’s impact is significant. Therefore, because the EIR NOP was published on April 18,
2025, this is the point in time that is used in this EIR to determine the baseline conditions. This
baseline includes the closure of the existing pier, the closure of the HS Lordship restaurant located
at 199 Seawall Drive, and intermittent closure of the Seawall Drive parking lot. This baseline reflects
the existing conditions at the time that the EIR NOP was published.
As part of the scoping process, the City received comments from the public requesting the use of a
different baseline (specifically one that pre-dates the closure of the pier, the HS Lordship’s
Restaurant and the intermittent closure of the Seawall Drive parking lot) due to concerns that an
analysis based on the actual baseline (existing conditions as of April 18, 2025) would not accurately
reflect potential impacts on parking. The pier has been closed since 2015, the HS Lordship
restaurant has been closed since 2018, and the Seawall Drive parking lot has been closed
intermittently since 2018. These facilities being open is not representative of the EIR NOP baseline
conditions. Lack of parking is not considered an environmental impact under CEQA. Given the
guidance from CEQA Guidelines Section 15125 and that the main concern raised by the public
requesting the use of a different baseline is for a non-CEQA topic, a baseline that differs from the
existing condition at the time of the NOP publication is not used for this analysis.

Format of the Environmental Analysis
This EIR provides analyses of impacts of those environmental topics for which the proposed project
could result in potentially significant effects. “Significant effect” is defined by CEQA Guidelines
Section 15382 as “a substantial, or potentially substantial, adverse change in any of the physical
conditions within the area affected by the project including land, air, water, minerals, flora, fauna,
ambient noise, and objects of historic or aesthetic significance. An economic or social change by
itself shall not be considered a significant effect on the environment. A social or economic change
related to a physical change may be considered in determining whether the physical change is
significant.”
Sections 3.1 through 3.14 discuss the environmental impacts that may result due to construction
and/or operation of the proposed project. The format of the environmental analysis for each
environmental topic in Sections 3.1 through 3.14 includes the subsections summarized below.

Introduction
This subsection summarizes what will be discussed in the respective environmental topic section
and states what informational documents are used as the basis for the section.

Environmental Setting
In accordance with CEQA Guidelines Section 15125(a), this subsection describes the existing,
baseline physical environmental conditions of the project site and vicinity (e.g., existing land uses,
transportation conditions, noise environment) with respect to each resource topic at the time the
NOP was issued. Conditions are described in sufficient detail to allow a general understanding of the
environmental impacts associated with construction and operation of the proposed project in order
to determine whether a significant environmental impact would occur (CEQA Guidelines Section
15126.2[a]). Extraneous setting information that does not shed light on the impact analysis is not
included in this EIR pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Section 15125[a]).



3-2
                                                                            Environmental Impact Analysis



Regulatory Framework
This subsection describes the relevant federal, California, regional, and local regulatory
requirements that are directly applicable to the environmental topic being analyzed. Where the
project site and its vicinity fall within the jurisdiction of federal, State, and local regulatory agencies,
the proposed project would be subject to the environmental-related laws, rules, regulations, and
policies of those agencies. These regulations are intended to reduce adverse effects on sensitive
environmental resources and/or offer general guidance on the protection of such resources.

Impacts and Mitigation Measures
This subsection evaluates the potential for the proposed project to result in direct and indirect
adverse impacts on the existing physical environment, with consideration of both construction and
operation impacts. The significance criteria questions for environmental impacts are listed at the
beginning of this subsection, followed by the discussion of the approach to the analysis (including
consideration of EIR scoping comments received) and specific thresholds of significance that have
been applied to evaluate the impacts of the proposed project, and finally by the discussion of
environmental impacts (both construction and operational) and identified mitigation measures.
Indirect impacts are discussed where they have the potential to occur.
Impacts are analyzed and the respective assessments and findings are provided, applying the
following levels of significance:
   No Impact. A determination of No Impact is reached if no potential exists for impacts or if the
    environmental resource does not occur in the project site or the area of potential impacts.
   Less Than Significant Impact. This determination applies if the impact does not exceed the
    defined significance criteria or would be eliminated or reduced to a less than significant level
    through compliance with existing local, State, and federal laws and regulations. No mitigation is
    required for impacts determined to be less than significant.
   Less Than Significant Impact with Mitigation. This determination applies if the proposed
    project would result in a significant impact, exceeding the established significance criteria, but
    feasible mitigation is available that would reduce the impact to a less than significant level.
   Significant and Unavoidable Impact. This determination applies if the proposed project would
    result in an adverse impact that exceeds the established significance criteria, and no feasible
    mitigation is available to reduce the impact to a less than significant level. Therefore, the
    residual impact would be significant and unavoidable.

Impacts are defined in terms of their context and intensity. Context is related to the uniqueness of a
resource; intensity refers to the severity of the impact. Where applicable, best management
practices or improvement measures, or both, are incorporated into the proposed project to limit the
potential for a significant impact. Where necessary, mitigation measures are identified for
significant impacts to limit the degree or lower the magnitude of the impact; rectify the impact by
repairing, rehabilitating, or restoring the affected environment; or compensate for the impact by
replacing or providing substitute resources or environments. These impacts conclude with a finding
of Less than Significant Impact with Mitigation. Where no mitigation measures are necessary,
relevant impacts are concluded to be Less than Significant or to have No Impact.
As part of the impact analysis, mitigation measures are identified, where necessary and feasible, for
impacts considered significant or potentially significant consistent with CEQA Guidelines Section
15126.4, which states that an EIR “shall describe feasible measures which could minimize significant

adverse impacts.” CEQA requires that mitigation measures have an essential nexus and be roughly
proportional to the significant impact identified in the EIR. The future project sponsors are required
to implement all mitigation measures identified in the Final EIR, and the lead agency (in this case,
the City of Berkeley) is responsible for overseeing implementation of such mitigation measures.
Impacts are numbered and shown in bold type. The corresponding mitigation measures, where
identified, are numbered and indented, and follow the impact statements. Impacts and mitigation
measures are numbered consecutively within each topic and include an abbreviated reference to
the impact section (e.g., “LU” for Land Use and Planning). The following abbreviations are used for

Cumulative Impacts
This subsection evaluates the potential for the proposed project in conjunction with other identified
cumulative projects to result in cumulative impacts. The projects identified in the Cumulative
Scenario Setting subsection below, in conjunction with the proposed project, are considered the
cumulative scenario for the analysis of cumulative impacts.
The goal of the cumulative impacts analysis is to determine whether the overall long-term impacts
of all such projects would be cumulatively significant, and to determine whether the proposed
project on its own would cause a “cumulatively considerable” incremental contribution to any such
cumulatively significant impacts. To determine whether the overall long-term impacts of all such
projects would be cumulatively significant, the analysis generally considers the following:
     The area in which impacts of the proposed project would be experienced;
     The impacts of the proposed project that are expected in the area;
     Other past, present, and reasonably foreseeable projects that have had or are expected to have
      impacts in the same area;
     The impacts or expected impacts of these other projects; and
     The overall impact that can be expected if the individual impacts from each project are allowed
      to accumulate.



3-4
                                                                          Environmental Impact Analysis



“Cumulative impacts” refers to two or more individual impacts that, when considered together, are
considerable, or that compound or increase other environmental impacts (CEQA Guidelines Section
15355). Cumulative impacts can result from individually minor but collectively significant impacts
taking place over time. If the analysis determines that the potential exists for the proposed project,
taken together with other past, present, and probable future projects, to result in a significant or
adverse cumulative impact, the analysis then determines whether the proposed project’s
incremental contribution to any significant cumulative impact is itself significant (i.e., “cumulatively
considerable”). The cumulative impact analysis for each individual resource topic is presented in
each resource section of this chapter immediately after the description of the direct impacts and
identified mitigation measures.
Pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Section 15130(a)(1), “As defined in Section 15355, a cumulative impact
consists of an impact that is created as a result of the combination of the project evaluated in the
EIR together with other projects causing related impacts. An EIR should not discuss impacts that do
not result in part from the project evaluated in the EIR.” Therefore, where the proposed project
would have no impact in a particular resource area, the proposed project could not contribute to a
cumulatively considerable impact, and cumulative impacts are not discussed further for that
resource topic.
CEQA Guidelines Section 15130(b)(1)(A)-(B) states that a discussion of cumulative impacts can either
include, “a list of past, present, and probable future projects producing related or cumulative
impacts, including, if necessary, those projects outside the control of the agency, or a summary of
projections contained in an adopted local, regional, or Statewide plan, or related planning
document, that describes or evaluates conditions contributing to the cumulative effect…”.
This EIR evaluates cumulative impacts using both approaches, depending on the environmental
resource topic. For example, cumulative impacts related to water supply demand consider the
projections from the East Bay Municipal Utility District’s Urban Water Management Plan, to account
for the overall cumulative water demand from the provider that would service the project. Please
refer to each environmental topic, which identifies the approach used for the cumulative impact
analysis therein.

Cumulative Scenario Setting
In determining the cumulative scenario setting, the City considered the geographic scope for each of
the environmental resource topics considered in this EIR. The geographic scope for each
environmental resource is included in Sections 3.1 through 3.14 of this EIR. The geographic scope
varies by each environmental topic. For example, the geographic scope for criteria air pollutants is
the entire San Francisco Bay Area Air Basin, whereas the geographic scope for hazardous materials
is the immediate vicinity of the project. With a few exceptions, and as explained in Sections 3.1
through 3.14 of this EIR, the geographic scopes of the project are within the immediate vicinity or
near the immediate vicinity of the project site. Where the geographic context is greater than the
immediate vicinity of the project site, for example for air quality or greenhouse gas emissions, the
cumulative impact analysis in this EIR describes how the regulatory thresholds account for
cumulative impacts. For these reasons, the cumulative projects shown in Figure 3-1 and Table 3-1
represent the cumulative projects within the immediate vicinity or near the immediate vicinity of
the project.
In determining the cumulative scenario setting, the City considered past, present, and probable
future projects. Past projects include the existing buildings and infrastructure on and near the
project site that have already been built. There are certain situations where past projects influence

Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project

the cumulative environmental impact analysis. For example, for toxic air contaminants, the
cumulative air quality analysis considers past projects that have already been built and currently
generate toxic air contaminants, in addition to the proposed project, pursuant to recommendations
from the Bay Area Air District. Please refer to the Cumulative Impacts discussions at the end of
Sections 3.1 through 3.14 of this EIR that describe which other cumulative projects would apply to
the specific cumulative environmental topic and analysis.
Present projects include projects that are currently under construction, and these were included in
Table 3-1. Reasonably foreseeable future projects are defined as those likely to occur during the
same period of time as construction and operation of the project and that could contribute to the
cumulative impact on a particular environmental resource. Reasonably foreseeable projects are
future projects (including those currently proposed) that are likely or probable, rather than those
that are merely possible. Generally, projects are reasonably foreseeable if they meet any one or
more of the following conditions:
     The project is a foreseeable future phase of an existing project.
     Applications for project entitlements or construction are pending with a government agency
      (these projects may have been analyzed in a recent environmental document).
     The project is included in regional transportation plans; regional transportation improvement
      programs; local long-range transportation plans; local land use, general, and specific plans; or an
      agency’s budget or capital improvement program.

Secondary Impacts

Mitigation Measures
Section 15126.4(a)(1)(D) of the CEQA Guidelines states that “if a mitigation measure would cause
one or more significant effects in addition to those that would be caused by the project as
proposed, the effects of the mitigation measure shall be discussed but in less detail than the
significant effects of the project as proposed.” As required by the CEQA Guidelines, this EIR
considers the potential secondary impacts from mitigation. Specifically, this EIR considers the
potential secondary impacts on Air Quality, Hazards and Hazardous Materials, and Utilities and
Service Systems due to Biological Resources mitigation for impacts associated with fill of the Bay.
Please refer to Section 3.3, Biological Resources for a discussion of the secondary impacts from
mitigation.

Parking
In compliance with CEQA and the CEQA Guidelines, as well as case-law, the City does not analyze
the loss of, or change in, parking capacity as a CEQA impact, and instead focuses on potential
secondary environmental impacts related to parking, such as drivers circling the area searching for
parking. Please refer to Section 3.2, Air Quality; Section 3.10, Noise; and Section 3.12,
Transportation, for an analysis of such potential secondary impacts. 3

Relationship with Draft Waterfront Specific Plan
The proposed Project can be built with or without the development associated with the Draft
Waterfront Specific Plan, and can offer recreational amenities and services to residents in Berkeley
and the region regardless of whether the Draft Waterfront Specific Plan is adopted. The proposed
Project and the Draft Waterfront Specific Plan are not interdependent, and each project can
proceed without the other. For example, the proposed Project can provide recreational amenities
and ferry service to people in Berkeley and the region, without implementation of the commercial
development contemplated by the Draft Waterfront Specific Plan. Accordingly, the proposed project
is a separate “project” under CEQA, because it constitutes the “whole of an action.” However, for
completeness, this EIR considers the potential contributions of other projects such as the Draft
Waterfront Specific Plan with respect to cumulative impacts.




3 Parking impacts, such as whether a project provides adequate parking, are exempt from CEQA review. As stated in San Franciscans

Upholding the Downtown Plan v. City & County of San Francisco (2002) 102 Cal.App. 656 at 697, “The social inconvenience of having to
hunt for scarce parking spaces is not an environmental impact; the secondary effect of scarce parking on traffic and air quality is. Under
CEQA, a project's social impacts need not be treated as significant impacts on the environment. An EIR need only address the secondary
physical impacts that could be triggered by a social impact.” Therefore, parking scarcity alone does not constitute a significant impact on
the environment. Instead, projects must be looked at on a case-by-case basis to determine whether there are secondary impacts related
to scarcity of parking (See, Save Our Access-San Gabriel Mountains v. Watershed Conservation Authority (2021) 68 Cal.App.5th 8).

3.1        Aesthetics
3.1.1      Introduction
This section describes existing conditions related to visual character, views, scenic views and
resources, and light and glare, as well as the relevant regulatory framework. This section also
evaluates potential impacts to aesthetics that could result from implementation of the proposed
project. Information in this section is based on information obtained from the Berkeley General
Plan, California State Scenic Highway System map, photographs taken of the project site, and
project-specific visual simulations.

3.1.2      Environmental Setting
Visual Character
Visual character in the CEQA context is an impartial description of the defining physical features,
landscape patterns, and distinctive physical qualities within a landscape. Visual character is
informed by the composition of land, vegetation, water, and structure and their relationship (or
dominance) to one another, and by prominent elements of form, line, color, and texture that
combine to define the composition of views. Visual character-defining resources and features within
a landscape may derive from notable landforms, vegetation, land uses, building design and façade
treatments, transportation facilities, overhead utility structures and lighting, historic structures or
districts, or panoramic open space.

Project Site
The project site and vicinity are located at and near the San Francisco Bay shoreline and are
generally characterized by a mixture of developed and natural waterfront elements. The project site
is generally surrounded by open water, except for a portion of the northern boundary which abuts
built structures, the Berkeley Marina, and open and recreational space (Shorebird Park, Horseshoe
Park, and McLaughlin Eastshore State Park). Available amenities in and around the project site
include recreational uses (such as Shorebird Park and beach, the Bay Trail Extension, picnic tables,
public sailing docks, and a nature center), restaurant buildings, surface parking areas, and open
water. Vegetation within the project site includes mature trees (such as Monterey pines and Torrey
pines), coyote brush scrub, ruderal vegetation, and low-lying ornamental shrubs and grasses.
The closed Berkeley Pier, which is in the western portion of the project site, extends approximately
3,000 feet into the Bay and is surrounded by open water to the north, south, and to the west. The
Berkeley Pier is shown in Figure 3.1-1, Photograph 1. The Pier is characterized by its extended, linear
form, which is emphasized by the wooden pier structure, vertical pilings, and the single row of
evenly spaced light standards running along the north side of the entire length of the pier. The
worn, established character of the Pier is defined by the sun-bleached wooden railings covered in
lichen and the moss-tinged concrete walkway.
An existing concrete and asphalt walking trail is located along the waterfront extending north and
south of the Pier, as shown in Figure 3.1-1 Photographs 2 and 3. Seawall Drive and parking spaces
are adjacent to these trails to the east. Adjacent to Pier to the north is the Skates on the Bay
restaurant (shown in Figure 3.1-1, Photograph 4, below). A parking lot is located to the east of the
Skates on the Bay restaurant; beyond that to the northeast is the Berkeley Marina which provides

1,000 leased private boat slips, 10 percent of which are live-aboard boats (Figure 3.1-1,

Recreational land uses proximate to the project site include brown gravel trails along the waterfront

Views
Views may be generally described as panoramic views of a large geographic area for which the field
of view can be wide and extend into the distance. Associated vantage points provide an orientation
from publicly accessible locations. Examples of distinctive views include urban skylines, valleys,
mountain ranges, or large bodies of water. Viewshed is a term used to describe a range of resources
and their context related to what people can see in the foreground, middle ground, and background
distances.

Project Site
VIEWS FROM AND THROUGH THE PROJECT SITE
Viewers recreating, driving, biking, sailing, swimming, or walking through or proximate to the
project site may be afforded views of the Berkeley Marina and the San Francisco Bay as well as more
distant views of the Golden Gate Bridge and the San Francisco City skyline as they visit Berkeley
parks (i.e., Shorebird Park, Horseshoe Park, and McLaughlin Eastshore State Park) and trails or travel
through Berkeley. Public views through the project site would vary based on location, proximity, and
weather clarity (i.e., fog density).
The Pier is currently closed to the public, however, the Pier and the waterfront area on the project
site and adjacent to the Pier provide varied distance views of the San Francisco Bay as well as
distant views of the Berkeley hills to the east, the Bay Bridge to the southwest, and the City of San
Francisco to the west on clear days.

VIEWS OF THE PROJECT SITE
Expansive views of the project site, including the Berkeley pier, are available from publicly accessible
waterfront points near the project site. Expansive views of the project site and the surrounding Bay
are also available from recreational viewing locations such as the Emeryville Marina and Point
Emery, located approximately 1.2 miles south and southeast of the project site, respectively.
Extended views of the project site are available from the waterfront recreational trails at Brickyard
Cove, located approximately 0.5 mile east of the project site. Views of the project site are also
available from César E. Chávez Park, located approximately 0.5 mile north of the project site,
although these views are intermittently obstructed by intervening trees.

Existing trees and vegetation along the edge of the project site block most views of the project site
from the Marina docks. In addition, public views of the project site vary based on location,
proximity, and weather clarity (i.e. fog density). However, in the vicinity, the project site is generally
visible from recreational trails and parks (Shorebird Park and Horseshoe Park) and shoreline areas.
The project site is also distantly visible from elevated publicly accessible viewpoints, such as those
afforded by hillside roadways and trails. Distant views of the project site are available from Grizzly
Peak Boulevard (approximately 5.5 miles east of the project site) and Stonewall Panoramic Trail.
Grizzly Peak Boulevard provides the public with panoramic summit views of the landscape, including
the city, the Bay, and the Bay Bridge, as well as access to local trailheads (e.g. Grizzly Peak Trail,
Seaview Trail) and Grizzly Peak Vista Point. The Stonewall Panoramic Trail, and other local trails,
provide similar viewsheds which encompass the expansive views of the area.

Scenic Resources and Scenic Views
Most communities identify scenic resources as important visual assets that contribute to community
identity. Visual resources are generally classified into two categories: scenic resources and scenic
views. These resources can include natural and open spaces, as well as the built environment,
specifically landforms, trees, water features, rock outcroppings, and historic buildings insofar as
they enhance and define the visual character of a landscape.
Scenic views are elements or components of the broader viewshed such as shorelines, mountain
ranges, valleys, and ridgelines. They are usually mid-ground or background elements of a viewshed
that can be seen from a range of viewpoints, often along a roadway or other corridor. Scenic
resources are specific features of a viewing area (or viewshed), such as trees. They are specific
features that act as the focal point of a viewshed and are usually foreground elements.

Project Site
The San Francisco Bay (Bay), which surrounds the project site to the north, south, and west, is
identified as a significant view in the Berkeley General Plan Urban Design and Preservation
Element. 1 In addition, in Policy UD-31 of the Berkeley General Plan identifies significant views of
landmarks, including of Golden Gate Bridge and Alcatraz Island, which are visible from the project
site. Additionally, the Berkeley General Plan Transportation Element identifies scenic routes within
Berkeley. Scenic routes are defined as a segment of an established regional network of routes which
traverse or provide the most efficient routes to or between areas of major scenic, recreation, or
cultural attractions. In the project vicinity, I-80, University Avenue, and Ashby Avenue are identified
as scenic routes that have views of the project site. 2

Scenic Highways
The California Scenic Highway Program designates scenic highways with the intention of protecting
these corridors from change that could diminish the aesthetic value of adjacent lands. The California
Department of Transportation (Caltrans) State Scenic Highway System includes a list of highways
that are either eligible for designation as scenic highways or have been officially designated. A
highway may be designated scenic depending upon how much of the natural landscape can be seen

Project Site
The nearest State-designated scenic highway is a portion of State Route 24 (SR 24), which is located

approximately 1.7 miles north of the project site. Similarly, due to intervening development and
landforms, the project site is not visible from I-80.

Light and Glare
In the context of CEQA, light is nighttime illumination that stimulates sight and makes things visible.
Glare refers to light that is so bright that it creates a nuisance or a hazard, or inhibits the ability to
see effectively, such as direct or reflected sunlight.

Project Site

LIGHT
Primary stationary sources of light at the project site include streetlights, parking lot and safety
lighting, pier lighting, and exterior building lights. Automobile headlights also create temporary,
mobile sources of light along proximate roadways and within on-site and nearby parking lots. Refer
to Figure 3.1-2, Photograph 1 for a representative photograph of the existing lighting on the pier.
Refer to Figure 3.1-2, Photograph 2 for a photograph of the Berkeley Waterfront, which shows the
nighttime lighting on the pier, as well as the Seawall Drive Parking lot (refer to the middle of the
photograph, to the peninsula located to the left of the pier).

GLARE
Current glare levels within the project site and the vicinity are consistent with urbanized
development. Primary sources of glare include sunlight reflected in the windows of buildings,
including glass façades, and the windshields of parked cars, as well as reflections on the Bay along
the waterfront.

3.1.3      Regulatory Framework
Federal Regulations
No federal plans, policies, regulations, or laws related to aesthetics are applicable, because the
project site is not located on federal lands and does not include scenic resources that are federally
regulated (i.e., historic resources or Wild and Scenic Rivers).

State Regulations

California Scenic Highway Program
The State Legislature created the California Scenic Highway Program, maintained by Caltrans, in
1963. The purpose of the State Scenic Highway Program is to protect and enhance the natural scenic
beauty of California highways and adjacent corridors, through special conservation treatment. The
State laws governing the Scenic Highway Program are found in the Streets and Highways Code,
Sections 260 through 263. The State Scenic Highway System includes a list of highways that are
either eligible for designation as scenic highways or have been officially designated as such. The
status of a proposed State Scenic Highway changes officially from eligible to officially designated
when the local governing body applies to Caltrans for scenic highway approval, adopts a Corridor
Protection Program, and receives notification that the highway has been officially designated a
Scenic Highway.

California Code of Regulations Title 24 - Building Lighting Characteristics
The California Building Standards Code (California Code of Regulations [CCR] Title 24) includes the
Building Energy Efficiency Standards (included in Parts 6 and 12 of CCR Title 24). Section 6.3 of the
Nonresidential and Multifamily Compliance Manual of the Building Energy Efficiency Standards
regulates lighting characteristics (i.e., maximum power/brightness, shielding, light sensor controls).
Different lighting standards are set by classifying areas by lighting zone. The classification is based
on 2010 United States Census population estimates. Areas can be designated as LZ0 (very low), LZ1
(low), LZ2 (moderate), LZ3 (moderately high), and LZ4 (high). Lighting requirements for dark and
rural areas are stricter in order to protect the areas from new sources of light pollution and light
trespass. The City of Berkeley falls under the “urban” standard and thus, is designated LZ3.

Regional and Local Regulations

Berkeley General Plan Open Space Element
The Berkeley General Open Space Element includes the following policy applicable to aesthetics:

Policy OS-12 Adjacent Uses
Ensure that land adjacent to parks is sensitively developed so that shade on the park is minimized,
safe access is maintained, and views are not significantly reduced. Actions:
A. Assure that new development along the shoreline recognizes its unique location, considers
   sensitive natural resources, and maintains adequate shoreline access and views.

Berkeley General Plan Urban Design Element
The Berkeley General Urban Design Element includes the following objectives and policies
applicable to aesthetics:

Objective 1: Protection of Existing Resources
Preserve historically or culturally important structures, sites, and areas and protect the character of
Berkeley’s neighborhoods and districts.

Objective 3: New Construction and Alterations
Ensure that new construction and alterations are well designed and respect and enhance the
existing environment.

Policy UD-3: Regulation of Neighborhood Character
Use regulations to protect the character of neighborhoods and districts, and respect the particular
conditions of each area.

Policy UD-7: Disaster Preparedness
Encourage and support the long-term protection of historically or architecturally significant
buildings to preserve neighborhood and community character.

Policy UD-16: Context
The design and scale of new or remodeled buildings should respect the built environment in the
area, particularly where the character of the built environment is largely defined by an aggregation
of historically and architecturally significant buildings.

Policy UD-18: Contrast and Cohesiveness
The overall urban experience should contain variety and stimulating contrasts achieved largely
through contrast between different areas each of which is visually cohesive.

Policy UD-19: Visually Heterogeneous Areas
In areas that are now visually heterogeneous, a project should be responsive to the best design
elements of the area or neighborhood.

Policy UD-22: Regulating New Construction and Alterations
Regulate new construction and alterations to ensure that they are individually well-designed and
that they are so designed and located as to duly respect and where possible enhance the existing
built environment.

Policy UD-23: Design Review
Ensure that the design review process ensures excellence in design and that new construction and
alterations to existing buildings are compatible with the best elements of the character of the area.

Policy UD-24: Area Character
Regulate new construction and alterations to ensure that they are truly compatible with and, where
feasible, reinforce the desirable design characteristics of the particular area they are in.

Policy UD-30: Planting
Ensure that, where feasible, new developments respect and contribute to the urban landscape by
retaining existing on-site trees and/or, if appropriate, planting suitable new ones on-site or in the
street right-of-way.

Policy UD-31: Views
Construction should avoid blocking significant views, especially ones toward the Bay, the hills, and
significant landmarks such as the Campanile, Golden Gate Bridge, and Alcatraz Island. Whenever
possible, new buildings should enhance a vista or punctuate or clarify the urban pattern.

Policy UD-35: Public Improvements
Undertake, and/or participate in, major improvement projects aimed at making the streetscape
more enjoyable, clarifying and strengthening the urban pattern, and generally enhancing Berkeley’s
physical character. Public works projects should be designed to make it easier for people to orient
themselves within Berkeley and understand and appreciate the city’s various districts and
neighborhoods, as well as to generally enhance the urban environment.

Policy LU-4: Discretionary Review

Berkeley Marina Master Plan
The Berkeley Marina Master Plan aims to provide long-term open space enhancement for the
Marina and includes the following guiding principles related to visual resources and aesthetics 5:
    Principle 1: Protect, restore, enhance, and expand wildlife habitat, open space, natural areas
     and biological resources.
      A. Protect, increase and enhance natural habitat and open space.
         − Maintain existing informal landscaping and provide new plantings. The Marina's
             landscaping conveys an informal, almost park-like setting comprised of extensive
             plantings of trees, shrubs, and open lawn areas. Future landscaping should continue this
             informal theme emphasizing native plants wherever possible. As needed, new plantings
             should concentrate on replacing dead or diseased plants and "filling out" areas of sparse
             plantings. Where new areas of planting are proposed their potential for view blockage
             and unwelcome shading should be considered. Plantings should be compatible in scale
             and color with the surrounding environment. Additional plantings should be installed to
             screen boatyard activities and parking lots and to enhance pedestrian pathways.

          B. Improve the Marina's landscaping, signage, and pedestrian amenities.
           − Enhance the Marina Entrance by installing new signage and plantings to create a sense
               of "arrival" at the Marina. The entrance to the Marina should be enhanced with
               landscaping to make it more appealing and signify arrival, while emphasizing views of
               the Bay, harbor, and boats. The PacBell building at the corner of Marina and University
               should be screened. Decorative pilings located at the entrance require removal for
               safety reasons. Incorporation of public art to replace the piles should be considered.
               Views into the Marina at its entry should be kept open.
           − Incorporate overlooks at the north end of Seawall Drive into a new pathway design for
               the area.

    Principle 3: Maintain and upgrade infrastructure.
      Improve restroom facilities. Restrooms should be sited and landscaped to minimize the
         visual impacts of the structures. Adequate signage should be installed to identify locations.
         All the Marina's restrooms should eventually be replaced to make them comply with ADA
         requirements. Like other buildings at the Marina, they are aging and have only received
         limited refurbishment. A facility should be located near the parking circle at the end of
         Spinnaker Way. 6, 7

     space, views, wetlands, tidal mudflats, seasonal ponds, wetlands-type environment, creeks,
     meadows, beaches, and the low-density character of the waterfront area of the City.
    Chapter 23 includes general development standards including the height, setback, and light and
     glare regulations.

San Francisco Bay Plan
The San Francisco Bay Plan 8 developed by the San Francisco Bay Conservation and Development
Commission (BCDC) aims to maintain and enhance the Bay as a body of water that affords scenic
enjoyment. Key aesthetics objectives in the form of findings and policies applicable to the proposed
project include the following:
    Public Access Findings and Policies
      Finding a. San Francisco Bay is a dominant feature of the nine-county Bay Area and affords a
        variety of habitats for many diverse plant and wildlife populations. It provides an
        environment for numerous forms of public enjoyment including viewing, photography,
        wildlife observation, nature study, fishing, wading, walking, bicycling, jogging, or just sitting
        beside the water. As an outstanding visual resource, the Bay is an important focal point for
        the entire region that serves to orient people to its various parts.
      Finding j. Although opportunities for views of the Bay from public access areas have
        increased since the Bay Plan was adopted in 1968, there are still a significant number of
        shoreline areas where there exists little or no visual access to the Bay.
      Policy 9. Public access improvements provided as a condition of any approval should be
        consistent with the project, the culture(s) of the local community, and the physical
        environment, including protection of Bay natural resources, such as aquatic life, wildlife and
        plant communities, and provide for the public’s safety and convenience. The improvements
        should be designed and built to encourage diverse Bay-related activities and movement to
        and along the shoreline, should provide barrier free access for persons with disabilities, for
        people of all income levels, and for people of all cultures to the maximum feasible extent,
        should include an ongoing maintenance program, and should be identified with appropriate
        signs, including using appropriate languages or culturally-relevant icon-based signage.
      Policy 11. Roads near the edge of the water should be designed as scenic parkways for slow-
        moving, principally recreational traffic. The roadway and right-of-way design should
        maintain and enhance visual access for the traveler, discourage through traffic, and provide
        for safe, separated, and improved physical access to and along the shore. Public transit use
        and connections to the shoreline should be encouraged where appropriate.

   Appearance, Design, and Scenic Views Findings and Policies
     Finding a. Much too often, shoreline developments have not taken advantage of the
       magnificent setting provided by the Bay. Some shoreline developments are of poor quality
       or are inappropriate to a waterfront location. These include uses such as parking lots and
       some industrial structures, which neither visually complement the Bay nor take advantage
       of a waterfront location. Over time, existing shoreline development of poor quality and
       inappropriate uses will be phased out or upgraded by normal market forces and by public
       action or a combination of both.
     Finding b. Unsightly debris, such as plastic bottles, old tires, and other refuse continues to
       mar the appearance of the shoreline, particularly of marshes, mudflats, and sloughs.
     Finding c. The appearance of the Bay, and people’s enjoyment of it as a scenic resource,
       contribute to the enjoyment of daily life in the Bay Area. As a special kind of open space, the
       Bay acts as both the unifying element of the entire Bay region and as a physical divider of its
       parts. The wide surface of the Bay, and the distant vistas it affords, offer relief from the
       crowded, often chaotic, urbanized scene and help to create a sense of psychological
       wellbeing.
     Finding d. Probably the most widely enjoyed “use” of the Bay is simply viewing it-from the
       shoreline, from the water, and from afar; a Bay view can add substantially to the value of a
       home, office, or apartment building. Also, the Bay is a major visitor attraction for the tourist
       industry.
     Finding e. As a world-renowned scenic resource, the Bay is viewed and appreciated from
       many locations in the region. However, full advantage has not been taken of the dramatic
       view potential from the hills and other inland locations surrounding the Bay, often because
       of poor road and street layout and poorly located buildings or landscaping. While some
       jurisdictions have adopted controls on building heights and locations, there is still no
       general attention to maximizing views from streets and roads and to obtaining public view
       areas. In particular, along many urban waterfronts, man-made obstructions such as
       buildings, parking lots, utility lines, fences, billboards, and even landscaping have eliminated
       or severely diminished views of the Bay and shoreline.
     Finding f. One of the visual attractions of San Francisco Bay is its abundance of wildlife,
       particularly birds which are constantly moving around the Bay waters, marshes, and
       mudflats in search of food and refuge. The navigable, deep water sites around the Bay are a
       unique and limited resource and should be protected for uses requiring deep draft ship
       terminals, such as water-related industries and ports.
     Policy 1. To enhance the visual quality of development around the Bay and to take
       maximum advantage of the attractive setting it provides, the shores of the Bay should be
       developed in accordance with the Public Access Design Guidelines.
     Policy 2. All bayfront development should be designed to enhance the pleasure of the user
       or viewer of the Bay. Maximum efforts should be made to provide, enhance, or preserve
       views of the Bay and shoreline, especially from public areas, from the Bay itself, and from
       the opposite shore. To this end, planning of waterfront development should include
       participation by professionals who are knowledgeable of the Commission’s concerns, such
       as landscape architects, urban designers, or architects, working in conjunction with
       engineers and professionals in other fields.

        Policy 3. In some areas, a small amount of fill may be allowed if the fill is necessary-and is

        Policy 4. Structures and facilities that do not take advantage of or visually complement the

         Design, and Scenic Views; and the Public Access Design Guidelines. City, county, regional,
         state, and federal agencies should be guided in their evaluation of bayfront projects by the

         appropriate arrangements and heights of all developments and landscaping between the
         view areas and the water. In this regard, particular attention should be given to all
         waterfront locations, areas below vista points, and areas along roads that provide good
         views of the Bay for travelers, particularly areas below roads coming over ridges and
         providing a “first view” of the Bay.
        Policy 15. Vista points should be provided in the general locations indicated in the Plan
         maps. Access to vista points should be provided by walkways, trails, or other appropriate
         means and connect to the nearest public thoroughfare where parking or public
         transportation is available. In some cases, exhibits, museums, or markers would be
         desirable at vista points to explain the value or importance of the areas being viewed.

   Transportation Policies
     Policy 4. Transportation projects on the Bay shoreline and bridges over the Bay or certain
        waterways should include pedestrian and bicycle paths that will either be a part of the Bay
        Trail or connect the Bay Trail with other regional and community trails. Transportation
        projects should be designed to maintain and enhance visual and physical access to the Bay
        and along the Bay shoreline.

3.1.4      Impacts Analysis
Significance Criteria
The City of Berkeley utilizes the following 2025 CEQA Guidelines Appendix G significance criteria
questions related to Aesthetics.
Would the proposed project:
a) Have a substantial adverse effect on a scenic vista?
b) Substantially damage scenic resources, including but not limited to, trees, rock outcroppings,
   and historic buildings within a state scenic highway?
c) In non-urbanized areas, substantially degrade existing visual character or quality of public views
   of the site and its surroundings? If the project is in an urbanized area, would the project conflict
   with applicable zoning and other regulations governing scenic quality?
d) Create a new source of substantial light or glare that would adversely affect day or nighttime
   views in the area?

Approach to Analysis
Visual resources are generally defined as including natural and built features in the visible
landscape. Landforms, water, and vegetation are among the natural elements that define an area’s
visual character. Buildings, roads, and other structures reflect human modifications to the natural
landscape. The assessment of aesthetic impacts involves qualitative analysis that is inherently
subjective in nature. Different viewers react to views and aesthetic conditions differently. This
evaluation is limited to public views, as impacts to private views do not constitute an environmental
impact under CEQA. This analysis evaluates changes to the existing visual environment resulting
from the project.

Scenic Vistas and Resources
For the purposes of analysis, a scenic vista is a view from a public place (roadway, designated scenic
viewing spot, etc.) that is expansive and considered by the City of Berkeley to be important. It can
be obtained from an elevated position (such as from a trail near the top of a hillside) or it can be
seen from a roadway with a longer-range view of the landscape. A significant impact could occur if a
proposed project component would block or otherwise damage the scenic vista upon
implementation. The City also considers whether a proposed project component would block views
from a scenic route or corridor toward a visual/scenic resource (i.e., shoreline, ridgeline). Thus, this
criterion is also analyzed as part of Impact AES-1.

Visual Character and Quality of Public Views / Consistency with Regulations
Governing Scenic Quality
The impacts on visual character or quality attributable to proposed project implementation were
evaluated relative to visual conditions under buildout, as estimated by existing experiences from
public viewpoints in and around Berkeley. Photographs of the project site were taken and
associated with visual simulations prepared to support this analysis.




Draft Environmental Impact Report                                                                 3.1-17
City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project

California Public Resource Code Section 21071 defines an urbanized area as:
1. An incorporated city that has either:
   a. A population of at least 100,000 persons, or
   b. A population of less than 100,000 persons if the population of that city and not more than
       two contiguous incorporated cities combined equals at least 100,000 persons.

2. An unincorporated area that is either:
   a. Completely surrounded by one or more incorporated cities and both of the following criteria
       are met:
       i. The population of the unincorporated area and the population of the surrounding
           incorporated city or cities equals at least 100,000 persons
       ii. The population density of the unincorporated area at least equals the population
           density of the surrounding city or cities.

     b. Located within an urban growth boundary and has an existing residential population of at
        least 5,000 persons per square mile.

Pursuant to California Public Resource Code Section 21071, the City of Berkeley is in an urbanized
area, because the city’s population is estimated at 128,348 in 2025, which exceeds 100,000
persons.9 Given that the proposed project would be developed in an urbanized area, the impact
discussion related to visual character and views is focused on consistency with applicable zoning and
other regulations governing scenic quality, such as those included in the Berkeley General Plan,
Municipal Code, and BCDC Bay Plan. Additionally, the City considers whether a proposed project
would be inconsistent with the character of a given plan area, or existing development in the
surrounding area, or would substantially alter existing natural topography. Since Berkeley also
regulates visual character and quality of public views through qualitative criteria, visual character is
also evaluated by considering whether a project would conflict with the surrounding area's
character or substantially alter natural topography. This criterion is analyzed as part of Impact AES-3.

Visual Simulations
To represent views that would be experienced from public locations, five key viewpoints (KVPs)
were selected for the simulation of post-project conditions. The location of the KVPs and the visual
simulations are shown in Impact AES-1. Each KVP presents a single viewpoint that depicts the visual
change that implementation of the project would have on viewers from the identified viewpoint
(sensitive receptors).
Visual simulations of the project from the identified KVPs were prepared by Environmental Vision
(2025) to provide a comparison of pre- and post-project conditions, as shown in Figure 3.1-4
through Figure 3.1-8. The visual simulations provided in these figures are the result of a computer
modeling process that combines gathered field data (photographs and measurements) with the
conceptual engineering design data to digitally model a simulated image of the project.

Light and Glare
The analysis of light and glare impacts focuses on the nature and magnitude of changes in light and
glare conditions associated with implementation of the proposed project on the project site and
surroundings. If the light and glare conditions of the proposed project and the existing environment
are similar, then the visual compatibility would be high. If the light and glare conditions of the
proposed project strongly contrast with the existing light and glare or applicable policies and
guidelines, then light and glare compatibility would be low and significant impacts may result.
Proposed design standards and guidelines as well as proposed project objectives are applied to
determine the significance of light and glare impacts associated with the proposed project.
Similarly, the City considers whether a proposed project would increase nighttime light or daytime
glare sources in a manner that would substantially affect nighttime or daytime views. Thus, this
criterion is analyzed as part of Impact AES-4.

EIR Scoping Comments Consideration
This section addresses comments received in response to the EIR NOP related to various concerns
regarding aesthetics.
One agency (BCDC) requested that the City consider policies related to aesthetics, including the
Public Access Design Guidelines for Shoreline Spaces when considering effects on scenic vistas and
scenic resources. The San Francisco Bay Plan subsection in Section 3.1.3, Regulatory Framework
includes a list of relevant policies from the Bay Plan and Impact AES-1 and AES-3 discuss consistency
with these policies.
Organizations and individuals provided general comments about addressing impacts on views,
aesthetics impacts from tree removal, and lighting. Impacts on views and impacts from the removal
of trees are addressed in Impact AES-1 and AES-3. Impacts related to lighting are addressed in
Impact AES-4.

Specific Thresholds of Significance
The City of Berkeley has not adopted quantitative thresholds specifically for the evaluation of
aesthetics. However, the City applies the following qualitative thresholds based on adopted policies
and guidelines to evaluate the significance of aesthetics impacts resulting from development.
   Permanent project infrastructure blocking or significantly altering existing views from a City- or
    State-identified scenic route or corridor toward a visual/scenic resource (i.e., Bay, skyline, or
    ridgeline)
   Substantially alter existing natural topography or damaging scenic resources, including but not
    limited to, trees, rock outcroppings, and historic buildings.
   Permanent project infrastructure being inconsistent with or degrading the visual character of
    the project site or existing development in the surrounding area or degrading the quality of
    public views of the project site.
   Construction or operation of facilities or infrastructure creating a new source of substantial light
    or glare that would adversely affect day or nighttime views for sensitive receptors (i.e.,
    residents) near the project site.

Construction
Impacts related to substantial permanent adverse effects on a scenic vista are limited to operational
impacts, because construction impacts would not result in permanent or long-term obstructions to
scenic vistas. No permanent substantial adverse effects on scenic vistas from construction would
result from implementation of the proposed project. Therefore, construction impacts related to
effects on a scenic vista would be less than significant.

Operation
Due to its placement on the water and low elevation compared to surrounding topographies and
viewing locations, the proposed project would be prominently visible from proximate streets and
the waterfront, and distantly visible from elevated viewpoints once constructed. As shown in
Figure 3.1-3 through Figure 3.1-8, the project would be visible from public views (or KVPs) identified
and shown in Figure 3.1-3. Additionally, views of the project would be available from numerous
trails and viewing points, such as those afforded from the Grizzly Peak Overlook and the Berkeley
Overlook.

path near Skates on the Bay, representing the view recreational visitors of the pier and waterfront,
water-based recreationalists, and motorists along Seawall Drive would have of the project site. As
shown in Figure 3.1-4, views of the San Francisco skyline would be affected; however, the San
Francisco skyline would remain visible. Additional views would be available from the proposed pier.
KVP 2 (Figure 3.1-5) depicts the view looking northwest toward the Pier from the waterfront path
near H.S. Lordships and the proximate parking area, representing the view visitors at H.S. Lordships,
water-based recreationalists, and motorists along Seawall Drive would have of the project site. As
shown in Figure 3.1-5, views of the Bay and ridgelines would remain visible. KVP 3 (Figure 3.1-6)
depicts the view looking north toward the Pier from the northernmost point of the Marina Park
Pathway, approximately 1.2 miles south of the project site across the Bay. KVP 3 represents the
view of the project site for recreational visitors along proximate waterfront pathways and trails;
water-based recreationalists and residents at Emeryville Marina and Harbor; and residents at
Watergate. As shown in Figure 3.1-6, no change would be readily visible with implementation of the
proposed project. KVP 4 (Figure 3.1-7) depicts the view looking west from the South Cove Sailing
docks, representing the view of the project site for land- and water-based recreational viewers. As
shown in Figure 3.1-7, the project would result in views of fewer trees and new visible solar
infrastructure, compared to existing conditions; however, scenic views of the Bay would remain.
KVP 5 (Figure 3.1-8) depicts the view looking south-southwest from César E. Chávez Park,

Horizontal features associated with the proposed project (i.e., the proposed pier and breakwater)
would not adversely affect scenic vistas (i.e., views of the Bay, Golden Gate Bridge, or Alcatraz
islands), because the limited height of these components would not obstruct public views. The
proposed project footprint is also similar to that of the existing Pier and amenities, and thus, visual
encroachment of the project on scenic views of the Bay, Golden Gate Bridge, and Alcatraz Island
would be minimal.
Policy OS-12, Action A, of the Berkeley General Plan provides that new development should
maintain adequate shoreline views. Vertical features associated with the proposed project include
solar panels above the parking stalls at the Seawall parking lot, a new restroom, and additional
trees. The proposed restroom would be approximately 18 feet long by 8 feet wide and 10 feet high,
located near the proposed public plaza in an area close to the proposed pier where there are
currently mature trees. Since the bathroom would be set back from the water and located in an
area where views of the Bay are blocked by existing vegetation, the bathroom would not present a
significant obstruction or adversely affect related to public views of the Bay.
Tree removal would be included as part of the proposed project. The project would also include
landscaping and planting new trees throughout the project site. Project landscaping would be
implemented in accordance with the guiding principles of the Berkeley Marina Master Plan,
including 1A, 1B, and 3, to enhance the visual setting of the waterfront and minimize the visual
prominence of restroom structures. Appearance, Design, and Scenic Views Policy 14 of the San
Francisco Bay Plan identifies that views of the Bay from vista points and from roads should be
maintained by appropriate arrangements and heights of all developments and landscaping between
the view areas and the water. Project landscaping would beneficially affect the visual quality of the
project area by providing additional, healthy vegetation to the area, and compliance with above-
described requirements would ensure that project landscaping does not detrimentally affect, or
block, public views. Therefore, operational impacts related to effects on a scenic vista would be less
than significant.

Construction and Operation
As described in Section 3.1.2, Environmental Setting, the nearest segments of designated (SR 24)
and eligible (I-80) State scenic highways are located approximately 5.5 miles and 1.7 miles from the
project site, respectively. Due to intervening development and landforms, the project would not be
visible from either roadway. The project would not result in damage to scenic resources including,
but not limited to, trees, rock outcroppings, and historic buildings within a State scenic highway
because there are no State scenic highways at the project site, and because the project site would
not be visible from a State scenic highway. Therefore, no construction or operational impacts
related to adverse effects on scenic resources or scenic views within locally designated scenic
roadway corridors would occur.

The Berkeley General Plan, Berkeley Marina Master Plan, Berkeley Municipal Code, and the San
Francisco Bay Plan contain policies that pertain to scenic quality, which are detailed in Section 3.1.3,
Regulatory Framework. The Berkeley General Plan policies related to aesthetics and visual resources
include those presented in the Open Space and Recreation Element and the Urban Design and


3.1-28
                                                                       Environmental Impact Analysis
                                                                                         Aesthetics

Preservation Elements. Protection and preservation of historically and architecturally significant
structures and visual character (UD-3, UD-7, UD-16, UD-24, UD-35, LU-1, LU-2, LU-3, and LU-43);
preservation of scenic views (OS-12 and UD-31); requires new development to be visually cohesive
(UD-18, UD-19, and UD-22); requires design review for new construction and alterations (UD-23 and
LU-4); and includes landscape and planting requirements for site development (UD-30). The
Berkeley Marina Master Plan includes guiding principles related to landscape implementation and
screening (Principle 1A), emphasizing views and scenic overlooks (Principle 1B), and reducing visual
impacts of infrastructure (Principle 3). The Berkeley Municipal Code includes rules and regulations
pertaining to use of the Berkeley Pier and Marina (Chapter 6.20); regulations for waterfront
development and view preservation (Chapter 11.56); and general development standards such as
height, setback, and light and glare regulations (Chapter 23). The San Francisco Bay Plan also
includes findings and policies which serve to maintain and enhance the Bay and its scenic attributes,
including but not limited to those related to visual and physical access to the Bay and waterfront,
provision of vista points, and project design review.

Construction
The construction phase of the project would require delivery trucks, vehicles, and construction
equipment, as well as storage, staging, and active work areas. The construction period is anticipated
to begin in April 2027 and last up to 21 months, with project completion proposed by the end of
2028. The location and use of equipment in active work areas would change during the construction
period depending on which components of the project site were under active construction.
Temporary construction activities would not have the potential to result in conflicts with zoning and
other regulations governing scenic quality. Therefore, project construction would not conflict with
applicable zoning and other regulations governing scenic quality, and no impact would occur.
Construction of the proposed project would cause a change in the existing visual character and
quality of the area by introducing a level of activity and heavy machinery to the waterside and
landside portions of the project site that is greater than that associated with existing conditions.
Although construction of the project would result in a degree of change to visual quality on the
project site, construction would not degrade or block any sensitive or unique visual resources,
landscapes, or public views. Furthermore, impacts associated with views of construction activities
and equipment would be temporary. Construction impacts related to visual character would be less
than significant.

Operation
Operation of new project infrastructure would represent a change in the existing visual character of
the project site compared to existing conditions. The project would alter waterside areas of the
project site with presence and operation of new permanent pier, breakwater, and ferry
infrastructure. In addition, the project would alter developed areas on the landside of the project
site for similar or complementary uses such as restrooms, parking areas, and public plaza as well as
for University Avenue, Seawall Drive, and Bay Trail Extension improvements. Substantial changes to
existing natural topography are not anticipated.

the proposed pier structures (e.g., pier surface, shade structure, railings, light fixtures) would
