McAteer-Petris Act
BCDC was given authority under the McAteer-Petris Act (Act) in 1968 to regulate development in
the following areas:
   San Francisco (SF) Bay itself, defined as all areas that are subject to tidal action, including:
    sloughs, marshlands lying between mean high tide and five feet above mean sea level, tidelands
    lying between mean high tide and mean low tide, and submerged lands lying below mean low
    tide, from the south end of SF Bay to the Golden Gate to the Sacramento River;
   A shoreline band of land extending inland for 100 feet from the shoreline of SF Bay (as defined
    above);
   Salt ponds, defined as all areas which have been diked off from the Bay and have been used
    during the three years immediately preceding November 11, 1969 for the solar evaporation of
    Bay water in the course of salt production (i.e., includes all levees, water conveyance channels,
    etc. used as part of the saltworks production;
   Managed wetlands, defined as areas which have been diked off from the Bay and have been
    maintained during the three years immediately preceding November 11, 1969 as a duck hunting
    preserve, game refuge, or for agriculture; and
   Certain waterways consisting of all areas that are subject to tidal action on named tributaries
    that flow into SF Bay, as listed in the Act.

The McAteer-Petris Act requires that any person or governmental agency wishing to place fill in, or
to extract materials exceeding $20 in value from, or make any substantial change in use of any land,
water, or structure within the area of BCDC jurisdiction must secure a permit from BCDC (as well as
any permit required from any city or county within which any part of the work is to be performed).
The Act provides that the BCDC shall grant a permit if it finds that the project is either: (1) necessary
to the health, safety, or welfare of the public in the entire SF Bay area; or (2) consistent with the
provision of Act and with the applicable provisions of the San Francisco Bay Plan.
The McAteer-Petris Act establishes a number of policies that must be met to authorize the
placement of fill in SF Bay and in its “certain waterways” jurisdiction, including the following:
   The public benefits from the proposed fill clearly exceeds the public detriment from the loss of
    water areas;
   Further filling should be limited to water-oriented uses (including but not limited to ports,
    water-related industry, airports, bridges, wildlife refuges, and water oriented recreation and
    public assembly) or minor fill for improving shoreline appearance or access to SF Bay;
   Fill should be authorized for any purpose only when no alternative upland location is available
    for such purpose;
   The water area to be filled should be the minimum amount necessary to achieve the purpose of
    the fill; and
   That the nature, location, and extent of any fill should be such that it will minimize harmful
    effects to the SF Bay area such as the reduction or impairment of the volume of surface area or
    circulation of water, water quality, fertility of marshes or fish or wildlife resources or other
    conditions impacting the environment.

The Act authorizes BCDC to designate in the shoreline band certain water-oriented priority land uses
that are essential to the public welfare of the SF Bay area. For a project within any portion of the

shoreline band that is located outside the boundaries of water-oriented priority land uses, the
McAteer-Petris Act provides that BCDC can deny a permit only if the proposed project fails to

The Act exempts the following activities from the need to obtain a BCDC permit:
   No permit is required for the construction within or upon any public highway or street of public
    service facilities within the area of the BCDC’s jurisdiction.
   No permit is required for ongoing uses within the BCDC’s shoreline band, salt ponds, and

BCDC also exercises its authority under Section 307 of the federal Coastal Zone Management Act (16

Public Trust Doctrine
The California State Lands Commission (SLC) manages 4 million acres of tide and submerged lands
and the beds of natural navigable rivers, streams, lakes, bays, estuaries, inlets, and straits. These
lands, often referred to as sovereign or Public Trust lands, stretch from the Klamath River and Goose
Lake in the north to the Tijuana Estuary in the south, and the Colorado River in the east, and from
the Pacific Coast 3 miles offshore in the west to world-famous Lake Tahoe in the east, and includes
California’s two longest rivers, the Sacramento and San Joaquin.
The SLC also monitors sovereign land granted in trust by the California Legislature to approximately
70 local jurisdictions that generally consist of prime waterfront lands and coastal waters. The SLC
protects and enhances these lands and natural resources by issuing leases for use or development,
providing public access, resolving boundaries between public and private lands. Through its actions,
the SLC secures and safeguards the public’s access rights to natural navigable waterways and the
coastline and preserves irreplaceable natural habitats for wildlife, vegetation, and biological
communities.
The SLC also protects state waters from marine invasive species introductions and prevents oil spills
by providing the best achievable protection of the marine environment at all marine oil terminals in
California and offshore oil platforms and production facilities.

SLC ENVIRONMENTAL PLANNING AND MANAGEMENT DIVISION
The Environmental Planning and Management Division provides policy and technical analysis to the
SLC and its Executive Officer and ensures compliance with CEQA. The Division prepares
Environmental Impact Reports, Mitigated Negative Declarations, and other environmental or public
trust documents for land use changes within the SLC’s jurisdiction, and routinely comments on
CEQA documents prepared by local, state, and federal agencies for projects impacting public trust
lands and resources.

SLC MARINE ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION DIVISION
The Marine Environmental Protection Division regulates and inspects all marine oil terminals in
California and bulk oil operations at these terminals to provide the best achievable protection of the
public health, safety, and the environment. Inspections are conducted on a daily, biennial, and

and operational personnel training. The Division also regulates large oceangoing vessels to protect
against the introduction of invasive (nonindigenous) species into state waters.

Regional and Local Regulations

San Francisco Bay Subtidal Habitat Goal Report, A 50-Year Conservation Plan
The San Francisco Bay Subtidal Habitat Goals Report: A 50‑Year Conservation Plan was developed
and led jointly by the California Coastal Conservancy/Ocean Protection Council, BCDC, NMFS, the
NOAA Restoration Center, and the San Francisco Estuary Partnership. These agencies together form
the Subtidal Goals Project Steering Committee, the group responsible for producing and guiding the
plan.

SOFT SUBSTRATE PROTECTION GOALS
1. Consider the potential ecological effects of contaminated sediments when developing, planning,
     designing, and constructing restoration projects or other projects that disturb sediments.
2.   Promote no net increase in disturbance to San Francisco soft bottom habitat.
3.   Promote no net loss of San Francisco Bay subtidal and intertidal sand habitats.
4.   Develop a coordinated, collaborative approach for regional sediment management of San
     Francisco Bay.
5.   Encourage the application of sustainable techniques in sand habitat replenishment or
     restoration projects.
6.   Encourage removal of artificial structures that have negative impacts on soft bottom habitat
     functions.

ARTIFICIAL STRUCTURES PROTECTION GOALS
1. Enhance and protect habitat functions and the historical value of artificial structures in San
   Francisco Bay.
2. Improve San Francisco Bay subtidal habitats by minimizing placement of artificial structures that
   are detrimental to subtidal habitat function.
3. Where feasible, remove artificial structures from San Francisco Bay that have negative or
   minimal beneficial habitats functions.
4. Promote pilot projects to remove artificial structures and creosote pilings at targeted sites in
   combination with a living shoreline restoration design that will use natural bioengineering
   techniques (such as native oyster reefs, stone sills and eelgrass plantings) to replace lost habitat
   structure.

SHELLFISH BEDS PROTECTION GOALS
1. Protect San Francisco Bay native shellfish habitats (particularly native oyster, Ostrea lurida)
   through no net loss existing habitat.
2. Protect areas in San Francisco Bay with potential shellfish expansion, restoration or creation.
3. Increase native oyster populations in San Francisco Bay with 8,000 acres of potential suitable
   subtidal area over a 50-year time frame through a phased approach conducted within a
   framework of adaptive management.

Expansion of Ferry Transit Service in the San Francisco Bay Area Program EIR
The Water Emergency Transportation Authority (WETA) – also known as San Francisco Bay Ferry –
prepared the Expansion of Ferry Transit Service in the San Francisco Bay Area Program EIR in 2003
(WETA Program EIR). The WETA Program EIR, which the City incorporates by reference herein,
included an analysis of the potential impacts on biological resources from the expansion of water
transit service and routes defined in the WETA Implementation and Operations Plan, which includes
expanded ferry service to Berkeley. The WETA Program EIR analyzed potential impacts and imposed
mitigation measures to address the impacts on habitat (jurisdictional wetlands, invasive species,
special aquatic sites), plankton productivity, benthic organisms, fish, birds, marine mammals, and
special-status species.
As part of the EIR process, WETA adopted a Mitigation Monitoring Plan, which WETA is required to
implement for the operation of ferry routes identified in their EIR. The Mitigation Monitoring Plan
includes a number of mitigation measures to reduce the potential for marine mammal strikes. Since
2003, WETA has worked closely with the Marine Mammal Center to ensure that implementation of
these mitigation measures reflects ongoing technological advances, evolving scientific
understanding of best practices, and updated NOAA guidance. 75

Approach to Analysis
Environmental impacts on biological resources have been assessed using impact significance criteria
from federal, State, and local regulations. CEQA, Chapter 1, Section 21001(c) states that it is the
policy of the State of California to “prevent the elimination of fish and wildlife species due to man’s
activities, ensure that fish and wildlife populations do not drop below self-perpetuating levels, and
preserve for future generations representations of all plant and animal communities.”
Environmental impacts relative to biological resources have been assessed using impact significance
criteria set forth in the CEQA Guidelines and federal, State, and local plans, regulations, and
ordinances.

Biological Resources
The analysis of impacts related on biological resources is based on review of available literature and
online record searches of the following databases: the CNDDB 76, Online Inventory of Rare,
Threatened and Endangered Plants of California 77, NWI 78, USFWS Critical Habitat Mapper 79, and
IPaC 80. The results from this analysis are summarized in Section 3.3.2, Environmental Setting.
Biologists evaluated impacts on biological resources based on the likelihood that special-status
species, sensitive habitats, wildlife corridors, and protected trees are present within the project site,
and the likely effects of project construction or operation on these resources. For the purposes of
this EIR, the word “substantial” as used in the significance thresholds below is defined by the
following three principal components:
    Magnitude and duration of the impact (e.g., substantial/not substantial);
    Uniqueness of the affected resource (rarity); and
    Susceptibility of the affected resource to disturbance.

For purposes of this analysis, the following thresholds are used to evaluate the significance of
biological resources impacts resulting from implementation of the proposed project.
   Result in direct take or habitat removal or alteration for candidate, sensitive, or special-status
    species.
   Cause injury or mortality to fish and aquatic mammals by increasing underwater noise.
   Degrade water quality through disturbance of sediment underwater or release of pollutants
    such that habitat or health of aquatic species are adversely affected.
   Adversely affect any riparian habitat or other sensitive natural community identified in local or
    regional plans, policies, and regulations or by CDFW, NMFS or USFWS.
   Remove, fill, or damage a federally protected wetland.
   Interrupt fish movement in the San Francisco Bay or impede migratory bird species movement
    via the Pacific Flyway.

Special-status Wildlife

Northwestern Pond Turtle, Double-Crested Cormorant, and Nesting Birds
Northwestern pond turtle (federally proposed threatened, SSC) has a low potential and double-
crested cormorant (CDFW Watch List) has a moderate potential to occur in terrestrial portions of
the project site. Nesting special-status bird species and/or nesting birds protected under the MBTA
and CFGC have potential to occur in the project site during the nesting season.
Northwestern pond turtle may occur at the mouth of Strawberry Creek and while unlikely, if
present, may move through upland areas on the project site adjacent to Strawberry Creek. No
impacts are expected to the Creek or northwestern pond turtle aquatic habitat, but there is a low
probability that turtles may move into adjacent upland areas that intersect with the project site.
Direct impacts to northwestern pond turtle could occur if individuals are moving through the work
area during road construction in the vicinity of Strawberry Creek. Construction activities in this area
could result in injury or mortality to pond turtles through collisions with construction equipment.
Impacts to northwestern pond turtle would be potentially significant and Mitigation Measures BIO-
1(a) and BIO-1(b) would be required.
Construction activities would include removal of trees that may provide nesting and roosting habitat
for native birds, including double-crested cormorant and raptors. Additionally, birds may nest or
roost in trees or structures on the project site and in the project vicinity. The project could result in
direct mortality through removal of active nests or increased disturbance levels (i.e., construction
noise and activity) that cause nest abandonment. Project construction activities would generally
take place between the hours of 7:00 A.M and 7:00 P.M. on weekdays and 9:00 A.M. and 8:00 P.M.
on weekends and holidays, in compliance with the City of Berkeley’s Municipal Code, and would
primarily occur during the daytime, which would limit the potential for construction-related
nighttime noise impacts. However, due to constructability constraints that require some work to be
completed under a single mobilization, limited nighttime work may be required for specific activities
such as pile driving. Nighttime construction noise has the same potential to adversely affect nesting
birds by increasing disturbance levels, disrupting normal behavioral patterns, and causing nest
abandonment. Impacts on nesting birds would be considered potentially significant.
However, implementation of Mitigation Measures BIO-1(a), BIO-1(b), and BIO-1(c) would require a
Worker Environmental Awareness Program, as well as preconstruction surveys for, and avoidance of
northwestern pond turtle and nesting birds. These mitigation measures would reduce construction-
related impacts to terrestrial special-status species (i.e., northwestern pond turtle) and birds
protected under the MBTA and CFGC to less than significant after mitigation.

Lighting Impacts
Nighttime construction lighting has the potential to disturb nesting birds and terrestrial wildlife. As
described in Section 2, Project Description, and Section 3.1, Aesthetics, construction activities would
largely occur during the daytime; nighttime illumination would be restricted to the minimum
needed for safety during pile-driving and for security at staging yards. Nighttime work is not
expected to exceed 50 nights. With implementation of Mitigation Measure AES-1, any required
nighttime lighting for project construction would be confined to the immediate work area (e.g., the
active pile installation location), would be temporary, and would use fully shielded fixtures that
direct light downward and toward the work zone. Therefore, the project would not introduce a
substantial new source of light capable of affecting nesting birds or terrestrial wildlife in the area.
Impacts would be less than significant after mitigation.

Special-status Fish

Pile Driving Noise
As discussed in Section 2, Project Description, the proposed project would require demolition of the
existing pier using a dead pull method or a vibratory hammer. The landside retaining wall and new
pier piles would require a combination of vibratory and impact pile driving.
Direct effects to fish species such as steelhead, chinook salmon, green sturgeon, and others could
occur in the form of injury and/or mortality due to use of the vibratory hammer and cable system to
remove pier pilings if fish were present at the time, and if sound levels are above that which can
cause injury or death in fish. The Agreement in Principal for Interim Criteria for Injury to Fish from
Pile Driving Activities 85 identifies the threshold for physical injury in fish from pile driving (including
vibratory hammers) noise (see Table 3.3-1).

 Source: California Department of Transportation. 2020. Technical Guidance for the Assessment of Hydroacoustic Effects of Pile Driving

 Notes: dB = decibel; Peak SPL = peak unweighted sound pressure level with reference to 1µPa; cSEL = cumulative sound exposure level

 * While not in the interim criteria, the Services have set 150 dB RMS as a guideline for where underwater sound pressure levels may
 result in behavioral (i.e., sub-injury) effects to fish.


Sound waves generated from in-water construction activities are defined as either impulsive (almost
instantaneous), like explosions or impact pile driving, or non-impulsive or continuous, like motors or
vibration, and generate different SPLs and frequencies, as well as vary over time and space.
Impulsive sounds typically have high amplitude but a short duration while continuous sounds
generally have lower amplitude but longer duration. The three SPL metrics commonly used in
evaluating hydroacoustic impacts on fish and other protected species are Peak SPL (LPEAK), Root
Mean Square (RMS), and sound exposure level (SEL). LPEAK is the maximum SPL measured in dB
referenced to 1 µPa and represents species exposure to high SPL pulses that can result in injury or
modified behavior of fish and wildlife from the compression or expansion of fluid filled membranes.
RMS is the square root of the sum of the squared pressures multiplied by the time increment and
divided by the impulse duration and represents the mean (average) pressure contained within a
85 Fisheries Hydroacoustic Working Group. 2008. Memorandum Agreement in Principal for Interim Criteria for Injury to Fish from Pile

Driving Activities. June 12.



3.3-44
                                                                                             Environmental Impact Analysis
                                                                                                     Biological Resources

defined period, typically calculated over the period of the pulse that contains 90 percent of the
acoustical energy and is termed the “effective pressure”. Cumulative SEL (SELcum or cSEL) is
calculated by summing the cumulative pressure squared over the time of the event and represents
the cumulative sound exposure level a species experiences over the duration of an activity. SELcum
is used to quantify injury limits to fish associated with acute barotrauma to hearing structures or
internal organs. Most sounds are composed of many different frequencies, referred to as the
frequency spectrum. Frequency spectra are important, because the frequency components of the
sound may affect the way wildlife respond to and are affected by the sound (in terms of physical
injury [hearing loss] as well as behavior). The frequency spectrum is also important when analyzing
sound propagation characteristics and ultimately the effect range to species.
Review of the predicted sound levels generated from the anticipated pile driving activities for each
of the pile types and sizes shows that impact pile driving of the 36-inch steel pipe piles would result
in exceedance of the Level A-injury criteria for instantaneous peak sound pressure levels (LPeak) for
all eight of the special-status fish species of concern within a 10 meter buffer. However, the
anticipated pile driving (both impact and vibratory) of the 24-inch concrete piles, 48-inch concrete
sheet piles, 24-inch and 36-inch steel pipe piles would not exceed the instantaneous peak (LPeak)
limit for fish but would exceed the cumulative sound level (SELCUM) injury limit for fish under 2 grams
(183 dB SEL), fish over 2 grams (187 dB SEL), and the single strike behavioral effect limit (150 dB
RMS) for both fish groups. At this 150 dB RMS threshold for continuous sound, behavioral effects
are expected only within about 200 meters of the pile-driving location. Because these levels surpass
the NOAA interim criteria, impacts to fish as a result of pile driving and vibratory hammers would be
considered potentially significant.
However, Mitigation Measure BIO-1(a) and BIO-1(d) would be required. Mitigation Measure
BIO-1(a), which requires a Worker Environmental Awareness Program (in part to support
implementation of Mitigation Measure BIO-1(d)), and Mitigation Measure BIO-1(d), which dictates
seasonal work windows, soft-start and ramp-up procedures, exclusion zones, and sound attenuation
measures during pile driving, would reduce impacts related to special-status fish to less than
significant with mitigation. In addition, the City would consult with NOAA Fisheries and CDFW during
the permitting process.

Pile Driving and Dredging Water Quality
Impacts on water quality (e.g., turbidity, suspended sediment) could also occur during pile driving
and dredging, and could affect fish species by reducing visibility, impairing foraging ability, or
clogging gills. Mechanical dredging can increase suspended sediment above background levels by 10
to 400 mg/L, with an average of 60 mg/L. 86 The Long Term Management Strategy for the Placement
of Dredged Material in the San Francisco Bay Region (LTMS) includes best management strategies,
such as work windows and review of dredging equipment stability by project site, to limit
environmental impacts. Indirect impacts to substrate or benthic prey could also occur from project
activities. Turbidity from in-water project activities would be temporary and localized, and turbidity
plumes are expected to disperse quickly due to tidal currents. Additionally, as discussed in Section
3.8 Hydrology and Water Quality, studies conducted in San Francisco Bay indicate that turbidity
generated by dredging activities, which is typically more intensive than pile installation or removal,
diminishes to background levels within a radius of approximately 600 feet within one tidal cycle for

(accessed February 2026)

singular events. 87 Because Bay waters are naturally highly turbid and experience substantial
fluctuations from tides, wind‑driven waves, and regional sediment transport, the temporary
turbidity generated by the project would be unlikely to affect foraging fish or clog gills, as these
species are highly mobile and can readily avoid localized turbidity plumes. Additionally, impacts
could occur if spills or leaks were allowed to enter marine habitats. Dredging would be subject to

Dredging activities would utilize mechanical methods (clamshell) and follow Dredge Material

Dredging Noise
As discussed in Section 2, Project Description, 400,000 cubic yards of dredged materials would be
generated and would require disposal. In-water noise associated with the dredging portion of the
construction phase would be comparable to the noise levels produced during the City’s federally
authorized dredging at the mouth of Berkeley Yacht Basin. Noise generated by dredging would be
short-term and temporary. Impacts to fish as a result of dredging noise would be potentially
significant and Mitigation Measure BIO-1(a) and BIO-1(d) would be required. Mitigation Measure
BIO-1(d) requires seasonal restrictions for dredging to avoid potential impacts on special-status fish.
Given the temporary nature of dredging noise and the seasonal restrictions, impacts would be less
than significant with mitigation.
In addition, the City would consult with NOAA Fisheries and CDFW during the permitting process.

Special-status Marine Mammals
The following analysis applies for the following species: harbor seal; California sea lion, harbor
porpoise; common bottlenose dolphin, gray whale, and humpback whale.

Pile Driving Noise
Similar to fish, impact pile driving of the 24-inch concrete piles, 48-inch concrete sheet piles, 24-inch
and 36-inch steel pipe piles would all exceed marine mammal cumulative SPL (SELcum) Level A -injury
effect levels, in the near field, and the Level B -Harassment effect levels at various distances in the
far field (at distance). Cumulative SPL Level A -injury and Level B -Harassment effect distances vary
depending on the hearing sensitivity of the different marine mammal hearing groups, pile type, size,
and driving method.
At the 120 dB RMS non-impulsive sound source threshold, behavior effects are estimated to be
within approximately 5,000 meters (5 kilometers or 3.1 miles). The most sensitive underwater limits
of various marine mammal hearing groups include high-frequency cetaceans (e.g., harbor
porpoises), which are sensitive to both impulsive and non-impulsive sound exposure at 159 dB/181
dB, and a peak limit of 202 dB. Moderately sensitive groups include Phocid pinnipeds (e.g., harbor
seals), which are sensitive to both impulsive and non-impulsive sound exposure at 183 dB/195 dB,
and a peak limit of 230 dB, and low-frequency cetaceans (e.g., gray whale and humpback whale).
The least sensitive groups include Otariid pinnipeds (e.g., sea lions), which are sensitive to both
impulsive and non-impulsive sound exposure at 185 dB/199 dB, and a peak limit of 222 dB. 91 Sound
propagation in the shallow, semi-enclosed waters of San Francisco Bay is expected to attenuate
more rapidly than in deeper oceanic environments; therefore, these distance estimates are
considered conservative.
No regular haul out sites for marine mammals occur in the project vicinity, but harbor seal and
California sea lion may use docks at the Berkeley Marina and narrow beaches along the shoreline to
the south of the project site to haul out. In-air acoustic thresholds cause behavioral disruption
(Level B) at 90 dB RMS for harbor seals and 100 dBRMS for California sea lion;91 therefore, these
species could be subject to harassment from in-air noise from pile driving that exceeds these
thresholds.

each marine mammal hearing group. 92 These thresholds represent the onset levels for permanent
threshold shifts (PTS), which are the sound levels at which auditory injury can occur.

Pile Driving and Dredging Water Quality
Impacts on marine mammals could also occur as a result of construction if water quality were
negatively affected. Similar to special-status fish, impacts to water quality as a result of increased
turbidity and/or chemical spills could occur during pile driving, dredging, or construction. However,
such turbidity and water quality effects would be temporary, localized, and would dissipate rapidly
under tidal mixing conditions. Marine mammals do not respire underwater and are highly mobile,
and therefore would not be adversely affected by short-term, localized increases in turbidity or
suspended sediments. Therefore, construction-related impacts on special-status marine mammals
as a result of turbidity and water quality related to pile driving and dredging would be less than
significant.

Dredging Noise
Impacts on marine mammals from dredging during construction would be similar to the impact on
fish, and include noise and reduced visibility. The project would be subject to the Long Term
Management Strategy for the Placement of Dredged Material in the San Francisco Bay Region 93 and
associated incidental take permit from CDFW (November 30, 1998), and Endangered Species Act
consultations with USFWS (May 28, 2004 and February 7, 2025) and NMFS (July 20, 2015).
Mechanical clamshell dredging could generate non-impulsive, short-term, and localized noise, and
marine mammals are mobile and would be expected to avoid localized areas of disturbance.
Therefore, impacts on marine mammals as a result of dredging noise during construction would be
less than significant.
Mitigation Measure BIO-1(d) would still apply to in-water work during construction, including
dredging, and provides general impact-avoidance requirements for fish and marine mammals. In
addition to the above requirements, the City would consult with NMFS to determine if an IHA would
be needed.

Harassment
Marine mammals such as harbor seal forage and pass through waters within the project site and
surrounding area and may haul out in the vicinity of the project site. If individuals are present during
construction, they may be disturbed by pile driving and tug boat operations, which could alter
behavior and disrupt normal activities. These impacts would be considered harassment and, thus,
be potentially significant.
In addition to the Worker Environmental Awareness Program required under Mitigation Measures
BIO-1(a), implementation of BIO-1(d), BIO-1(e), and HYD-1 would also be required to mitigate
impacts on marine mammals during construction. The MMMP developed under BIO-1(e) would
apply the project’s hydroacoustic analysis to establish Level A and Level B protection zones and
integrate these with the soft-start procedures and observation protocols identified in Mitigation
Measure BIO-1(d). These measures would require soft-start techniques, a sound curtain, buffer
zones, and biological monitoring to address impacts due to pile driving noise. Mitigation Measure
BIO-1(d) would ensure that any impacts to marine mammals would avoid injury and be limited to
behavioral impacts, and would thus be less than significant. Mitigation Measure HYD-1 would
reduce negative effects to water quality from pile driving and dredging by requiring best

Operation

TERRESTRIAL

Special-Status Wildlife
The proposed project would primarily occur withing existing developed areas, and would not involve
significant new levels of disturbance to the mouth of Strawberry Creek, the sole location of suitable
habitat for northwestern pond turtle within the project site. This species is typically found in slow,
calm waters of ponds and lakes with basking sites and emergent vegetation, but is not typically
found outside of ponds or lakes or out in the open waters of the San Francisco Bay. Therefore,
impacts on northwestern pond turtle due to operation would be less than significant.
Impacts on nesting birds, including double-crested cormorant, from operation would also be
minimal. Any additional lighting added as part of the project, as discussed in Section 3.1, Aesthetics,
under Impact AES-4, would be designed in accordance with City ordinance, and would be similar to
existing levels of lighting present on the project site. The ferry would operate in open water, and the
existing use of the project site for recreation would continue with similar levels of activity and
disturbance. Wake generated by ferry operation would be consistent with existing vessel operations
in the Bay and not result in disturbance to nesting or roosting habitats above the existing shoreline
riprap armoring. Therefore, impacts on nesting birds due to operation would be less than significant.
Operation of the project would introduce additional vehicles to the project site; however, the
overall flow of traffic would be similar to the existing setting of the project site, which has roadways
and parking lots with vehicles moving throughout the project site. Therefore, the vehicle traffic from
the project site would result in less than significant impacts on special-status species. Similarly, the
noise associated with operation of the project would be similar to the existing setting. Therefore,
noise impacts to special-status species from operation of landside project elements would be less
than significant.

MARINE
As noted above, WETA adopted the Expansion of Ferry Transit Service in the San Francisco Bay Area
Program Mitigation Monitoring Plan which addresses operation of ferry vessels throughout San
Francisco Bay.

Special-status Fish
Operation of ferry vessels would result in limited disturbance to marine habitats potentially
supporting special-status fish. The electric ferry vessels are expected to generate substantially less
noise than traditional diesel engines, especially lower frequency sounds. Underwater noise
measurements made of various hybrid electric and conventional ferry vessels indicate that a ship
retrofitted with electric motors, generators, and batteries (Tellus) radiated less underwater noise


Draft Environmental Impact Report                                                                 3.3-51
City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project

than a ship with a conventional diesel propulsion system (Neptunus). A report from 2024 prepared
by Silent@Sea notes the following: "according to our measurements, Tellus radiates less
underwater noise than Neptunus, with up to 10 dB [difference].” A 10dB difference is a halving of
noise, as if a wall or barrier has been put in place. The report states: “This is an indication that
retrofitting ships with modern hybrid propulsion is a potential way to reduce their noise
radiation.” 94 Additionally, operation of ferry vessels would occur at the surface, where fish could
easily avoid vessels and noise. Artificial lights on the ferry would be consistent with existing lighting
on vessels that travel in the project area and lighting installed on the dock could have potential to
attract fish and their predators, but the slow speeds required for docking vessels would allow
animals to safely swim out of the way. Thus, any additional lighting would have a less than
significant impact. Therefore, impacts on special-status fish due to operation of ferry vessels in the
project area would be less than significant.

Special Status Marine Mammals
Similar to the discussion regarding impacts of additional project lighting on fish above, no significant
impacts are expected due to project lighting.
While the electric ferry vessels would introduce a new noise source, they would generate
significantly less noise, especially at lower frequency sounds, than traditional diesel engines.
Underwater noise measurements made of various hybrid electric and conventional ferry vessels
indicate that a ship retrofitted with electric motors, generators, and batteries (Tellus) radiated less
underwater noise than a ship with a conventional diesel propulsion system (Neptunus). A report
from 2024 prepared by Silent@Sea notes the following: "according to our measurements, Tellus
radiates less underwater noise than Neptunus, with up to 10 dB [difference].” A 10dB difference is a
halving of noise, as if a wall or barrier has been put in place. The report states: “This is an indication
that retrofitting ships with modern hybrid propulsion is a potential way to reduce their noise
radiation.” 95 Therefore, in-water noise impacts on marine mammals due to operation of ferry
vessels would be less than significant.
The east side of the Central Bay (north of the South Bay and south of the Golden Gate Strait, which
connects to the Pacific Ocean), which comprises the project vicinity is generally shallow with a flat
bottom and -30.0 to 3.2 feet MLLW. 96 In contrast, the Golden Gate Strait exceeds 300 feet in depth
and supports more frequent sightings of larger marine mammals such as whales and dolphins.
Therefore, marine mammal activity, particularly for whales, is expected to be lower in the project
vicinity than elsewhere in the Bay.
Operation of ferry vessels would occur at the surface level, and the project proposes to operate two
vessels on the weekday route between the Berkeley terminal and San Francisco, and one vessel for
Larkspur, and one vessel for San Francisco on the weekends. New ferryboat trips would include
eight peak-direction ferry trips in the morning (Berkeley to San Francisco) and six in the evening, and

Mitigation Measures

MITIGATION MEASURE BIO-1(A): IMPLEMENT WORKER ENVIRONMENTAL AWARENESS PROGRAM PRIOR TO
AND DURING CONSTRUCTION

Prior to initiation of all construction activities (including staging and mobilization), all personnel
associated with project construction shall attend a Worker Environmental Awareness Program
training, conducted by a City-approved qualified biologist, to aid workers in recognizing special-
status biological resources that may occur in the project area. This training will include information
about northwestern pond turtle, special-status fish, marine mammals, and nesting birds potentially
occurring in the project site.
The specifics of this program shall include identification of special-status species and habitats, a
description of the regulatory status and general ecological characteristics of special-status
resources, and review of the limits of construction and measures required to avoid and minimize
impacts to biological resources within the work area. A fact sheet conveying this information shall
also be prepared for distribution to all contractors, their employees, and other personnel involved
with construction of the project. All employees shall sign a form provided by the trainer
documenting they have attended the Worker Environmental Awareness Program and understand
the information presented to them. The crew foreman shall be responsible for ensuring crew
members adhere to the guidelines and restrictions designed to avoid impacts to special-status
species.

MITIGATION MEASURE BIO-1(B): CONDUCT NORTHWESTERN POND TURTLE SURVEY AND AVOIDANCE PRIOR
TO CONSTRUCTION

No less than seven days prior to the start of any construction activities within 500 feet of Strawberry
Creek (including staging and mobilization), a City-approved qualified biologist will conduct a
preconstruction survey for northwestern pond turtle within suitable habitat on the project site as
feasible. If any northwestern pond turtle are identified within the work area, they will be allowed to
leave the work site on their own. CNDDB Field Survey Forms will be submitted to the CDFW for all
special-status animal species observed.
If any northwestern pond turtles are observed by construction personnel within or adjacent to
(within 50 feet) the project site, all work within the vicinity of the observation will be halted and the
qualified biologist will be notified immediately to evaluate the occurrence and relocate the animal
as necessary. Only a qualified biologist will capture and relocate wildlife. Construction personnel are
not permitted to handle said animals. If northwestern pond turtles become federally-listed at the
time of construction, no individuals shall be handled without approval from USFWS.
A report of all pre-construction survey efforts will be submitted to the City within 30 days of
completion of the survey effort to document compliance. The report will include the dates, times,
weather conditions, and personnel involved in the surveys and monitoring. The report will also
include for each captured special-status animal, the Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM)
coordinates and habitat descriptions of the capture and release sites (in UTM coordinates), the
length of time between capture and release, and the general health of the individual(s).
This measure may be modified or supplemented by permit conditions from applicable regulatory
agencies.

MITIGATION MEASURE BIO-1(C): CONDUCT NESTING BIRD SURVEY AND AVOIDANCE PRIOR TO
CONSTRUCTION
If ground disturbing project activities begin within the nesting season (February 1 through August
31), then no more than seven days prior to the initiation of project activities, a nesting bird pre-
construction survey shall be conducted by a City-approved qualified biologist within the disturbance
footprint, plus a 300-foot buffer. During construction within the nesting season, an additional
focused survey shall be conducted prior to tree removal to identify active nests with the subject
tree(s). If no active nests are observed, no further action would be required. Ground-disturbing
project activities that are initiated outside of the nesting season may continue into the nesting
season without requiring new nesting bird surveys.
Pre-construction nesting bird surveys shall be conducted by a qualified biologist during the time of
day when birds are most active and should be of sufficient duration to reliably conclude presence or
absence of nesting birds on the project site and within the designated buffer. A report of the nesting
bird surveys results shall be submitted to the City for review and approval prior to clearance for
mobilizing equipment. If nests are found, their locations shall be flagged (if possible) and recorded
with the use of a GPS unit. Avoidance buffers shall be established around active nests. Depending
upon the species, suitable minimum buffers may be 50 feet for non-raptor species and 300 feet for
raptor species, or as determined by the qualified biologist based on species sensitivity, construction
activities, and other factors.
If active nests are present, all project work shall be conducted outside the established avoidance
buffer zone from the nest until it is no longer active. No staging of large equipment shall occur
within the avoidance buffer until the qualified biologist confirms that breeding/nesting is complete

and all the young have fledged. If buffer zones are determined to be infeasible, a City-approved

MITIGATION MEASURE BIO-1(D): CONDUCT PILE DRIVING IMPACT AVOIDANCE TO FISH AND MARINE
MAMMALS PRIOR TO AND DURING CONSTRUCTION
In-water work, including pile driving and dredging, shall be limited to the window of June 1 through
November 30. The soft-start, ramp-up, exclusion-zone and sound attenuation procedures described
below apply to pile-driving and pile-extraction activities. A “soft-start” technique will be used to allow
fish and marine mammals to vacate the area before the pile driver reaches full power. For vibratory
hammers, the contractor will initiate the driving for 15 seconds at reduced energy, followed by a 1-
minute waiting period when there has been downtime of 30 minutes or more. This procedure shall
be repeated two additional times before continuous driving is started. This procedure would also
apply to vibratory pile extraction. For impact driving, an initial set of three strikes would be made by
the hammer at 40 percent energy, followed by a 1-minute waiting period, then two subsequent
three-strike sets before initiating continuous driving. Pile-driving activity shall not begin at any
location if any marine mammal is observed within the applicable safe-zone distance for its hearing
group, as defined for the specific pile‑driving method (e.g., pile diameter, vibratory or impact
installation, and number of piles installed per day). Safe‑zone distances shall follow the most current
NMFS‑approved guidance and the Marine Mammal Monitoring Plan prepared pursuant to Mitigation
Measure BIO‑1(E). In all cases, a minimum exclusion distance of no less than 10 meters shall be
maintained around the pile‑driving location. If a marine mammal moves within the safe zone after
pile driving has begun, the contractor shall implement the appropriate delay or shutdown as
described in Mitigation Measure BIO-1(E). A sound curtain, or bubble curtain, shall be employed
during impact pile driving to break up sound waves, as feasible. The sound curtain would consist of a
perforated hose laid in a circle to release air bubbles around the pile and diesel impact hammer.
Jetting methods using pressurized water and/or wood cushion block methods shall also be employed
as feasible to minimize impacts.
If the intensity of the pile-driving activity needs to be increased or a marine mammal is within the
safe zone buffer for the activity, pile-driving shall be “ramped-up”, which is a slow increase in the
intensity of pile-driving. At the start of pile-driving for each pile at all locations, the pile shall be
struck once with the hammer and the second pile strike delayed long enough to permit adequate
time for any marine mammals within the safe zone to leave the area prior to the start of sustained
pile-driving activities.
This measure, including the technique and the size of the safe zone, may be modified or
supplemented by permit conditions from applicable regulatory agencies.

MITIGATION MEASURE BIO-1(E): PREPARE MARINE MAMMAL MONITORING PLAN PRIOR TO CONSTRUCTION
AND IMPLEMENT RECOMMENDATIONS DURING CONSTRUCTION

Prior to construction, the City shall prepare a Marine Mammal Monitoring Plan (MMMP) to avoid
and minimize potential adverse impacts on marine mammals during pile driving and tug operations.
The MMMP shall implement general guidelines set forth in the MMPA and incorporate the


Draft Environmental Impact Report                                                                    3.3-55
City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project

hydroacoustic modeling results developed for the project to define site-specific protection zones
and avoid exposure of marine mammals to underwater sound levels exceeding the most up to date
Level A (injury) thresholds identified by NOAA Fisheries. The MMMP shall include the following:
   Protection and Monitoring Zones: Using the hydroacoustic modeling results, the MMMP shall
    define shutdown and disturbance zones for each marine mammal hearing group. These zones
    will be tailored to the pile type, size, and driving method and will correspond to the Level A and
    Level B effect distances developed for the project. The plan will describe how these protection
    zones will be verified and monitored in the field, integrating them with the soft-start and
    observation procedures described in Mitigation Measure BIO-1(d).
   Vessel Operation Protocols: The MMMP shall include vessel-operation measures consistent
    with the MMPA. Construction vessels under power shall remain at least 300 feet from whales
    and 150 feet from dolphins, porpoises, seals, and sea lions. When marine mammals are
    encountered, vessel operators shall reduce speed to no-wake, shift to neutral, and allow the
    animals to pass safely before resuming operations.
   On-Site Monitoring and Response: A qualified biologist shall be present on site, either
    observing from the pier or aboard a vessel, during all pile-driving and tug operations. The
    biologist shall document all marine-mammal observations, note behavioral responses, and
    immediately alert project personnel if a whale enters the modeled harassment distance or
    comes within 300 feet, or if any other marine mammal enters the modeled harassment distance
    or comes within 150 feet, whichever is greater. Upon such an observation, the contractor shall
    implement the appropriate delay or shutdown procedures identified in the MMMP.
   Adaptive Management and Coordination: The MMMP shall outline communication and
    reporting protocols, including stop-work notification procedures and coordination with NMFS
    Protected Species Division. Results from daily monitoring will be used to assess the
    effectiveness of the protection zones and adjust them, if needed, in consultation with NMFS.

This measure may be modified or supplemented by permit conditions from applicable regulatory
agencies.

Impact BIO-2               THE PROJECT COULD HAVE A SUBSTANTIAL ADVERSE EFFECT ON SENSITIVE NATURAL
COMMUNITIES IDENTIFIED IN LOCAL OR REGIONAL PLANS, POLICIES, OR REGULATIONS, OR BY THE CALIFORNIA
DEPARTMENT OF FISH AND WILDLIFE OR US FISH AND WILDLIFE SERVICE. IMPACTS WOULD BE LESS THAN
SIGNIFICANT WITH MITIGATION INCORPORATED.


Construction
There are no terrestrial sensitive natural communities, riparian areas, or critical habitats within, or
immediately adjacent to the project site. Therefore, there would be no impact on sensitive
terrestrial habitats.
Marine habitats within the project site include EFH for Pacific Coast Salmon, considered HAPC, and
critical habitat for the southern DPS of green sturgeon and the Sacramento River winter-run ESU of
Chinook salmon. Impacts on sensitive marine habitats could occur during construction due to spills
and leaks that may affect water quality or through the introduction of non-native species. Spills and
leaks can occur if construction vehicles and equipment are improperly maintained, used, or stored,
and could negatively affect water quality and toxicity for marine species. Temporary impacts on EFH
and HAPC could also include changes to water quality (e.g., turbidity, pH, dissolved oxygen),
increased noise, and other increased human activity during construction. Impacts on water quality
would be potentially significant. Additionally, the San Francisco Bay includes several important ports
for marine shipping. Therefore, the San Francisco Bay is vulnerable to the spread of invasive species,
and has been heavily impacted by non-indigenous species. 100 The introduction of invasive species
through dirty equipment or contaminated ballast water could affect habitat quality and degrade
EFH, estuaries, and marine and estuarine SAV, including eelgrass beds. Impacts on EFH, estuaries
and marine and estuarine SAV would be considered potentially significant.
Mitigation Measures BIO-1(a), BIO-2, and HYD-1 would be required and would reduce impacts to
EFH for Pacific Coast Salmon and marine Habitat Areas of Particular Concern by requiring a Worker
Environmental Awareness Program, best management practices, and avoidance of invasive species
introduction during construction. Therefore, construction impacts related to sensitive marine
habitats would be less than significant with mitigation.

Operation
The proposed project includes electric ferryboats, which would limit the potential for accidental fuel
spills or leaks within marine habitats during operations. Vessel operators would be required to
comply with all USCG and RWQCB requirements for ferry operations including hazardous material
handling, spill prevention, route inspections, maintenance, monitoring, and reporting. Additionally,
the project’s new ferryboat trips occur in the San Francisco Bay, which is a major port for
commercial shipping, and existing recreation and ferryboat use. Vessel operators would be required

to comply with all USCG and RWQCB requirements for ferry operations. Therefore, operational
impacts related to sensitive marine habitats would be less than significant.
Most invasive marine species in the San Francisco Bay are transported by ballast water via large
commercial ships, cargo vessels, and recreational boats. 101 The electric ferryboats proposed by the
project do not use ballast water systems. Hull fouling, the buildup of algae and sessile marine
invertebrates on a vessel’s submerged surfaces, is another common pathway for the spread of
marine invasive species. Routine maintenance such as regular hull cleaning, anti‑fouling coatings,
and dry‑dock inspections required for electric ferryboat operations prevent these organisms from
accumulating, reducing the potential for vessels to transport invasive species within the Bay. The
San Francisco Bay is widely recognized as one of the most heavily invaded estuaries in the world,
with more than 230 introduced species documented in the Bay‑Delta system. 102 The project would
operate only two ferry vessels, with regular service to San Francisco and limited weekend service to
Larkspur, resulting in a negligible incremental increase in the already heavily trafficked and highly
invaded bay. Given the absence of ballast‑water use, the routine hull‑maintenance requirements for
electric ferryboats, and the negligible increase in boat trips in the broader San Francisco Bay
context, the potential for the project to contribute to the spread of marine invasive species would
be less than significant.

Construction

FILL AND DREDGING IMPACTS
There are no State or federally protected wetlands or waters within terrestrial areas of the project
site. Therefore, there would be no impact on terrestrial wetlands or waters.
The project site occurs within tidal waters of the San Francisco Bay, which are waters of the U.S.;
waters of the State; and are regulated by the USACE under Section 404 of the CWA and Section 10
of the Rivers and Harbors Act, by the RWQCB under Section 401 of the CWA and Porter-Cologne Act,
and by BCDC pursuant to the McAteer-Petris Act.
The project would require a maximum of approximately 400,000 cubic yards of dredging, which
would be conducted in compliance with LTMS and associated permits. Sediment sampling
conducted under DMMO oversight has indicated that dredged materials are suitable for beneficial
reuse, and the City would coordinate with the LTMS agencies to beneficially reuse dredged material
to the extent feasible. All dredging and material placement would occur in accordance with
applicable regulations and permit conditions to minimize adverse effects on water quality and
aquatic habitat.
The project would remove approximately 1,280 linear feet of the existing pier, which is equivalent
to approximately 28,160 square feet. The project would install a new pier, breakwater, universal
charging floats, and landing ramps and platforms, with an area of approximately 45,210 square feet.
Table 3.3-4 provides a summary of the proposed removal and addition of this cover area within tidal
waters of the San Francisco Bay. The project would result in a net increase of approximately 17,050
square feet of fill and/or cover area within the San Francisco Bay. The increase in fill and cover
within the Bay would result in temporary or permanent loss of tidal waters by area and associated
ecological functions and services, which would be a potentially significant impact.
Mitigation Measure BIO-3 would require the removal of additional portions of the existing pier to
address project impacts associated with fill and cover in the San Francisco Bay. The City would also
obtain the appropriate permits from the USACE, RWQCB, and BCDC; these permits will include
avoidance, minimization, and compensatory mitigation requirements to achieve no net loss of
jurisdictional waters. Because implementation of Mitigation Measures BIO-3 would result in no net
loss of jurisdictional waters, impacts would be less than significant with mitigation.

WATER QUALITY
As discussed under Impact BIO-1 above, demolition of the old pier and construction of the new pier
and breakwater could also result in impacts on water quality due to increased turbidity from pile
driving and dredging, and accidental spills, which could degrade waters of the U.S. and State, and
their beneficial uses and would be considered a potentially significant impact.
However, Mitigation Measure HYD-1 would reduce impacts on tidal waters of the San Francisco Bay
by requiring best management practices for water quality. Therefore, construction-related fill and
dredging impacts on waters would be less than significant with mitigation.

Operation

SHADING AND SOFT BOTTOM HABITAT IMPACTS
The proposed project would replace the existing pier in place, and would result in additional square
feet of shading and loss of soft bottom habitat. This impact would be considered potentially
significant.
However, Mitigation Measure BIO-3 would be required to remove additional areas of the existing
pier at a ratio of at least 1:1 so that there is no increase in shading or loss of soft bottom habitat.
The project would add hard substrate for algal growth, sessile invertebrates, and seaweeds with the
creation of the breakwater, which could benefit ecological function. Therefore, operation-related fill
shading and soft bottom habitat impacts would be less than significant with mitigation.

IMPACTS FROM FERRY VESSEL WAKE
The Central Bay sees substantial wind-driven waves and wakes from existing marine traffic. The
shoreline at the project site is armored with rip-rap that absorbs this energy and would likewise
diffuse the wakes of the new electric ferry vessels. The armored shoreline that would be subject to
the wakes of the new electric ferry vessels are in good condition, with no failures visible. Because
the shoreline is armored and maintained, the added wake energy would not measurably increase
erosion, disturb aquatic habitats, or result in loss of jurisdictional waters. Therefore, impacts on
jurisdictional waters from the wake associated with ferry vessels would be less than significant.

Mitigation Measures

MITIGATION MEASURE BIO-3: PROVIDE COMPENSATORY MITIGATION FOR LOSS OF JURISDICTIONAL WATERS
PRIOR TO OPERATION
The City shall avoid a net loss of jurisdictional waters due to project implementation by demolishing
additional portions of the existing pier to offset new fill and cover. Compensatory mitigation shall be
required for impacts on tidal waters of the San Francisco Bay to achieve no net increase in Bay fill.
Compensatory mitigation shall be provided at a minimum 1:1 ratio (by square foot of impact)
through removal of existing pier piles and decking, as approved by the regulatory agencies.
Mitigation may be achieved through removal of additional areas of the existing pier, including the
concrete pier deck and pilings. Compensatory mitigation shall be implemented prior to or
concurrently with construction of the new pier.
The City shall develop a mitigation plan documenting the existing pier footprint, the proposed pier
footprint, and the required additional demolition needed to meet the mitigation goal. This plan shall
be developed by a qualified regulatory specialist prior to project construction and submitted to the
appropriate agencies for review and approval during permitting.
This measure may be modified or supplemented by permit conditions from applicable regulatory
agencies.

MITIGATION MEASURE HYD-1: INCLUDE AND IMPLEMENT ADDITIONAL BEST MANAGEMENT PRACTICES IN THE
SWPPP PRIOR TO AND DURING PIER DEMOLITION
See Section 3.8, Hydrology and Water Quality, for mitigation measure details.

Secondary Impacts from Mitigation
Demolition of additional areas of the existing pier as required by Mitigation Measure BIO-3 would
result in substantially similar impacts as those evaluated under the proposed project for
construction of the new pier. Accordingly, it would not introduce new impact mechanisms, but
would incrementally increase the duration and spatial extent of the temporary construction‐phase
effects already disclosed for the project. Below is a summary of the potential secondary impacts
from implementation of Mitigation Measure BIO-3.
The project would require demolition of the existing pier resulting in potentially significant impacts
to special-status fish and marine mammals. These impacts are the same as those that would occur
from the removal of the pier, just increased in scale. All impacts would remain short-term, localized,
and fully mitigated to a less-than-significant level through application of the same measures
identified for the project under Impact BIO-1 and Impact BIO-2. In the long term, the additional
demolition would be environmentally beneficial because it would remove legacy fill and shading,
thereby improving tidal circulation, light penetration, and benthic habitat quality within San
Francisco Bay.
The project would require additional construction in order to remove additional portions of the pier.
The air quality analysis in Section 3.2, Air Quality of this EIR includes conservative assumptions
about the construction schedule and demolition volumes that account for additional removal of the
pier from Mitigation Measure BIO-3. Therefore, the conclusions identified in Section 3.1, Air Quality
include the potential emissions from implementation of Mitigation Measure BIO-3. The proposed
project would not result in any more emissions beyond those already identified in Section 3.2, Air
Quality.

Wildlife Movement Corridors

Significance Criterion d: Would the proposed project interfere substantially with the movement of
                          any native resident or migratory fish or wildlife species or with

                          use of native wildlife nursery sites?

Impact BIO-4         THE PROJECT WOULD NOT SUBSTANTIALLY IMPEDE WILDLIFE MOVEMENT AREAS OR
NATIVE WILDLIFE NURSERY SITES. IMPACTS WOULD BE LESS THAN SIGNIFICANT.


Construction

TERRESTRIAL
The project site is located within filled Baylands adjacent to marine foraging habitat. Trees within
the project site and the closed pier may provide roosting habitat for migratory birds in the Pacific
Flyway; however, most of the site is developed for recreational and commercial use (including
substantial parking areas) and does not contain sensitive upland, riparian, or marsh areas where
terrestrial wildlife movement corridors typically occur. No native wildlife nursery sites (e.g., rookery
or den) have been identified within the project footprint or immediate vicinity. The project site is
also surrounded by open waters on three sides, limiting the opportunity for terrestrial movement.
There would be temporary disturbance to migratory birds during construction, including from the
removal of trees (see Impact BIO-5 for a discussion of tree impacts) and demolition of the closed
pier; however, these impacts would be localized and suitable foraging, roosting, and nesting habitat
in the vicinity of the site would remain available during construction. Therefore, construction
impacts related to terrestrial wildlife movement would be less than significant.

                                                                           Environmental Impact Analysis

MARINE
Demolition of the existing pier and pile driving for construction of the new pier would generate
noise and vibration in water that could disrupt fish and marine mammal movement within and in
the vicinity of the project. However, the project site is located along the shoreline of the southeast
corner of the Central Bay, where the water is shallower than other portions of the Bay
(approximately -30 to 3.2 feet MLLW), and approximately 3.75 miles from deeper waters of the
Golden Gate Strait. 103 Given the shallow waters within the project site, and its location along the
shoreline where no connection to spawning grounds are present, the project site is on the periphery
of the migratory corridor for anadromous fish that exists in the San Francisco Bay. The project site is
not within a designated or regionally significant movement corridor for anadromous fish migrating
between marine and freshwater habitats, or for marine mammals moving between haul-out or
breeding sites. Given the localized and temporary nature of construction activity, and the absence
of critical movement pathways, construction impacts related to marine wildlife movement would be
less than significant.

Operation

TERRESTRIAL
Operation of the project would include vehicles, bicycles, and pedestrians using University Avenue,
Seawall Drive, and parking lots. These uses of the project site would be consistent with existing
recreation and commercial uses. No new barriers or disturbances to terrestrial wildlife movement
are proposed. Therefore, there would be no operational impact related to terrestrial wildlife
movement.

MARINE
Operation of ferry vessels would occur at the water surface level, with some incremental increase in
ferry boat noise and lighting within the project area. The project proposes to operate two ferry
vessels with regular service to San Francisco and weekend service to Larkspur, that are both active
shipping ports with existing recreational and ferryboat use. Therefore, the project would represent
an incremental increase in existing boat trips on the Bay. Special-status fish and marine mammals,
specifically whales, are likely habituated to existing levels of boat trip levels and would avoid new
ferry boat service. In addition, as described under Impact BIO-1, WETA would continue to
implement best practices to reduce the potential for whale strikes including through the
implementation of practices that reflect ongoing technological advances, evolving scientific
understanding of best practices, and updated NOAA guidance. Therefore, the minimal increase in
operational in-water activities compared to existing conditions represents a less than significant
impact related to marine wildlife movement.

No mitigation would be required.

3.3.5         Cumulative Impacts
The geographic scope of the cumulative biological resources analysis is the central San Francisco Bay
and the immediate vicinities. The cumulative analysis considers the nearby past, present, and
reasonably foreseeable future plans and projects listed in Table 3-1 (refer to Chapter 3,
Environmental Impact Analysis).

Special-status Wildlife and Plant Species

Terrestrial
Most of the local cumulative projects would be located in developed urban areas that have limited
potential to support terrestrial special-status wildlife and plant species. There are open areas that
provide habitat for special-status species of flora and fauna, including César E. Chávez Park,
McLaughlin Eastshore State Seashore, Brickyard Cove, Aquatic Park, and the Albany Waterfront.
Open space within the cumulative project and project areas are relatively small and generally
isolated areas surrounded by urban development. Cumulative projects listed in Table 3-1 consist
predominantly of redevelopment of existing facilities including parking, transportation, and
recreational facility improvements. Development and projects planned within the cumulative
projects area would occur in similar, disturbed habitat common in urban areas. However, due to the
presence of habitat for some special-status species in and near Berkeley, including western
burrowing owl, monarch butterfly, Crotch’s bumble bee and tricolored blackbird, these species also
have the potential, albeit low, to occur within the cumulative projects area. Additionally, nesting
birds protected by the MBTA, and special-status bat species have the potential to occur within the
vicinity of the project. Standard pre-construction surveys and, if necessary, avoidance procedures
would be required for cumulative projects with the potential to impact nesting birds and other
special-status species. While there are isolated pockets of natural habitat that can support special-
status wildlife and plant species, the urban and developed nature of the City as well as the other
cumulative projects precludes the possible adverse cumulative impacts to biological resources
related to special-status wildlife and plant species. Therefore, cumulative projects in combination
with implementation of the proposed project would result in a less than significant cumulative
impact with respect to terrestrial special-status wildlife and plant species.

Marine
Marine areas within the Central Bay, where the project lies, provide habitat for special-status fish
and marine mammals, such as salmonids, whales, dolphins, and seals. Cumulative projects would be
required to adhere to existing laws and regulations pertaining to fill and development within the
project vicinity and to protection of marine habitats, special-status species, and water quality where
cumulative projects have the potential to impact marine habitats. The current level of boat traffic,
including existing ferry vessels, container shipping through the Port of Oakland and other smaller
ports, and recreational boating, as well as the other cumulative projects within the Berkeley Marina
are indicative of a very active environment. Possible adverse cumulative impacts to biological


3.3-66
                                                                        Environmental Impact Analysis
                                                                                Biological Resources

resources related to marine special-status wildlife species is unlikely because existing activity from
these many and varied vessels is such that species are habituated to a high level of activity;
therefore, the proposed project would not result in any measurable change to marine special-status
wildlife behavior. In general, in proximity to an active waterfront such as the Berkeley Marina, fish
are habituated to boating activity. Therefore, cumulative projects in combination with
implementation of the proposed project would result in a less than significant cumulative impact
with respect to marine special-status wildlife.

Sensitive Natural Communities and Waters of the United States and State

Terrestrial
Within the project vicinity, the City of Berkeley contains several creeks and riparian areas that would
be considered jurisdictional waters, wetlands, and/or sensitive natural communities. Cumulative
projects listed in Table 3-1 consist of predominantly redevelopment or infill projects, including
commercial and residential development, and transportation projects. Cumulative development
would occur in similar, disturbed habitat common in urban areas. Additionally, no terrestrial
sensitive natural communities, freshwater wetlands or waters, or federally designated critical
habitats are present within the project site. Therefore, cumulative projects in combination with
implementation of the proposed project would result in a less than significant cumulative impact
with respect to terrestrial sensitive natural communities, associated riparian habitat, or wetlands or
waters.

Marine
Marine habitats within the project site and vicinity are EFH for Pacific Coast Salmon, considered
HAPC, and critical habitat for the southern DPS of green sturgeon and the Sacramento River winter-
run ESU of Chinook salmon. Waters of the San Francisco Bay within the project site are also waters
of the U.S. and State under the jurisdiction of the USACE and RWQCB, and BCDC. Cumulative
projects would be required to adhere to existing laws and regulations pertaining to fill and
development within the San Francisco Bay, and measures to protect marine habitats and water
quality. Therefore, cumulative projects in combination with implementation of the proposed project
would result in a less than significant cumulative impact with respect to marine sensitive natural
communities including EFH, HAPC, and critical habitat.

Wildlife Movement Corridors

Terrestrial
Berkeley and its surrounding vicinity contain a variety of creeks and open space areas that act as
potential movement corridors for fish and wildlife, including in riparian areas. Any future cumulative
development that occurs within the City would have to consider the potential impact on these
corridors. Cumulative projects listed in Table 3-1 consist of predominantly redevelopment or infill
projects, including commercial and residential development, and transportation projects.
Cumulative development would occur in similar, disturbed habitat common in urban areas. The
areas surrounding the potential corridors within Berkeley and its surroundings in the Bay Area are
highly developed, further impeding the movement of species out from these areas. Therefore,
cumulative projects in combination with implementation of the proposed project would result in a
less than significant cumulative impact with respect to terrestrial wildlife movement corridors.

Marine
The Central Bay in the vicinity of the project contains shallow and deepwater habitats that provide
corridors for movement among estuarine and freshwater habitats of the San Francisco Bay. Within
the project area there are recreational boaters and commercial boats. Given the existing levels of
boat traffic within the Central Bay due to existing commercial boats and recreational boating,
cumulative projects in combination with implementation of the proposed project would result in a
less than significant cumulative impact with respect to marine wildlife movement corridors.

Local Biological Resources Policies or Ordinances Consistency
Development may require the removal of or encroachment on certain protected trees as listed by
the City of Berkeley ordinances. Cumulative plans and projects listed in Table 3-1 consist of
predominantly general plan buildouts, including commercial and residential development, and
active transportation projects. Development and projects planned within the cumulative projects
area would occur in similar, disturbed habitat common in urban areas. Future projects that occur in
or near undeveloped areas may require an arborist report to determine the identity of trees
planned for removal or encroachment. Therefore, the project, in conjunction with other cumulative
projects, would be required to adhere to applicable tree ordinances and regulations of the City of
Berkeley 104 and nearby Cities of Albany 105 and Oakland 106 that require permits for removal of
protected tree species (Coast live oak), compliance with species- and size-based protection
thresholds, and preparation of arborist reports to evaluate and mitigate impacts related to
protected trees. Therefore, cumulative projects in combination with implementation of the
proposed project would result in a less than significant cumulative impact with respect to protected
trees. For a discussion of cumulative impacts related to consistency with the BCDC Bay Plan, please
refer to Section 3.9, Land Use and Planning.

Habitat or Natural Community Conservation Plans Consistency
Because the project results in no impact related to a conflict with a Habitat Conservation Plan,
Natural Community Conservation Plan, or other approved habitat conservation plan; the project
could not contribute to a cumulative impact. Therefore, no cumulative impact would occur.

3.4             Cultural Resources
3.4.1           Introduction
This section describes the existing setting related to cultural resources within the project site and
adjacent areas as well as the relevant regulatory framework. This section also analyzes the potential
impacts to cultural resources anticipated to result from implementation of the proposed project.
Information in this section is based on archival and database research, a California Historical
Resources Information System records search, a search of the Sacred Lands File (SLF) by the Native
American Heritage Commission (NAHC), bathymetric remote sensing data analysis, and pedestrian
field survey results. California Department of Parks and Recreation forms prepared to document the
project site and its eligibility as a historical resource are included in Appendix D.

3.4.2           Environmental Setting
Cultural Resources Definitions
The term “cultural resources” under the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) encompasses
historic and archaeological resources as well as burial sites. Below is a brief summary of each
definition:
    Historical Resources: Historical resources are resources listed in, or determined eligible for
     listing in, the California Register of Historical Resources (CRHR); a resource included in a local
     register of historical resources or identified in a historical resources survey; or any object,
     building, structure, site, area, place, record, or manuscript that a lead agency determines to be
     historically significant. Historical resources may include eligible built environment resources of
     the precontact 1 or historic periods. For the purposes of this section, historical resources are
     associated with the recent past. Specifically in California, historical resources are typically
     associated with the Spanish, Mexican, and American periods in the State’s history and are
     generally less than 200 years of age.
    Archaeological Resources: Archaeology is the study of artifacts and material culture with the
     aim of understanding human activities and cultures in the past. Archaeological resources may
     be associated with precontact indigenous cultures as well as post-contact historic periods.
    Burial Sites and Cemeteries: Burial sites and cemeteries are formal or informal locations where
     human remains have been interred.

Overall Cultural Setting
The following is a brief overview of the indigenous history and post-contact history of the project
site and adjacent areas, including the rest of the City of Berkeley and general San Francisco Bay
Area. This section is not intended to be a comprehensive review of the current resources present;
rather, it serves as a general overview. Further details can be found in ethnographic studies, mission
records, and major published sources.




1 Precontact refers to the period prior to European settler contact with Native Americans, in this case specifically in California.
