Presence of Contaminants in Fill, Soil, Sediment, and Water

Fill Contaminants at the Project Site
According to historical topographic maps provided by the United States Geological Survey, the
project site and adjacent land was mainly undeveloped land, roads, creeks/canals, and open water
from at least 1895 to 1915. According to aerial photographs provided by Berkeley Historical Society,
commercial/industrial buildings were developed east of the project site by 1930 to 1952, and ﬁll
material appears to have been placed in several areas along the Berkeley Marina, west of present-
day I-80. By 1965, additional ﬁll material appears to have been placed in the northeast portion of the
Berkeley Marina, north of the project site, creating a conﬁguration similar to present day, and
commercial/industrial buildings were developed in this area from the late 1960’s to the late 1970’s.
Adjacent and nearby property uses appear to have remained similar to present day since at least the
late 1970’s, including the former Berkeley Landﬁll that ceased operations in the mid 1980’s and was
developed into North Waterfront Park by 1991 and renamed César E. Chávez Park in 1994.
Based on historical records (aerial photographs and topographic maps), land within the project site,
south of University Avenue was once open water, which has been ﬁlled with dredge spoils, as well as
ﬁll materials and soil of unknown origin from the 1950s through the 1980s. Artiﬁcial ﬁll is considered
heterogeneous, contains debris, and placed without engineered compaction. Fill material within the
project site and adjacent land may contain various contaminant concentrations exceeding State
regulatory thresholds, and waste generated from the disturbance of soil at these locations may need
to be regulated as a hazardous waste.

Soil Contaminants at the Project Site
Aerially deposited lead (ADL) was historically deposited by cars burning leaded gasoline and is often
found in the soil adjacent to highways and roads. Elevated concentrations of ADL may be present
along existing roadways, including those near the eastern portion of the project site, near I-80. Soil
along the eastern boundary of the project site may contain concentrations of lead exceeding state
regulatory thresholds, and any waste generated from the disturbance of soil in these locations may
be regulated as a non-hazardous or hazardous waste. Soil within the project site may be
contaminated with ADL due to the proximity of I-80, located adjacent to the eastern boundary of the
project site. The highway location in relation to the project site is shown in Figure 3.7-1.
According to the Geotechnical Report prepared by ENGEO dated December 16, 2024, soil corrosion
testing was completed on two samples of soil located at the intersection of University Avenue and
Sewall Drive. 15 Based on the resistivity measurements and chloride ion concentration from the
collected samples, ENGEO classiﬁed the soil as severely corrosive to buried metal and concrete per
ASTM D1498, D4972, G57, and D4327 standards. 16

Sediment and Water Contaminants at the Project Site
Sediments in bays and estuaries are commonly impacted by a variety of pollutants originating from
multiple sources, including ship fuel releases and industrial, agricultural, municipal wastewater, and
storm water discharges. According to the 2021 San Francisco Estuary Institute report, there are
several contaminants present in Bay Area sediments that are routinely found at elevated

Presence of Contamination in Transformers, Utility Poles, and Pier Piles

Contamination in Transformers and Utility Poles at the Project Site
Within the project site, there is a pad-mounted transformer, located east of Seawall Drive and that
may contain PCBs. PCBs are regulated by the United States Environmental Protection Agency
(USEPA) under the Toxic Substances Control Act, which governs the use, cleanup, and disposal of
PCBs, as discussed in Section 3.7.3, Regulatory Framework, below.

Contamination in Pier Piles at the Project Site
Within the project site, there are pier pilings supporting the existing pier that may be treated with
chemicals, including creosote for preservation and durability.

Proximity to Schools
School locations require consideration because children are particularly sensitive to hazardous
materials exposure. Additional protective regulations apply to projects that could use or disturb
potentially hazardous products near or at schools. The California Public Resources Code Section
21151.4 and California Government Code Section 15186(b) require projects that would be located
within a quarter mile of a school and might reasonably be expected to emit or handle hazardous
materials to consult with the school district regarding potential hazards. The closest school is located
approximately one half mile east of the project site, and there are no schools located within a
quarter mile of the project site.

Oakland International Airport is the closest airport to the project site, located approximately 11

Wildfire-conducive Conditions at the Project Site

Existing Vegetation
Due to the substantial open space areas and associated vegetation and wildlife habitats throughout
the State, California is subject to ﬁre hazards. Grassland or other vegetation in California is easily
ignited, particularly in dry seasons. Wildﬁre is a serious hazard in high dry fuel load areas,
particularly near areas of natural vegetation. The project site is located near Shorebird Park, which
contains open space and vegetation. However, the project site is located east, north, and south of
the San Franisco Bay, creating a buﬀer for wildﬁre-conductive conditions.
As discussed in greater detail in Section 3.3, Biological Resources, vegetation is mostly absent from
both developed and riprap areas of the project site, with the exception of sparse landscaping and
ruderal vegetation in developed areas, and pickleweed in riprap areas. The coyote brush scrub
vegetation community is on ﬁlled Baylands and is dominated by coyote brush (Baccharis pilularis),
with small scrubby coast live oaks (Quercus agrifolia), American bird's foot trefoil (Acmispon
americanus), and seaside wooly sunﬂower (Eriophyllum staechadifolium), as well as non-native
ornamentals. Ruderal areas are primarily found along the edges of roadways and trails within the
project site and have been heavily disturbed or altered such that natural vegetation has largely been

Existing Slope and Aspect
Wildﬁre is also a serious hazard in areas with steep slopes, since ﬁres tend to burn more rapidly on
steeper terrain. The existing slope across the project site is predominantly ﬂat. Its engineered
shoreline has produced terrain with minimal elevation and a primarily west-facing aspect oriented
toward the San Francisco Bay. 24 The project site is also located outside of a State-designated
earthquake-induced landslide hazard zone.

Existing Weather and Atmospheric Conditions
Wind, temperature, and relative humidity are the most inﬂuential weather elements in ﬁre behavior
and susceptibility. 25 Wildﬁre is also a serious hazard in areas of high wind, given that ﬁres will travel
faster and farther geographically when winds are higher. Extreme wildﬁre events are expected to
increase in frequency with the eﬀects of increased global temperature, although changes in speciﬁc
ﬁre-prone areas are diﬃcult to predict with any certainty. In particular, Alameda County is
experiencing longer and drier summer conditions. Historically, Berkeley’s climate has been
characterized by cool, wet winters with annual rainfall averaging 26.74 inches and approximately 85
percent of precipitation occurring between November and March. Warm, dry summers occurring
from June to October, with an average high of 75 degrees Fahrenheit are also typical for Berkeley. 26

Existing Fuel and Energy Lines
Wildﬁre is more likely in areas where electric power lines are located above ground and could ignite
vegetation where it comes into contact. Wildﬁre could also spread in areas of fuel lines, which could
fail (whether due to earthquake or error) and ignite a ﬁre. No natural gas transmission or hazardous
material liquid pipelines are on the project site. 27

3.7.3         Regulatory Framework
Hazardous materials and waste can pose a potential hazard to human health and the environment
when improperly treated, stored, transported, disposed of, or otherwise managed. Federal, State,
and local programs that regulate the use, storage, and transportation of hazardous materials and
hazardous waste are in place to prevent unwanted consequences. These regulatory programs are
designed to reduce the risk that hazardous substances may pose to people and businesses under
normal daily circumstances and as a result of emergencies and disasters.

Federal Regulations
Primary Federal agencies with responsibility for hazardous materials management include the
United States Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA), U.S. Department of Labor’s Occupational
Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), and the U.S. Department of Transportation (USDOT). The
major laws enforced by these agencies are described below.

Toxic Substances Control Act (1976) and the Resource Conservation and Recovery
Act of 1976
These acts established a program administered by the USEPA for the regulation of the generation,
transportation, treatment, storage, and disposal of hazardous waste. Congress enacted the Toxic
Substances Control Act (TSCA) of 1976, codiﬁed in CFR Title 40, to give USEPA the ability to track the
75,000 industrial chemicals currently produced or imported into the United States. USEPA
repeatedly screens these chemicals and can require reporting or testing of those that may pose an
environmental or human-health hazard. USEPA can ban the manufacture and import of those
chemicals that pose an unreasonable risk. More speciﬁcally, in California, PCBs are regulated by both
State (Title 22 of the California Code of Regulations [CCR]) and federal (TSCA) rules. TSCA has banned
the manufacture, processing, use, and distribution in commerce of PCBs. TSCA gives USEPA the
authority to develop, implement, and enforce regulations concerning the use, manufacture, cleanup,
and disposal of PCBs. TSCA also establishes USEPA’s Lead Abatement Program regulations, which
provide a framework for lead abatement, risk assessment, and inspections. Those performing these
services are required to be trained and certiﬁed by USEPA.
The Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA) was amended in 1984 by the Hazardous and
Solid Waste Act, which aﬃrmed and extended the “cradle to grave” system of regulating hazardous
wastes. Among other things, the use of certain techniques for the disposal of some hazardous
wastes was speciﬁcally prohibited by the Hazardous and Solid Waste Act.

U.S. Environmental Protection Agency
The USEPA is the agency primarily responsible for enforcement and implementation of Federal laws
and regulations pertaining to hazardous materials. Applicable Federal regulations pertaining to
hazardous materials are contained in the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) Titles 29, 40, and 49.
Hazardous materials, as deﬁned in the CFR, are listed in 49 CFR 172.101. The management of
hazardous materials is governed by the following laws:
1. Resource Conservation and Recovery Act of 1976 (42 USC 6901 et seq.)
2. Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act of 1980 (also called
   the Superfund Act) (42 USC 9601 et seq.)
3. Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (7 USC 136 et. Seq.)
4. Superfund Amendments and Reauthorization Act of 1986 (Public Law 99 499)

These laws and associated regulations include speciﬁc requirements for facilities that generate, use,
store, treat, and/or dispose of hazardous materials. USEPA provides oversight and supervision for
Federal Superfund investigation/remediation projects, evaluates remediation technologies, and
develops hazardous materials disposal restrictions and treatment standards.

U.S. Department of Transportation Regulations
USDOT prescribes strict regulations for the safe transportation of hazardous materials, including
requirements for hazardous waste containers and licensed haulers that transport hazardous waste
on public roads. The Secretary of the USDOT receives the authority to regulate the transportation of
hazardous materials from the Hazardous Materials Transportation Act (HMTA), as amended and
codiﬁed in in 49 U.S. Code (U.S.C.) Section 5101 et seq. The Secretary is authorized to issue
regulations to implement the requirements of 49 U.S.C. The Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety
Administration, formerly the Research and Special Provisions Administration, was delegated the
responsibility to write the hazardous materials regulations, which are contained in Title 49 of the
CFR Parts 100-180. Title 49 of the CFR, which contains the regulations set forth by the HMTA,
speciﬁes requirements and regulations with respect to the transport of hazardous materials. It
requires that every employee who transports hazardous materials receive training to recognize and
identify hazardous materials and become familiar with hazardous materials requirements. Under the
HMTA, the Secretary "may authorize any oﬃcer, employee, or agent to enter upon, inspect, and
examine, at reasonable times and in a reasonable manner, the records and properties of persons to
the extent such records and properties relate to: (1) the manufacture, fabrication, marking,
maintenance, reconditioning, repair, testing, or distribution of packages or containers for use by any
'person' in the transportation of hazardous materials in commerce; or (2) the transportation or
shipment by any 'person' of hazardous materials in commerce.

Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970
The U.S. Department of Labor’s OSHA was created to assure safe and healthful working conditions
by setting and enforcing standards and by providing training, outreach, education, and assistance.
OSHA provides standards for general industry and construction industry on hazardous waste
operations and emergency response. The Occupational Safety and Health Act, which is implemented
by OSHA, contains provisions with respect to hazardous materials handling. Federal Occupational
Safety and Health Act requirements, as set forth in Title 29 of the CFR Section 1910, et. seq., are
designed to promote worker safety, worker training, and a worker’s right-to-know. OSHA has
delegated the authority to administer OSHA regulations to the State of California.


3.7-12
                                                                                               Environmental Impact Analysis
                                                                                             Hazards and Hazardous Materials

Title 49 of the CFR, which contains the regulations set forth by the Hazardous Materials
Transportation Act of 1975, speciﬁes additional requirements and regulations with respect to the
transport of hazardous materials. Title 49 of the CFR requires that every employee who transports
hazardous materials receive training to recognize and identify hazardous materials and become
familiar with hazardous materials requirements. Drivers are also required to be trained in function
and commodity-speciﬁc requirements.

Clean Air Act

Federal Disaster Mitigation Act
The Federal Disaster Mitigation Act of 2000 created the framework for state, local, tribal, and
territorial governments to engage in hazard mitigation planning to receive varying forms of non-
emergency disaster assistance. The Act establishes a national disaster hazard mitigation program
aimed at reducing loss of life, property, and disaster assistance costs. It emphasizes the need for
identifying risks, implementing measures to reduce losses, and ensuring critical services continue
after disasters. The act provides funding to assist states, local, tribal and territorial governments in
implementing eﬀective hazard mitigation measures through federal contributions and the hazard
mitigation grant program which states may administer, provided they meet certain criteria such as
an approved mitigation plan.

National Fire Protection Association
The National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) is a nonproﬁt organization established in 1896 to
create standards and codes for use by local governments, including building codes, hazardous
response procedures, and battery energy storage systems (BESS). The following NFPA standards are
relevant to safe management battery energy storage systems 32:
    NFPA 1, Fire Code, Chapter 52;
    NFPA 70 (National Electrical Code), Article 706;
    NFPA 111, Stored Electrical Energy Emergency and Standby Power Systems; and
    NFPA 855, Standard for the Installation of Energy Storage Systems.

State Regulations

Hazardous Materials Transportation
California has adopted U.S. Department of Transportation regulations for the intrastate transport of
hazardous materials, which are found in Title 26 of the California Code of Regulations. The state also
regulates the movement of hazardous waste both originating in and passing through California.
The California Highway Patrol (CHP) and Caltrans are the primary agencies responsible for enforcing
these regulations and responding to transportation-related hazardous materials incidents. CHP
oversees labeling, packaging, vehicle inspections, and documentation to prevent leaks and ensure
proper response in case of accidents. Caltrans maintains chemical spill response teams at up to 72
locations statewide.
Under California Vehicle Code Section 32000, CHP licenses common carriers that transport over 500
pounds of hazardous materials for hire, or over 1,000 pounds if not for hire, when placarding is
required. Hazardous waste packaging must meet performance standards simulating travel
conditions, including resistance to water exposure, impact, compression, pressure changes, and
temperature extremes.

Senate Bill 1383 (SB 1383) – Maintenance and Operation Standards for BESS
Adopted in 2022, SB 1383 mandates the California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) to establish
and enforce state-level safety standards for the maintenance and operation of BESS located in
California. To comply with SB 1383, the California Public Utilities Commission modiﬁed General
Order 167 to explicitly include BESS facilities under its jurisdiction.

California Public Utilities Commission General Order 167
The CPUC ensures access to safe, clean, and aﬀordable utility infrastructure and services throughout
California. Enacted on March 13, 2025, CPUC modiﬁed General Order 167 to add new safety
standards for the maintenance and operation of BESS, as required by SB 1383. The updated General
Order 167 requires adherence to new maintenance and operation standards, safety reporting and
inspections, and coordination with local emergency agencies. The CPUC also requires that battery
storage facility owners must develop emergency response and action plans pursuant to SB 38.
Facilities 50 MW and larger are subject to the full scope of GO 167 while smaller facilities may be
exempt from certain provisions.

Senate Bill 38 – Emergency Response and Action Plans for BESS
Adopted in 2023, SB 38 amends Section 761.3 of the California Public Utilities Code to require that
all battery energy storage facilities in California develop and implement Emergency Response and
Emergency Action Plans in coordination with local emergency management agencies, Certiﬁed
Uniﬁed Program Agencies (CUPAs), and local ﬁrst responder agencies to be submitted to the county
and/or city where the facility is located. These plans must cover the entirety of the BESS facility,
establish procedures for equipment malfunction, include safety protocols for surrounding
communities, and deﬁne notiﬁcation procedures with local emergency agencies.

Department of Toxic Substances Control
As a department of the CalEPA, the DTSC is the primary agency in California that regulates hazardous
waste, oversees cleanup of existing contamination by responsible parties, and looks for ways to
reduce the hazardous waste produced in California. DTSC regulates hazardous waste in California
primarily under the authority of RCRA and the California Health and Safety Code.
The DTSC also administers the California Hazardous Waste Control Law (HWCL) to regulate
hazardous wastes. While the HWCL is generally more stringent than RCRA, until the USEPA approves
the California program, both state and federal laws apply in California. The HWCL lists 791 chemicals
and approximately 300 common materials that may be hazardous; establishes criteria for
identifying, packaging, and labeling hazardous wastes; prescribes management controls; establishes
permit requirements for treatment, storage, disposal, and transportation; and identiﬁes some
wastes that cannot be disposed of in landﬁlls.
Government Code Section 65962.5 requires the DTSC, the State Department of Health Services, the
SWRCB, and CalRecycle to compile and annually update lists of hazardous waste sites and land
designated as hazardous waste sites throughout the state. The Secretary for Environmental
Protection consolidates the information submitted by these agencies and distributes it to each city
and county where sites on the lists are located. Before the lead agency accepts an application for any
development project as complete, the applicant must consult these lists to determine if the site at
issue is included.
If any soil is excavated from a site containing hazardous materials, it would be considered a
hazardous waste if it exceeded speciﬁc criteria in CCR Title 22. Remediation of hazardous wastes
found at a site may be required if excavation of these materials is performed, or if certain other soil
disturbing activities would occur. Even if soil or groundwater at a contaminated site does not have
the characteristics required to be deﬁned as hazardous waste, remediation of the site may be
required by regulatory agencies subject to jurisdictional authority. Cleanup requirements are
determined on a case-by-case basis by the agency taking jurisdiction.

California Occupational Safety and Health Act – California Labor Code, Section
6300 et seq.
The California Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1973 addresses California employee working
conditions, enables the enforcement of workplace standards, and provides for advancements in the
ﬁeld of occupational health and safety. The Act also created the California Occupational Safety and
Health Administration (CalOSHA), the primary agency responsible for worker safety in the handling
and use of chemicals in the workplace. CalOSHA’s standards are generally more stringent than
federal regulations. Under the former, the employer is required to monitor worker exposure to listed
hazardous substances and notify workers of exposure. The regulations specify requirements for
employee training, availability of safety equipment, accident-prevention programs, and hazardous
substance exposure warnings. At sites known or suspected to be contaminated by hazardous
materials, workers must have training in hazardous materials operations and a Site Health and Safety
Plan must be prepared, which establishes policies and procedures to protect workers and the public
from exposure to potential hazards at the contaminated site.

California Health and Safety Code, Division 20, Chapter 6.95
At the State level, California Health and Safety Code Division 20, Chapter 6.95 establishes the
Hazardous Materials Business Plan (HMBP), which is administered at the local level by appointed
Certiﬁed Uniﬁed Program Agencies (CUPAs) under the oversight of CalEPA. CUPAs work in tandem
with other agencies such as the DTSC and the SWRCB and are empowered to conduct inspections,
enforce compliance, and carry out corrective action when necessary. The HMBP program requires
business handling hazardous materials above speciﬁed quantities to prepare and submit a business
plan including an inventory of hazardous materials, site maps, emergency response procedures, and
employee training protocols to be submitted through the California Environmental Reporting System
and reviewed by the appropriate CUPA.
The TMD is the CUPA for the City of Berkeley. TMD administers various CUPA and other
environmental programs and maintains documents related to the Emergency Planning. 35 The TMD
maintains HMBP ﬁles for Berkeley facilities. In addition, the TMD maintains inspection and
enforcement history for this and other CUPA programs and the industrial stormwater pollution
prevention program.

California Code of Regulations, Title 22, Hazardous Waste Management
At the State level, under CCR Title 22, Division 4.5, DTSC regulates hazardous waste in California
primarily under the authority of the Federal RCRA and the California Health and Safety Code. The
Hazardous Waste Control Law (HWCL), under CCR 22, Chapter 30, establishes regulations that are
similar to RCRA but more stringent in their application and empowers the DTSC to administer the
State’s hazardous waste program and implement the federal program in California. The DTSC is
responsible for permitting, inspecting, ensuring compliance, and imposing corrective action
programs to ensure that entities that generate, store, transport, treat, or dispose of potentially
hazardous materials and waste comply with federal and State laws. The DTSC deﬁnes hazardous
waste as waste with a chemical composition or other properties that make it capable of causing
illness, death, or some other harm to humans and other life forms when mismanaged or released
into the environment. The DTSC shares responsibility for enforcement and implementation of

California Code of Regulations Title 23, Chapter 15 Discharges of Hazardous Waste
to Land Section 2511(b)
CCR 23, Chapter 15 Discharges of Hazardous Waste to Land Section 2511(b) pertains to water quality
aspects of waste discharge to land. The regulation establishes waste and site classiﬁcations as well as
waste management requirements for waste treatment, storage, or disposal in landﬁlls, surface
impoundments, waste piles, and land treatment facilities. Requirements are minimum standards for
proper management of each waste category, which allows regional water boards to impose more
stringent requirements to accommodate regional and site-speciﬁc conditions. In addition, the
requirements of CCR 23, Chapter 15 applies to cleanup and abatement actions for unregulated
hazardous waste discharges to land (e.g., spills).

California Accidental Release Prevention Program
The purpose of the California Accidental Release Prevention (Cal ARP) program is to prevent
accidental releases of substances that can cause serious harm to the public and the environment, to
minimize the damage if releases do occur, and to satisfy community right-to-know laws. The Cal ARP
requires any business that handles more than threshold quantities of an extremely hazardous
substance per California regulations to develop a Risk Management Plan (RMP). The RMP is
implemented by the business to prevent or mitigate releases of regulated substances that could
have oﬀ-site consequences through hazard identiﬁcation, planning, source reduction, maintenance,
training, and engineering controls. The RMP contains the following elements:
   Safety Information
   A Hazard Review
   Operating Procedures
   Training Requirements
   Compliance Audits
   Incident Investigation Procedures

The RMP must also consider the proximity to sensitive populations located in schools, residential
areas, general acute care hospitals, long-term health care facilities, and child day care facilities. The
RMP must also consider external events such as seismic activity. The Certiﬁed Uniﬁed Program
Agencies determine the level of detail in the RMPs, review the RMPs, conduct facility inspections,
and provide public access to most of the information. There are three program levels identiﬁed by
Cal ARP and they are dependent on the type of business, potential impact, and accident history,
among other factors.
If an accidental release occurs, the owner/operator of a facility shall ensure that response actions
have been coordinated with local emergency planning and response agencies.

California Fire and Building Code
The California Building Code establishes the minimum requirements consistent with nationally
recognized good practices to safeguard the public health, safety, and general welfare for the hazards
of ﬁre, explosion, or dangerous conditions in new and existing buildings, structures and premises,
and to provide safety and assistance to ﬁreﬁghters and emergency responders during emergency

and demolition of every building or structure or any appurtenances connected or attached to such

The 2022 California Fire Code, found in Title 24, Part 9 of the California Code of Regulations
establishes enforceable standards for minimizing ﬁre, explosion, and hazardous material risks in

California State Hazard Mitigation Plan
The 2023 California State Hazard Mitigation Plan (SHMP) builds upon the state’s commitment to
reduce or eliminate potential risks and impacts of natural and human-caused disasters to help
communities with their mitigation and disaster resiliency eﬀorts. The plan identiﬁes and proﬁles
various hazards, including earthquakes, wildﬁres, ﬂoods, drought, extreme heat, and climate change
impacts, and establishes mitigation goals, objectives, and actions to encourage community
resilience. The SHMP provides guidance for local jurisdictions to develop their own hazard mitigation
plans and ensures California’s eligibility for federal disaster assistance and mitigation funding. 36

California Emergency Plan
The California Emergency Plan, developed by the California Governor’s Oﬃce of Emergency Services,
provides a comprehensive framework for statewide emergency management. It explains the state’s
approach to preparing for, mitigating, responding to, and recovering from various hazards, including
natural disasters, technological incidents, and human-caused events. The plan details the roles and
responsibilities of state agencies, local governments, and other stakeholders. The California
Emergency Plan also includes provisions for mutual aid, public information dissemination, and
continuity of government during emergencies to improve California’s resilience during times of
emergency response and recovery eﬀorts.

Regional and Local Regulations

PG&E Electric and Gas Service Requirements (Greenbook)

projects within PG&E’s service area, for their interconnection, metering, and switchgears. Appendix C
of the Greenbook includes engineering documents relevant to BESS design and installation.

Bay Area Air District Regulation 11, Rule 2
The Bay Area Air District regulates demolition and renovation of asbestos-containing materials
(ACM) through Rule 2, which applies to any planned renovation that involves 100 square feet, 100
linear feet, or 35 cubic feet or more of ACM, as well as to all demolitions regardless of ACM content.
The requirements include a noticing period, the conducting of a pre-demolition survey for ACM
materials by a certiﬁed inspector, and a general prohibition on demolition until ACM has been
abated and removed from the location and requires that abatement be conducted by persons with
speciﬁc asbestos certiﬁcation (primarily Asbestos Hazard Emergency Response Act certiﬁcation).

Expansion of Ferry Transit Service in the San Francisco Bay Area Program EIR
The Water Emergency Transportation Authority (WETA) – also known as San Francisco Bay Ferry –
prepared the Expansion of Ferry Transit Service in the San Francisco Bay Area Program EIR in 2003
(WETA Program EIR). The Water Resources Section of the WETA Program EIR, which the City
incorporates by reference herein, included an analysis of the potential impacts on water resources
from accidental spills due to the operation of ferry vessels. The WETA Program EIR imposed
mitigation that would require continued implementation of safety planning and contingency
planning to minimize the potential for accidental spills from the operation of ferry vessels.

Berkeley Municipal Code
Title 15 of the Berkeley Municipal Code includes the Berkeley Hazardous Materials Code. The intent
of this title is to provide regulations and standards for certain operations, enterprises or activities
which, if not regulated, may adversely aﬀect public health and safety. Berkeley’s TMD is a Certiﬁed
Uniﬁed Program Agency and implements Chapter 6.11 of Division 20 of the California Health and
Safety Code and Title 15 of the BMC. The TMD has created Berkeley’s Hazardous Materials Business
Plan, which is meant to satisfy federal and state Community laws and provides detailed information
for use by emergency responders.
TMD also oversees projects located in Environmental Management Areas (EMA or EMAs), which are
zones designated by the City of Berkeley where there is known or suspected groundwater
contamination. Projects within these areas are subject to speciﬁc permit requirements established
by the City to ensure the safe handling of contaminated soil and groundwater to prevent public
health risks. As a condition of development approval, the EMA designation requires that
construction and development activities in these zones follow stringent protocols to manage and
mitigate contamination eﬀectively. These requirements include:
   Site Assessment: Conducting thorough environmental site assessments to identify the extent of
    contamination and potential risks.
   Soil and water management: Implementing protocols for handling contaminated soil and
    groundwater, including proper disposal and treatment methods.
   Health and safety plans: Developing health and safety plans to protect workers and the public
    from exposure to hazardous materials.
   Monitoring and reporting: establishing monitoring programs to track contamination levels and
    reporting ﬁndings to relevant authorities.
   Permit compliance: obtaining necessary permits and approvals from the City’s Toxics
    Management Division, who will notify the responsible agency if a soil or groundwater
    management plan is necessary, before commencing work.

Berkeley Local Hazard Mitigation Plan (LHMP)
Berkeley is exposed to several natural and human-caused hazards that vary in their intensity and
impacts on the city. The LHMP addresses earthquake, wildland-urban interface, extreme heat, poor
air quality, high wind, rainfall-triggered landslide, tsunami, sea level rise, ﬂoods, utility interruption,
hazardous materials release, and infectious disease. The 2024 LHMP speciﬁes that the City has not
recently experienced hazardous materials releases as a cascading impact of a natural hazard, and
that climate change is no longer treated as a standalone hazard. Instead, climate change is

The City of Berkeley’s 2024 LHMP serves three main functions:
    The 2024 LHMP documents the City’s current understanding of the hazards present in Berkeley,

3.7.4            Impacts Analysis
Significance Criteria
The City of Berkeley utilizes the following 2025 CEQA Guidelines Appendix G signiﬁcance criteria
questions related to hazards and hazardous materials. Would the project:
a) Create a signiﬁcant hazard to the public or the environment through the routine transport, use,
   or disposal of hazardous materials?
b) Create a signiﬁcant hazard to the public or the environment through reasonably foreseeable
   upset and accident conditions involving the release of hazardous materials into the
   environment?
c) Emit hazardous emissions or handle hazardous or acutely hazardous materials, substances, or
   waste within one-quarter mile of an existing or proposed school?
d) Be located on a site that is included on a list of hazardous materials sites compiled pursuant to
   Government Code Section 65962.5 and, as a result, would create a signiﬁcant hazard to the
   public or the environment?
e) For a project located within an airport land use plan or, where such a plan has not been
   adopted, within two miles of a public airport or public use airport, result in a safety hazard or
   excessive noise for people residing or working in the project area?
f) Impair implementation of or physically interfere with an adopted emergency response plan or
   emergency evacuation plan?
g) Expose people or structures, either directly or indirectly, to a signiﬁcant risk of loss, injury, or
   death involving wildland ﬁres?

Note that wildﬁre impacts related to being located in or near a State Responsibility Area or lands
classiﬁed as very high ﬁre hazard severity zones are discussed in Section 3.15, Eﬀects Found Not to
be Signiﬁcant.

Approach to Analysis
Environmental impacts related to hazards and hazardous materials have been assessed using impact
signiﬁcance criteria from federal, State, and local regulations. The impact analysis is based on
available literature regarding the existing plans, policies, and resources in the project site. Criteria
used during this analysis are described below.
   Hazards (Speciﬁc to Hazardous Materials Upset and Exposure Risk). This evaluation focuses on
    whether the proposed project would result in changes to the physical environment that would
    cause or exacerbate adverse eﬀects related to the use, transportation, disposal, accidental
    release, or emission of hazardous materials. Potential construction-related and operational
    impacts from existing hazardous materials in soils, sediments, groundwater, and surface water
    are evaluated using available information from the DTSC and the SWRCB.
   Hazards (Speciﬁc to Aviation Safety and Noise Exposure Risk). The airport safety zones and noise
    contours for the closest airport to the project site (Oakland International Airport) were reviewed
    to determine potential impacts from exposure to aviation-related hazards and noise.
   Emergency Evacuation and Response. The evaluation includes a determination of whether the
    changes to the physical environment caused by the proposed project would impair or interfere
    with emergency response plans, including the Berkeley Local Hazard Mitigation Plan.
   Wildﬁre Exposure Risk. The California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection Hazard
    Severity Maps were consulted in determining the project’s proximity to State Responsibility
    Areas or lands classiﬁed as very high ﬁre hazard severity zones. Impacts related to wildﬁre
    hazards and risks were evaluated using Fire Hazards Severity Zone mapping for Alameda County,
    aerial imagery, and topographic mapping.

     an evacuation route, such as I-80 or the I-80 Bicycle/Pedestrian Overcrossing, University Avenue,

    Location of the project in or near area of susceptible vegetation, steep slopes, high-wind areas,
     fuel and power lines, or previous wildﬁre burn areas leading to greater wildﬁre risk.

Construction
The following discussion addresses the transport, use, storage, and disposal of hazardous materials
during construction activities; the potential for release of existing contaminated materials during
construction; and the potential for exposure to lead-based paint or ACM during demolition or
construction.

TRANSPORTATION, USE, STORAGE, AND DISPOSAL 38
Construction associated with the project may include the temporary transport, storage, and use of
potentially hazardous materials including demolition debris, dredged material, fuels, lubricating
ﬂuids, cleaners, or solvents. If spilled, these substances could pose a risk to the environment and to
human health. However, the transport, storage, use, or disposal of hazardous materials is subject to
various federal, state, and local regulations designed to reduce risks associated with hazardous
materials, including potential risks associated with upset or accident conditions. Hazardous materials

would be required to be transported under U.S. DOT regulations (U.S. DOT Hazardous Materials
Transport Act, 49 Code of Federal Regulations), which specify the types of containers, labeling, and
other restrictions to be used in the movement of such material on interstate highways. DTSC
regulates hazardous waste, cleans up existing contamination, and looks for ways to control and
reduce the hazardous waste produced in California. It does this primarily under the authority of
RCRA and in accordance with the California Hazardous Waste Control Law (California Health and
Safey Code Division 20, Chapter 6.5) and the Hazardous Waste Control Regulations (Title 22,
California Code of Regulations, Divisions 4 and 4.5). DTSC also oversees permitting, inspection,
compliance, and corrective action programs to ensure that hazardous waste managers follow federal
and State requirements and other laws that aﬀect hazardous waste speciﬁc to handling, storage,
transportation, disposal, treatment, reduction, cleanup, and emergency planning. Compliance with
existing regulations would reduce the risk of potential release of hazardous materials during
construction. Therefore, construction impacts related to hazardous materials exposure due to
transport, use, storage, or disposal of hazardous materials during construction would be less than
signiﬁcant.

RELEASE – LANDSIDE
Portions of the project on land are in an EMA as identiﬁed by the City’s TMD, which identiﬁes areas
known or suspected of having groundwater contamination. 39 There are no hazardous material sites
or release cases located within the project site. There are, however, three closed LUST Cleanup Site
cases that resulted in impacted groundwater and gasoline-impacted soil are within 580 feet of the
project site. In addition, soil within the project site and adjacent to I-80 may be aﬀected by
contamination from ADL, a contaminant historically deposited by cars burning leaded gasoline that is
often found in the soil adjacent to highways and roadways. Furthermore, based on the project site
location within and adjacent to artiﬁcial ﬁll lands, elevated concentrations of other hazardous
materials, such as petroleum hydrocarbons, volatile organic compounds, polycyclic aromatic
hydrocarbons, heavy metals, pesticides, or polychlorinated biphenyls may also be present in artiﬁcial
ﬁll, soil, and sediment at the project site.
Demolition, excavation, grading, and construction activities may result in exposure of construction
workers to contaminants through the mobilization of sediment, dust, and/or soil in and adjacent to
the project site. However, construction within an EMA requires project review by the TMD prior to
issuance of permits. All projects requiring discretionary review, such as this project, would be subject
to the following City of Berkeley Standard Condition of Approval:
Toxics. The City shall coordinate with the Toxics Management Division (TMD) to determine which of

B. Soil and Groundwater Management Plan
   1. A Soil and Groundwater Management Plan (SGMP) shall be submitted to TMD for all non-
        residential projects that: (1) are in the EMA and (2) propose any excavations deeper than 5
        feet below grade. The SGMP shall be site speciﬁc and identify procedures for soil and
        groundwater management including identiﬁcation of pollutants and disposal methods. The
        SGMP will identify permits required and comply with all applicable local, state and regional
        requirements.
   2. The SGMP shall require notiﬁcation to TMD of any hazardous materials found in soils and
        groundwater during development within 24 hours of the discovery of any previously
        undiscovered contamination. The SGMP will provide guidance on managing odors during
        excavation. The SGMP will provide the name and phone number of the individual
        responsible for implementing the SGMP and post the name and phone number for the
        person responding to community questions and complaints.
   3. TMD may impose additional conditions as deemed necessary. All requirements of the
        approved SGMP shall be deemed conditions of approval of this Use Permit.

C. Building Materials Survey
   4. Prior to approving any permit for partial or complete demolition and renovation activities
       involving the removal of 20 square or lineal feet of interior or exterior walls, a building
       materials survey shall be conducted by a qualiﬁed professional. The survey shall include, but
       not be limited to, identiﬁcation of any lead-based paint, asbestos, polychlorinated biphenyl
       (PBC) containing equipment, hydraulic ﬂuids in elevators or lifts, refrigeration systems,
       treated wood and mercury containing devices (including ﬂuorescent light bulbs and mercury
       switches). The Survey shall include plans for hazardous waste or hazardous materials
       removal, reuse or disposal procedures to be implemented that fully comply with state
       hazardous waste generator requirements (22 California Code of Regulations 66260 et seq).
       The Survey becomes a condition of any building or demolition permit for the project.

       be submitted to TMD within 30 days of the completion of the demolition. If asbestos is
       identiﬁed, Bay Area Air District Regulation 11-2-401.3 a notiﬁcation must be made and the J
       number must be made available to the City of Berkeley Permit Service Center.

RELEASE – WATERSIDE
There are also several contaminants present in Bay Area sediments that are routinely found at
elevated concentrations, above sediment quality guidelines. These chemicals include PCBs,
polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, pesticides (e.g., dieldrin and chlordane), and several metals (e.g.,
copper, mercury, lead, and zinc). A 2023 sediment sampling analysis conducted during the Berkeley
Marina Dredging Project identiﬁed mercury, total PCBs, and dioxins/furans in Bay Area sediments. 42
In addition, sediments were sampled and analyzed in 2025 within the ﬁve dredge units within the
project vicinity in accordance with the Inland Testing Manual, 43 site-speciﬁc requirements for the
proposed reuse sites, and the United States Army Corps of Engineer’s Dredged Material
Management Oﬃce. 44 The sampling and analysis included evaluation of the sediments for
placement at disposal sites in San Francisco Bay, the Cullinan Ranch Restoration Project (CRRP), and
the Montezuma Wetlands Restoration Project (MWRP) beneﬁcial reuse sites. Based on the ﬁndings
of the sampling and analysis the sediments are suitable for reuse as summarized below:
    Dredge Unit 1: Unconﬁned aquatic disposal in San Francisco Bay and MWRP
    Dredge Units 2, 3, and 5: Unconﬁned aquatic disposal in San Francisco Bay and CRRP, and MWRP
    Dredge Unit 4: CRRP and MWRP

Metals, organochlorine pesticides, polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons, polychlorinated biphenyls,
and dioxins/furans were detected in sediment samples analyzed; however, the concentrations did
not exceed California or Federal hazardous waste criteria.
Based on the ﬁndings of the sediment sampling and analysis, there are not anticipated to be
signiﬁcant impacts related to the handling of the sediments should the sediments be limited to
reuse within the reuse sites in which they were determined to be suitable.

In addition, there is the potential for other unknown impacts to Bay Area sediments from
surrounding land uses and wastewater/stormwater discharges. There is the potential for the
sediments that are dredged to be contaminated, which could result in health hazard impacts to
workers or the environment if not properly managed. However, the project would be subject to the
City of Berkeley Standard Condition of Approval discussed above in “Release of Contaminated
Materials During Construction – Landside.” Compliance with these requirements and with federal,
state, and local regulations pertaining to the transport, use, storage, and disposal of hazardous
materials would minimize the risks associated with potentially contaminated sediments, and impacts
would be less than signiﬁcant.
Additionally, pier pilings for the existing pier within the project site may have been treated with
chemicals, such as creosote, that have the potential to lead to toxicity in the surrounding water and
sediment as the treated wood breaks down over time. Demolition materials from portions of the
existing pier pilings may contain hazardous materials that could result in health hazard impacts on
workers or the environment if not properly managed. However, compliance with existing regulations
would minimize the potential risk associated with piles that have been treated with creosote, which
is also known as Treated Wood Waste or TWW. California Health and Safety Code Sections
25143.1.5, 25150, and 25230 require that TWW is managed as hazardous waste unless speciﬁcally
exempted. These provisions require that employees managing TWW be trained in the proper
methods of identifying and segregating TWW, safely handling TWW, and the proper disposal of
TWW. Furthermore, the California Code of Regulations, Title 22, Division 4.5, Chapters 12-14and
Health and Safety Code Section 25150 include requirements related to how TWW can be stored,
proper labeling of TWW, and timelines for disposal, which the City would be required to adhere to.
In addition, the California Code of Regulations Section 25150 and Health and Safety Code Chapter 13
require that TWW be managed as a non-RCRA hazardous waste and transported to Class I Hazardous
Waste Landﬁll. TWW must be identiﬁed with a state hazardous waste code on the hazardous waste
manifest, and its disposal must comply with DTSC requirements. Although demolition of the existing
pier pilings may result in a potential health hazard to workers and the environment, overall, the
removal of creosote piles would provide an environmental beneﬁt by removing a hazardous material
from the San Francisco Bay, and potential impacts would be limited to the handling, transportation,
and disposal of these piles. Through adherence to existing regulations that regulate the handling,
transportation, and disposal of these piles, impacts would be less than signiﬁcant.
With compliance with existing regulations for the removal, transport, storage, use, or disposal of
hazardous materials, construction impacts associated with release of contaminated materials during
waterside construction would be less than signiﬁcant.

LEAD-BASED PAINT EXPOSURE
Roadways in the City of Berkeley that were paved prior to the 1970s may contain lead-based
materials in the striping paint historically used. Proposed circulation improvements along University
Avenue and Seawall Drive would include repaving and restriping activities, which may involve the
disturbance or removal of existing asphalt and associated paint. Such activities could result in health
hazard impacts to workers if not properly managed.
Projects in Berkeley are subject to CalOSHA regulations regarding lead-based materials. The
California Code of Regulations, Title 8, Section 1532.1, requires testing, monitoring, containment,
and disposal of lead-based materials, such that exposure levels do not exceed CalOSHA standards.
Therefore, with implementation of standard CalOSHA lead safety protocols, construction impacts
related to lead exposure speciﬁc to roadway improvements would be less than signiﬁcant.



3.7-28
                                                                           Environmental Impact Analysis
                                                                         Hazards and Hazardous Materials

ASBESTOS-CONTAINING MATERIALS EXPOSURE
Berkeley contains numerous residential and commercial structures that, due to their age, may
contain asbestos and/or lead-based paint. Structures built before the 1970s typically contained
asbestos-containing materials (ACM). Given the age of the existing Berkeley pier, there is potential
for asbestos contamination in the concrete pilings. Demolition of these structures could result in
health hazard impacts to workers if not remediated prior to construction activities. However, the
project would be subject to the City of Berkeley Standard Conditions of Approval above, which
includes a Building Materials Survey prior to approval of permits for complete or partial demolition.
The condition of approval requires that a building materials survey be conducted by a qualiﬁed
professional. The survey must include plans on hazardous waste or hazardous materials removal,
reuse or disposal procedures to be implemented that fully comply with state hazardous waste
generator requirements. The project would also be required to adhere to Bay Area Air District
Regulation 11, Rule 2, which governs the proper handling and disposal of ACM for demolition,
renovation, and manufacturing activities in the Bay Area. With adherence to the Standard
Conditions of Approval and Bay Area Air District policies regarding ACM, construction impacts
related to asbestos exposure speciﬁc to pier pilings demolition would be less than signiﬁcant.

Operation
The risk of hazardous materials creating a signiﬁcant hazard to the public or the environment would
primarily occur during construction, if contaminated surface water, groundwater, sediment, or soil
were disturbed on-site. Once the proposed project is operational, the contaminated media would be
removed or covered and would no longer pose a risk to the public or the environment.

TRANSPORTATION, USE, STORAGE, AND DISPOSAL
While it is possible that proposed pier and associated infrastructure operation could result in a
nominal increase in the frequency of maintenance and inspection trips, it would not result in an
increase in hazardous material conditions or disruption of hazardous materials within the project
site. Although the proposed ferry service would be electric, which would not require a backup
generator or diesel fuel, potential discharges from onboard systems represent a minor but
conceivable source of hazardous waste. Discharges could include lubricants, hydraulic ﬂuids, or
sewage, which could occur with WETA’s existing ﬂeet. As described in Section 3.7.3, Regulatory
Framework, WETA has analyzed the potential impacts from accidental spills due to the expansion of
ferry transit. With the implementation of mitigation requiring safety planning and contingency
planning to minimize the potential for accidental spills from the operation of ferry vessels, impacts
were found to be less than signiﬁcant in the WETA Program EIR. As part of its WETA Program EIR,
WETA will continue to implement safety planning and contingency planning as part of the expanded
ferry service to Berkeley. In addition, ferry vessels would be maintained oﬀ-site, at the Central Bay
Operations and Maintenance Facility in Alameda, California. Beyond the transport of onboard
sewage systems, which would comply with applicable regulations, operation and maintenance
would not require the routine use, storage, transport, or disposal of hazardous materials. Therefore,
operational impacts related to transportation, use, storage, and disposal of hazardous materials
would be less than signiﬁcant.

RELEASE – BATTERIES
The all-electric ferry service will rely on the use of lithium-ion batteries. While there is a potential risk
of upset and accidental release of hazardous chemicals contained within the batteries due to a ﬁre or



Draft Environmental Impact Report                                                                     3.7-29
City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project

damage to lithium-ion batteries from physical impact, exposure to certain temperatures, and/or
improper charging, the project incorporates multiple safety features to address these risks. As
discussed below in Impact HAZ-6, the project site is not prone to ﬁre hazards, and the project design
includes ﬂame suppression features. For example, the Universal Charging Float or UCF is equipped
with a dedicated ﬁre suppression system to address potential hazards associated with the use and
storage of batteries under reasonably foreseeable upset or accident conditions. In addition, in the
event of a ﬁre incident, the pier will include water lines and hose bibs that will be available to
extinguish ﬂames, and the pier itself will be designed to accommodate ﬁre trucks and emergency
vehicles.
Lithium-ion batteries are regulated by the USDOT as Class 9 Miscellaneous Dangerous Goods. The
transport, use, storage, and disposal of batteries during operation and maintenance of the project
would be subject to all applicable federal, State, and local laws, regulations, standards, and guidelines
established by the USEPA, the State of California, and the City related to storage, use, and disposal of
hazardous materials. Applicable laws include the HMTA, RCRA, 40 CFR Parts 260- through 273, 49 CFR
171 through 180, and CCR Title 22 (as described in Section 3.7.3, Regulatory Framework). TMD is the
Certiﬁed Uniﬁed Program Agency for the City and performs inspections to prevent exposure to
environmental health hazards for businesses and residents in Berkeley. California Governor’s Oﬃce of
Emergency Services provides emergency response to hazardous materials incidents occurring in the
applicable planning area. Adherence to applicable regulations, including preparation of a HMBP,
would be required to reduce potential consequences of operational accidents involving hazardous
materials and the potential consequences of any such accidents. As discussed above, an HMBP would
be required by the City’s Standard Condition of Approval.
Compliance with applicable federal, state, and local requirements, and implementation of ﬁre
protection protocols, would result in a less than signiﬁcant hazard to the public through the
accidental release of hazardous materials associated with lithium-ion batteries during operation.
Operational impacts related to the release of hazardous materials speciﬁc to electric batteries would
be less than signiﬁcant.

hazardous materials or waste during operation. For this reason, and because there are no schools
within 0.25 mile of the project site, operation of the proposed project would not emit hazardous
emissions or handle hazardous or acutely hazardous materials, substances, or waste within 0.25 mile

improvements along University Avenue would potentially contribute to traﬃc during this phase of
construction, these actions would be temporary and would serve to improve circulation and safety
along this egress route.
While the new ferry terminal would not result in additional people living and working in the Berkeley
Waterfront, it would result in more people coming to the Berkeley Waterfront in order to access the
ferry or the recreational resources. If an emergency event, such as a tsunami, happened during a
peak period before people had embarked on the ferry, those people along with all other people in
the Berkeley Waterfront would need to evacuate the area, because the Waterfront is designated by
the California Geological Survey and California Governor’s Oﬃce of Emergency Services as a Tsunami
Inundation Zone. 49 The National Tsunami Warning Center monitors potential tsunami activity and
issues alerts to notify oﬃcials and the public about the potential for a tsunami using a tiered alerting
system with the highest level of alert being a warning. The most recent tsunami evacuation of the
Berkeley Waterfront occurred on December 5, 2024, following a magnitude 7.0 earthquake oﬀ the
coast of Mendocino, California.
In a report published February 20, 2025, the City of Berkeley provides an after-action review of its
response to the December 5, 2024, tsunami warning and summarizes community feedback to the
City’s response. The report emphasizes that the City’s emergency response protocols are developed
based on best practice guidance from the State of California and how these protocols were
operationalized during the tsunami warning to ensure safety of residents and property at the
Waterfront. 50 Upon receipt of the National Tsunami Warning Center warning notiﬁcation, County
and City staﬀ mobilized to evacuate Waterfront residents by activating its Emergency Operations
Center (EOC), which includes the Fire Department, Police Department, Department of Parks,
Recreation, and Waterfront, Department of Public Works, and the City Manager’s Oﬃce. The EOC
also coordinated with external agencies including the California Highway Patrol, AC Transit, Berkeley
Uniﬁed School District, American Red Cross, City of Albany, UC Berkeley, the Lawrence Berkeley
National Lab, and the Alameda County Sheriﬀ’s Oﬃce.
Alameda County and the City of Berkeley used the following tools to communicate with residents
about evacuation protocols:

In addition to the egress routes listed in the LHMP, the EOC coordination with the California Highway
Patrol and AC Transit facilitated a streamlined evacuation protocol by shutting down I-80 oﬀramps
into Berkeley and bringing additional buses to Marina areas to oﬀer residents near the tsunami
inundation zone with an alternate mode of evacuation. Traﬃc concerns were identiﬁed in the
December 2024 evacuation as background traﬃc continued to enter Berkeley. To address this, the
City updated its protocols to request immediate shutdown of I-80 oﬀramps into Berkeley at the
onset of a tsunami warning event and continues to coordinate with transportation partners to
further clarify protocols for tsunami evacuation support. 51
The LHMP identiﬁes that operation of the proposed project will enhance emergency access at the
Berkeley Waterfront, because the proposed project provides an alternative westward emergency
evacuation route in the event of an emergency closure of the surrounding roads. This is particularly
important in landside emergencies where eastward evacuation may be compromised.
Furthermore, as discussed in Chapter 2, Project Description, WETA has a legislative mandate to
operate and coordinate emergency water transit when regional transportation systems are
disrupted due to disaster or other events. Emergency operations may involve the rapid deployment
of survivors, ﬁrst responders, and disaster service personnel following a major emergency. In such
scenarios, WETA would oversee and operate water-based transportation routes linking ferry
terminals as part of a broader emergency transit network, facilitating access to care centers or base
camps. The transport of emergency personnel into aﬀected areas to deliver critical life-saving
services would likely require shuttle connections, as many of these individuals would be stationed at
base camps located away from the primary incident zones.

WETA ferry vessels have been deployed during emergencies in the past that disrupted other
transportation systems. Following the 1989 Loma Prieta Earthquake, which disabled the Bay Bridge
and BART Transbay Tube, ferry service operated overnight during inspections, and additional ferry
vessels were brought in from Catalina Island and Puget Sound to help support ferry service while the
Bay Bridge was repaired. In 2013, ferry ridership tripled as Bay Area residents used the ferry service
to commute throughout BART strikes and increased by 79 percent over a ﬁve day-long BART closure
in 2015. 52
Despite the pinch points described in the LHMP, construction and operation of the project would not
impair implementation of or physically interfere with an adopted emergency response or evacuation
plan. Instead, it would support emergency response capabilities by providing an alternative
evacuation route via water transit in scenarios where landside routes are constrained or
inaccessible, aligning with the City of Berkeley’s LHMP and WETA’s emergency operations mandate.
Therefore, this impact would be less than signiﬁcant.

and would involve the use of water for equipment cleaning and dust suppression. The use of water
in construction would assist in maintaining safe equipment use as well as managing vegetation
through soil moisture retention, which would reduce the likelihood of ignition in hot or dry
conditions. Therefore, impacts related to wildland ﬁre risk during construction would be less than
signiﬁcant.

3.7.5      Cumulative Impacts
The geographic scope of the cumulative hazards, hazardous materials, and wildﬁre analysis is the
vicinity of the project site. The cumulative analysis considers the nearby past, present, and
reasonably foreseeable future plans and projects listed in Table 3-1 (refer to Chapter 3,
Environmental Impact Analysis) located in Berkeley and surrounding areas in addition to the project
site.

Hazardous Materials Release and Exposure Risk
In general, exposure to hazardous materials can cause localized adverse eﬀects; however, a
combination of federal, state, and local regulations limit or minimize the potential for exposure to
hazardous materials. Cumulative plans and projects listed in Table 3-1 are primarily located within
the Berkeley Waterfront and Marina area and include infrastructure upgrades, recreational
improvements, and the maximum development potential associated with the Draft Waterfront
Speciﬁc Plan. Cumulative projects located in this vicinity would be subject to regulations for
development in the Berkeley EMAs, would not involve large quantities of hazardous materials or
activities that transport or handle hazardous materials, and would not be sited on known hazardous
materials sites. In addition, there are no hazardous materials sites or land uses at or in the vicinity of
the project site that are known to utilize large quantities of hazardous materials or involve hazardous
activities, and there are no schools proximate to the project site that could experience a cumulative
hazardous materials exposure. However, cumulative plans and projects may include demolition of
structures and infrastructure that have the potential to contain hazardous building materials such as
asbestos and lead-based paint. Any cumulative project involving such disturbance would be subject
to standard regulatory requirements, including hazardous building materials surveys and compliance
with applicable federal and State regulations for asbestos, lead-based paint, and other
contaminants, and all applicable environmental health and safety regulations, including those
enforced by DTSC, RWQCB, and the City of Berkeley. Therefore, cumulative development in
combination with implementation of the proposed project would result in a less than signiﬁcant
cumulative impact with respect to hazardous materials release and exposure risk would be less than
signiﬁcant.

Emergency Response and Evacuation Plans Consistency
The LHMP governs emergency response and evacuation planning at the Berkeley Waterfront and
Marina. Cumulative plans and projects listed in Table 3-1 are primarily located within the Berkeley
Waterfront and Marina area and include infrastructure upgrades, recreational improvements, and
the maximum development potential associated with the Draft Waterfront Speciﬁc Plan that in
combination with the proposed project would increase the number of visitors to the Berkeley
Waterfront. As discussed above under Impact HAZ-5, the project site is located along University
Avenue and adjacent to I-80, both of which serve as designated evacuation routes. The LHMP
identiﬁes that egress routes in the area are relatively constrained, particularly the segment of
University Avenue between Marina Boulevard and West Frontage Road, which serve as the only
eastward driving option out of the Berkeley Waterfront.
The project in combination with cumulative development would increase the number of visitors to
the area, which represents a potentially signiﬁcant cumulative impact related to evacuation
capabilities.

However, the project would not introduce new permanent residents or inhabitable structures.

Wildland Exposure and Exacerbation Risk
A combination of federal, state, and local regulations limits or minimize the potential for exposure to
wildﬁres by reducing the amount of development in wildland urban interface areas, ensuring new
development is developed according to California Building Code and California Fire Code, and
incorporating requirements for ﬁre-safe construction into land use planning.
As discussed above, the proposed project site is located at the Berkeley Waterfront, where the risk
of wildﬁre ignition and spread is relatively low due to its coastal setting and buﬀers of the San
Francisco Bay and I-80. Cumulative projects considered in this analysis (see Table 3-1) are primarily
located within the Berkeley Marina and Waterfront area, which is not within or adjacent to a
designated Very High Fire Hazard Severity Zone as mapped by CalFire. 55 These cumulative projects,
such as dock replacements, restroom and pathway improvements, park enhancements, and the
maximum development potential associated with the Draft Waterfront Speciﬁc Plan are located in
areas that are already developed and do not contain signiﬁcant levels of dry fuel or topographic
conditions conducive to wildland ﬁre spread. Cumulative plans and projects would be located in
areas that are already developed and do not contain signiﬁcant levels of dry fuel susceptible to
ignition. Cumulative project construction would adhere to respective city building codes designed to
minimize potential for uncontrolled ﬁres. Adherence to respective city building codes would ensure
that California Fire Code standards including automatic sprinkler systems are included in
development. Given the relatively low risk of wildland ﬁres, as well as compliance with existing
regulations by cumulative projects, cumulative projects in combination with implementation of the
proposed project would result in a less than signiﬁcant cumulative impact with respect to wildﬁre
exposure risk.

3.8            Hydrology and Water Quality
3.8.1          Introduction
This section describes the existing hydrology and water quality setting in the watershed and within
the project site and adjacent areas as well as the relevant regulatory framework. This section also
evaluates the potential impacts related to surface and groundwater quality, groundwater supplies
and recharge, erosion and siltation, flooding, pollutant discharge, and conflict with water quality
and groundwater plans that could result from implementation of the proposed project. The
information in this section is based, in part, on information from the San Francisco Bay Basin
Regional Water Quality Control Board (RWQCB) Water Quality Control Plan (Basin Plan), the San
Francisco Bay Region Municipal Stormwater National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System
(NPDES) Permit, the East Bay Plain Subbasin Groundwater Sustainability Plan (GSP), and the
Berkeley Municipal Code.

3.8.2          Environmental Setting
Surface Water Hydrology and Drainage

Definitions
Surface water “hydrology” refers to how water moves across the surface of land, whereas
“stormwater” refers to surface flows that occur in response to storm events. The project site is
located adjacent to and within the San Francisco Bay (the Bay). The San Francisco Bay Watershed
waterways, wetlands, and bays are located within the United States' fourth-largest metropolitan
region. The Bay functions as the main drainage outlet for waters of these metropolitan areas. 1

San Francisco Bay
The Bay is comprised of three distinct hydrographic areas: the South Bay, which extends from the
San Francisco Bay Bridge to the southern terminus of the San Francisco Bay in San Jose, the Central
Bay which extends from the San Francisco Bay Bridge north to the Richmond-San Rafael Bridge, and
the North Bay that connects the Delta and the Pacific Ocean. 2 The project site is located within the
Central Bay. Within the Central Bay, several subwatersheds 3 connect to and drain to the San
Francisco Bay. As shown in Figure 3.8-1, the area due east of the project site is within the
Strawberry Creek Subwatershed, which comprises the main branch and various tributaries that
drain the Berkeley hills. Stormwater management and stream channel culverting have altered
drainage paths throughout the Strawberry Creek Subwatershed. Strawberry Creek drains to the San
Francisco Bay through the eastern portion of the project site via the outlet shown in Figure 3.8-1.
The San Francisco Bay Watershed and Strawberry Creek Subwatershed are discussed below.

                                                                                                  Hydrology and Water Quality


The Central Bay is characterized by strong tidal exchange, persistent wind, and complex underwater
currents that routinely mobilize fine sediments and contribute to naturally elevated and highly
variable turbidity levels. The U.S. Geological Survey has a long-running water-quality monitoring
program in San Francisco Bay that tracks turbidity and suspended-sediment concentrations and
notes that tidal currents change direction four times daily and wind direction/intensity fluctuate on
a daily cycle, contributing to spatial and temporal variability in turbidity throughout the Bay. 4
External factors such as tidal currents, waves, and wind affect water quality alongside freshwater
and marine influences. These dynamic hydrodynamic conditions result in frequent resuspension of
bottom sediments from wind waves, vessel traffic, and tidal currents, such that background
turbidity levels are already influenced by ongoing natural and anthropogenic processes.

San Francisco Bay Watershed
The Bay encompasses approximately 1,600 square miles and is the largest estuary on the west coast
of the United States. The primary watershed in the San Francisco Bay Area is the San Francisco Bay
Watershed, a 4,600 square mile watershed that drains to the San Francisco Bay and encompasses all
or major portions of Alameda, Contra Costa, Marin, Napa, San Francisco, San Mateo, Santa Clara,
Solano, and Sonoma Counties. For regulatory purposes, the RWQCB designates hydrologic planning
areas. As designated by the RWQCB, the project site is located within the San Francisco Bay Central
Planning Area. 5
Multiple watersheds are tributary to the San Francisco Bay and convey water from the San Joaquin
and Sacramento rivers through the Sacramento-San Joaquin Bay Delta, the San Francisco Bay, and
into the Pacific Ocean. The watersheds that contribute surface flows to the San Francisco Bay,
including the Strawberry Creek Watershed, cover a total area of approximately 75,000 square miles,
including the San Francisco Bay Watershed. 6 The Sacramento and San Joaquin rivers, which enter
the San Francisco Bay system through the Delta at the eastern end of Suisun Bay, contribute almost
all the freshwater inflow to the San Francisco Bay. Suisun Bay is a shallow tidal estuary that lies at
the confluence of the Sacramento and San Joaquin Rivers. On its western end, Suisun Bay is drained
by the Carquinez Strait, which connects to San Pablo Bay located in the northern portion of the San
Francisco Bay. 7

Strawberry Creek Subwatershed
The project site is located just west of the Strawberry Creek Subwatershed, which is part of the
larger San Francisco Bay Watershed. The Strawberry Creek Subwatershed encompasses 3.0 square
miles, and flows through the City of Berkeley from Grizzly Peak in the Berkeley Hills down to the San
Francisco Bay. 8 The outfall of Strawberry Creek discharges into Central San Francisco Bay at the

eastern end of the project site, as shown in Figure 3.8-1. The Strawberry Creek Subwatershed
originates on the western slopes of the Berkeley Hills, where a series of small springs and
tributaries, including the prominent North Fork and Hamilton Gulch converge. These waters flow
through Strawberry Valley and onto the University of California, Berkeley (UC Berkeley) campus. The
North Fork merges with Strawberry Creek at the eucalyptus grove in the campus's center. From this
confluence, the creek enters a City culvert at Oxford Street and flows underground, except for a
daylighted segment through Strawberry Park, before continuing westward beneath Berkeley until
emptying into Central San Francisco Bay near University Avenue. 9

Project Site
As discussed previously, the project site is adjacent to and discharges to the Strawberry Creek
Watershed outfall. The Strawberry Creek discharge point is shown in Figure 3.8-1. The project site
lies entirely within the San Francisco Bay coastal zone, where hydrology is dominated by tidal action
rather than upland watershed runoff. The immediate water bodies influencing hydrology include
the Berkeley Marina Basin, open San Francisco Bay waters to the west and south, and the North and
South Sailing Basins within McLaughlin Eastshore State Park. Water elevations and movement in
these areas are controlled by twice-daily tidal cycles, wind-driven waves, and, during storm events,
additional inflows from upland storm drain systems.
Freshwater inputs to the site’s vicinity are minimal and primarily consist of urban stormwater
conveyed via storm drain infrastructure along University Avenue, Seawall Drive, and adjacent
parking lots. The surrounding shoreline is armored in many places with riprap, bulkheads, and
constructed marina facilities, which limit natural bank erosion and sediment transport but focus
flows toward existing outfall locations.
Within the project site and adjacent areas, surface water hydrology is defined by existing
development and stormwater management, which is provided through operation and maintenance
of the existing stormwater drainage system.
Impervious surfaces, including paved parking lots, roadways, sidewalks, and building roofs, produce
the majority of runoff. Stormwater generally flows via sheet flow from paved surfaces to curb inlets
connected to an underground storm drain network. These storm drains convey runoff to outfalls
discharging directly to adjacent Bay waters or marina basins. Landscaped areas (road medians, park
edges) provide limited infiltration capacity but are small in area compared to impervious cover. In
low-lying areas immediately adjacent to the shoreline, drainage may be influenced by tidal
backwater effects during high tides or storm surge events, temporarily slowing discharge from
outfalls. Internal pedestrian and bicycle pathways drain laterally toward adjacent landscaped swales
or storm drain inlets, ultimately connecting to the same bayfront outfall network. There are existing
stormwater management features throughout the project site, including but not limited to the
gutters, storm drains and pipelines, as well as vegetated swales and pervious areas built into the
existing development and maintained by the City of Berkeley’s Streets and Utilities Division.

Jurisdictional Features
Definitions
Jurisdictional features for the San Francisco Regional Water Quality Control Board primarily relate to
watersheds and "waters of the State" that include surface waters like rivers, lakes, streams, and
wetlands (as defined by State and federal law). Specific watershed and waters of the State
boundaries are defined by the California Porter-Cologne Water Quality Control Act and federal
Clean Water Act Section 401 and established by the State Water Board for purpose of water quality
protection across surface waters within respective hydrologic regions.

Overview
Berkeley is located within the hydrologic jurisdiction of the San Francisco Bay Basin (Region 2)
RWQCB, which manages beneficial uses 10 and quality objectives, as well as strategies for achieving
these objectives, in accordance with the Basin Plan for the San Francisco Bay Basin. 11 In addition,
the RWQCB administers the NPDES stormwater permitting program and regulates stormwater in
the San Francisco Bay Basin.

Project Site
