San Francisco Bay
CONTAMINANTS AND RUNOFF
The most recent San Francisco Estuary Institute (SFEI) Regional Monitoring Program (RMP) data
indicated top known contamination issues being faced in the San Francisco Bay waters include:
    Bacteria levels during and after storm events
    Nutrients, and resulting algal blooms and low oxygen levels
    Mercury and selenium
    Polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), dioxin, and furan compounds
    Emerging contaminants, including per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS)
    Plastics, including microplastics, bisphenols, and organophosphate esters, and trash

Many of these contaminants, nutrients, and waste reach the Bay via stormwater flows and runoff.
The RWQCB has adopted several Total Maximum Daily Loads (TMDLs) for the San Francisco Bay, and
tributaries to the San Francisco Bay, that are applicable to the Bay, including TMDLs for mercury,
PCBs, and diazinon and pesticide-related toxicity in urban creeks. 15 The City of Berkeley joined other
jurisdictions to form the Alameda Countywide Clean Water Program, referred to as the “Alameda
Permittees,” under the San Francisco Bay Region Municipal Stormwater NPDES Permit (Order No.
Order No. R2-2022-0018; NPDES No, CAS612008). 16 The City is tasked with implementing a
stormwater program to control stormwater flows and minimize related adverse water quality.

SEDIMENT
Bay sediment quality is a concern, because of the influence the sediment quality can have on the
quality of overlying waters. Bay sediment can be a source of and sink for pollutants and trace
compounds. Resuspension of sediments can remobilize particulate-bound pollutants into Bay
waters. Waste generated from the disturbance of soil at these locations may cause water quality
concerns, as discussed in Section 3.7, Hazards and Hazardous Materials.

TIDES AND CURRENTS 17
The Bay is characterized by a mixed semi-diurnal tidal pattern, wherein two high and two low tides
occur within a 24-hour period. Tidal currents in the San Francisco Bay are driven primarily by the
interaction of oceanic tides and freshwater inflows from the Sacramento and San Joaquin Rivers.
These currents can reach high velocities, particularly in the narrow entrance at the Golden Gate.
Water levels throughout the San Francisco Bay, including the project site, can fluctuate by 2 meters
from mean sea level. The tidal influence extends throughout the San Francisco Bay, with stronger
currents near the mouth and progressively weaker flows further inland. Currents play a critical role
in sediment transport, salinity distribution, and nutrient mixing across the San Francisco Bay.

SEDIMENT
Based on historical records, land within the project site, south of University Avenue was once open
water, and has since been filled with fill materials and soil of unknown origin. The land was built up
from at least the 1950s through the 1980s, and the artificial fill materials/soil likely remains within
the project site and adjacent land. Twenty-three feet of artificial fill exists at the Marina. Young Bay
Mud (YBM) and recent deposits are soft, easily disturbed, and contain shells/organics—sediments
that could be resuspended during in-water work. 18 Artificial fill is considered heterogeneous,
contains debris, and placed without engineered compaction. Potential for legacy contaminants in fill
and bay sediments is implied in material descriptions.
In 2025, sediment sampling and analysis was conducted within five dredge units in the project
vicinity in accordance with the Inland Testing Manual, 19 site-specific requirements for proposed
reuse sites, and United States Army Corps of Engineers Dredged Material Management Office
protocols. 20 Sediment samples obtained in this analysis were found to contain metals,
organochlorine pesticides, polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons, PCBs, and dioxins/furans. However,
concentrations of these contaminants did not exceed State or Federal hazardous waste criteria.
Although contaminants were present, the concentrations of such contaminants indicate that
sediments are not likely to pose significant hazards if managed according to reuse site
requirements.

TIDE AND CURRENTS
The Berkeley Waterfront experiences mixed semidiurnal tides, with water levels ranging from
approximately +6.8 feet mean lower-low water (MLLW) during average higher-high tide conditions
to about +10.3 feet MLLW under 100-year extreme tide events. The design still water level, which
accounts for astronomical tides, storm surge, and projected sea level rise through 2075, is estimated
at +11.9 feet MLLW. Currents at the site are generally mild with surface velocities averaging
approximately 1 knot, primarily driven by tidal exchange rather than persistent wind force. Winds in
the region vary seasonally. During autumn and winter months, winds are milder and vary
directionally. In spring and summer months, prevailing winds follow a south-southwest pattern and
intensify, frequently exceeding 12 knots. By comparison, exposed areas such as San Francisco can

Groundwater Levels
Definitions
A groundwater basin is an underground area where water is naturally stored and then slowly moves
through layers of soil, sand, and gravel (called aquifers). Groundwater basins provide a buffer during
droughts by storing water that replenishes aquifers via permeable materials capable of both holding
and yielding groundwater. Groundwater basins are managed to ensure sustainable water supply for
communities, businesses, and agriculture.
Santa Clara Valley – East Bay Plain Groundwater Subbasin
The East Bay Plain Subbasin exists within the Santa Clara Groundwater Basin and covers 77,800
acres in Alameda County, and is managed by the East Bay Municipal Utility District Groundwater
Sustainability Agency (GSA) and City of Hayward GSA. 22 The Subbasin extends across multiple
jurisdictions, including all or portions of the Cities of Alameda, Albany, Berkeley, El Cerrito,
Emeryville, Hayward, Oakland, Piedmont, Richmond, San Leandro, and San Pablo.
The East Bay Plain Subbasin deep aquifer was a key water source for the region from the 1800s
through the 1920s, including for industrial areas. By the early 20th century, substantial agricultural
development had occurred in the southern portion of the groundwater basin. Since then, the area
has undergone extensive urbanization, and East Bay Municipal Utility District has imported surface
water to supplement water supplies in the area, now characterized by industrial, commercial, and
residential land uses. 23
Groundwater pumping in the East Bay Plain Subbasin has decreased over time, groundwater levels
are considered stable, and groundwater in the Subbasin is considered sustainable. There are three
major aquifer zones within the Subbasin: the Shallow Aquifer Zone, Intermediate Aquifer Zone, and
Deep Aquifer Zone (within the southern half of the Subbasin only, outside the project site). Most of
the yielding production wells have been constructed within the Deep Aquifer Zone and within the
lower portion of the Intermediate Aquifer Zone in the southern portion of the Subbasin. The
Shallow Aquifer Zone and upper to middle portions of the Intermediate Aquifer Zone have geologic
conditions that typically lead to lower yielding wells. 24 The GSAs are not aware of any customers
who solely depend on groundwater for a drinking water supply. 25 No sole source aquifers exist in
the region. 26

Project Site
As shown in Figure 3.8-2, the eastern portion of the project site is located within the northwestern
portion of the East Bay Plain Subbasin of the Santa Clara Valley Groundwater Basin. Depth to
groundwater at the project site is between 5 and 13.4 feet, depending on exact location and
elevation. Fluctuations in the level of groundwater occur as a result of variations in rainfall,
irrigation practice, tidal influences, and other variables. Perched groundwater can also result in
locally shallower groundwater conditions. 27

Groundwater Quality

East Bay Plain Subbasin
Overall groundwater quality in the intermediate aquifer of the East Bay Plain Subbasin is considered
of good quality, with contamination of total dissolved solids, chloride, nitrate, arsenic and
manganese limited to the shallow aquifer. 28 Major constituents in the Subbasin are as follows:
    Total Dissolved Solids: Total dissolved solids have secondary MCLs of 500 mg/L (recommended)
     and 1,000 mg/L (maximum). In the Subbasin, average concentrations are generally less than
     1,000 mg/L, except in localized areas near the San Francisco Bay (primarily in the Shallow
     Aquifer Zone).
    Chloride: Chloride has secondary MCLs of 250 mg/L (recommended) and 500 mg/L (maximum).
     The distribution of chloride concentrations, potentially serving as an indicator for seawater
     intrusion, generally have concentrations less than 500 mg/L, except near the San Francisco Bay
     in the Shallow Aquifer Zone.
    Nitrate: Available data for wells in the Intermediate and Deep Aquifer Zones suggest that nitrate
     levels are below the primary Maximum Contaminant Level (MCL) of 10 mg/L for nitrate.
    Arsenic: Most wells with data have arsenic concentrations below the arsenic primary MCL of 10
     ug/L; however, there are one or more wells in each depth zone with an average arsenic
     concentration above the MCL.

Flood Hazard Areas

Definitions and Events
The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) National Flood Hazard Layer is a geospatial
database that contains current effective flood hazard data. Special Flood Hazard Areas are defined
to show the extent of flood waters that would occur in response to the magnitude flood that has a
one percent chance of occurring in any given year; this is also commonly referred to as the 100-year
floodplain or 100-year Flood Hazard Area. FEMA has produced Flood Insurance Rate Maps (FIRMs)
covering Alameda County, which define the 100-year Flood Hazard Areas for insurance purposes,
and to guide land use planning to consider public and property safety as related to the potential for
damage from flood events.
Urban flooding can occur when storm-drains and small channels become obstructed or
overwhelmed during intense, short-duration rainfall events. In addition, tsunamis and seiches are
two types of water waves that are generated by earthquake events. Tsunamis are broad-wavelength
ocean waves, and seiches are standing waves within confined bodies of water, typically reservoirs.
Furthermore, the Department of Water Resources Division of Safety of Dams regulates dam safety
and evaluates risks associated with potential for inundation resulting from dam failure.

3.8.3      Regulatory Framework
Federal Regulations

Clean Water Act
The Federal Water Pollution Prevention and Control Act of 1948 was the first major law to address
water pollution in the United States. In 1972, the Federal Water Pollution Control Act was amended
and became known as the Clean Water Act. The Clean Water Act established the basic structure for
regulating discharges of pollutants into the waters of the United States with the intent “to restore
and maintain the chemical, physical, and biological integrity of the Nation's waters.” The Clean
Water Act gave the EPA the authority to implement federal pollution control programs, such as
setting water quality standards for contaminants in surface water, establishing wastewater and
effluent discharge limits for various industry contaminants in surface water, establishing wastewater
and effluent discharge limits for various industry categories, and imposing requirements for
controlling nonpoint-source pollution. At the federal level, the Clean Water Act is administered by
the EPA and United States Army Corps of Engineers (USACE).
The federal Clean Water Act places the primary responsibility for the control of water pollution and
for the planning of development and use of water resources with the states, although it does
establish certain guidelines for the states to follow in developing their programs. At the state and
regional levels in California, the Clean Water Act is enforced by the State Water Resources Control
Board (SWRCB) and the nine RWQCBs.

SECTION 303—WATER QUALITY STANDARDS AND TOTAL MAXIMUM DAILY LOADS (TMDLS)
Section 303(c)(2)(b) of the Clean Water Act (CWA) requires states to adopt water quality standards
for all surface waters of the United States based on the water body’s designated beneficial use.
Where multiple uses exist, water quality standards must protect the most sensitive use. Water
quality standards are typically numeric, although narrative criteria based on biomonitoring methods
may be employed where numerical standards cannot be established or where they are needed to
supplement numerical standards.
CWA Section 303(d) requires states to develop a list of water quality impaired segments of
waterways. The list includes waters that do not meet water quality standards necessary to support a
waterway’s beneficial uses even after the minimum required levels of pollution control technology
have been installed. Listed water bodies are to be priority ranked for development of a TMDL. A
TMDL is a calculation of the total maximum daily load (amount) of a pollutant that a water body can
receive on a daily basis and still safely meet water quality standards. The TMDLs include waste load
allocations for urban stormwater runoff as well as municipal and industrial wastewater discharges,
with allocations apportioned for individual Municipal Separate Storm Sewer Systems (MS4s) and
wastewater treatment plants. For stormwater, load reductions would be required to meet the TMDL
waste load allocations within the 20 years required by the TMDLs.
The EPA, SWRCB, and RWQCBs are responsible for establishing TMDL waste load allocations and
incorporating approved TMDLs into water quality control plans, NPDES permits, and Waste
Discharge Requirements in accordance with a specified schedule for completion. The San Francisco
Bay RWQCB adopted TMDLs that apply to the City of Berkeley through the Alameda Countywide
Clean Water Program.




3.8-14
                                                                        Environmental Impact Analysis
                                                                         Hydrology and Water Quality

SECTION 401—WATER QUALITY CERTIFICATION
Section 401 of the Clean Water Act regulates discharges of fill and dredged material to waters of the
United States. Under Section 401, the SWRCB and RWQCBs have regulatory authority over actions in
waters of the United States through the issuance of water quality certifications, which are issued in
conjunction with any federal permit (e.g., permits issued by the USACE under Section 404 of the
Clean Water Act, described below). Section 401 provides the SWRCB and the RWQCBs with the
regulatory authority to waive, certify, or deny any proposed activity that could result in a discharge
to surface waters of the State. To waive or certify an activity, these agencies must find the proposed
discharge would comply with State water quality standards, including those protecting beneficial
uses and water quality. If these agencies deny the proposed activity, the federal permit cannot be
issued.

SECTION 402—NATIONAL POLLUTION DISCHARGE ELIMINATION SYSTEM PERMIT
Section 402 of the Clean Water Act establishes the NPDES regulations for stormwater and other
pollutant discharges. Section 402 prohibits discharge of pollutants to waters of the United States
unless they are regulated by an NPDES permit. Stormwater discharges are regulated under a variety
of NPDES permits, including municipal, agricultural, industrial, construction, and low-threat
discharge permits. In 1987, Congress amended the Clean Water Act to require the implementation
of a two-phased program to address stormwater discharges. Phase I of the NPDES program,
promulgated by the USEPA in November 1990, requires NPDES permits for stormwater discharges
from MS4s serving populations of 100,000 or greater, construction sites disturbing greater than five
acres of land, and 10 categories of industrial activities.
The USEPA recognized that smaller construction projects (disturbing less than five acres) and small
MS4s (serving populations smaller than 100,000) were also contributing substantially to pollutant
discharges nationwide. Therefore, in order to further improve stormwater quality, the USEPA
promulgated the NPDES Phase II program in January 2000, which requires NPDES permits for
stormwater discharges from regulated small MS4s and for construction sites disturbing between
one and five acres of land. In California, the NPDES program is administered by SWRCB through the
nine RWQCBs. Further discussion of the NPDES program and permits in California relevant to the
project are provided in discussion of state and local regulations, below.

SECTION 404- DISCHARGE OF DREDGE OR FILL
Section 404 of the Clean Water Act requires a permit be issued by USACE before dredged or fill
material may be discharged into waters of the United States, unless the activity is exempt from
Section 404 regulations (e.g. farming activities, maintenance activities, construction of temporary
sedimentation basins, construction and maintenance of forest roads or temporary mining roads).
Waters of the United States generally include tidal waters, lakes, ponds, rivers, streams (including
intermittent streams), and wetlands (with the exception of isolated wetlands).

National Flood Insurance Program
FEMA oversees floodplains and administers the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) under the
National Flood Insurance Act of 1968. The NFIP makes federally subsidized flood insurance available
to property owners within communities who participate in the program. FEMA defines areas of
special flood hazard, or “Flood Hazard Areas,” as those areas that are subject to inundation by a
100-year flood event, or the magnitude flood with a one percent chance to occur in any given year.
Flood Hazard Areas are defined on regulatory flood maps titled Flood Insurance Rate Maps (FIRMs).


Draft Environmental Impact Report                                                                3.8-15
City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project

The NFIP mandates that development cannot occur within a Flood Hazard Area if it would result in
more than a one-foot increase in flood elevation. In addition, development is not allowed in
delineated floodways within the regulatory floodplain. Local agencies are responsible for
administering their community’s floodplain management regulations. The Alameda Flood Control &
Water Conservation District manages local storm drain facilities and is responsible for regional flood
control planning within Berkeley, California.

State Regulations

Porter-Cologne Water Quality Control Act
California’s primary statute governing water quality and water pollution is the Porter-Cologne Water
Quality Control Act of 1970 (Porter-Cologne Act). The Porter-Cologne Act grants the SWRCB and
nine RWQCBs broad powers to protect water quality and is the primary vehicle for the
implementation of the Clean Water Act in California. The Porter-Cologne Act grants the SWRCB and
RWQCBs the authority and responsibility to adopt plans and policies, regulate discharges to surface
water and groundwater, regulate waste disposal sites, and require cleanup of discharges of
hazardous materials and other pollutants. The Porter-Cologne Act also establishes reporting
requirements for unintended discharges of any hazardous substance, sewage, oil, or petroleum
product. Each RWQCB must adopt and implement a Water Quality Control Plan (Basin Plan) for its
region in conformance with the policies set forth in the Porter-Cologne Act.

California Toxics Rule and State Implementation Policy
The California Toxics Rule, adopted in 2000, established numeric water quality criteria for
approximately 130 priority pollutant trace metals and organic compounds. The California Toxics
Rule criteria are regulatory criteria adopted for inland surface waters, enclosed bays, and estuaries
in California that are on the CWA Section 303(c) list for contaminants. The California Toxics Rule
includes criteria for the protection of aquatic life and human health. Human health criteria (water-
and organism-based) apply to all waters with a Municipal and Domestic Water Supply beneficial use
designation as indicated in the Basin Plans. The Policy for Implementation of Toxics Standards for
Inland Surface Waters, Enclosed Bays, and Estuaries of California, also known as the State
Implementation Policy, was adopted by the SWRCB in 2000. It establishes provisions for translating
the California Toxics Rule criteria, National Toxics Rule criteria, and Basin Plan water quality
objectives for toxic pollutants into:
   NPDES permit effluent limits;
   Effluent compliance determinations;
   Monitoring for 2,3,7,8-tcdd (dioxin) and its toxic equivalents;
   Chronic (long-term) toxicity control provisions;
   Site-specific water quality objectives; and
   Granting of effluent compliance exceptions.

The goal of the State Implementation Plan is to establish a standardized approach for permitting
discharges of toxic effluent to inland surface waters, enclosed bays, and estuaries.




3.8-16
                                                                                                Environmental Impact Analysis
                                                                                                 Hydrology and Water Quality

Antidegradation Policy
The State Antidegradation Policy (Resolution No. 68-16) was adopted by SWRCB in 1968 to protect
surface water and groundwater from degradation. The Antidegradation Policy applies to the
disposal of waste to high-quality surface water and groundwater. The Antidegradation Policy
requires the water quality of these water bodies to be maintained unless SWRCB finds the change
will be consistent with maximum benefit to the people of the state, will not unreasonably affect
present and anticipated beneficial uses of the waters, and will not result in water quality less than
that prescribed in policies regulating water quality. The Antidegradation Policy also requires the
best practicable treatment or control of discharges to high-quality waters to assure pollution or
nuisance will not occur and the highest possible water quality will be maintained.

Construction Stormwater General Permit
The California Construction Stormwater Permit (Order WQ 2022-0057-DWQ; NPDES No.
CAS000002) regulates construction activities that disturb at least one acre of land, authorizing
stormwater discharges to surface waters while prohibiting non-stormwater discharges and
hazardous substances above regulatory limits. Project proponents must complete a risk assessment,
eliminate or reduce non-stormwater discharges, and develop a Stormwater Pollution Prevention
Plan (SWPPP) detailing Best Management Practices (BMPs) to minimize pollution. To obtain
coverage under the NPDES permit, project proponents must electronically file permit registration
documents, including a Notice of Intent, risk assessment, site map, SWPPP, and fee, with the SWRCB
before construction begins. The SWPPP must include erosion control measures, sediment control,
pollutant management, and post-construction runoff management, along with a program for BMP
inspection and maintenance.
Attachment J establishes specific requirements for construction dewatering discharges, including
authorization for pumping or siphoning groundwater or stormwater from excavations and
foundations; compliance with receiving water limitations; monitoring for pH (6.5–8.5) and turbidity
(≤250 Nephelometric Turbidity Unit) during discharges; and the ability to halt dewatering if numeric
action levels are exceeded. The Construction Stormwater General Permit also requires notification
to the Regional Water Board prior to dewatering, incorporation of BMPs to minimize pollutant
mobilization, and timely SWPPP updates. 33

California Sustainable Groundwater Management Act
The Sustainable Groundwater Management Act (SGMA), enacted in September 2014, establishes a
framework for sustainable management of California's groundwater over a 50-year planning
horizon, ensuring groundwater use without causing undesirable results. SGMA requires the creation
of Groundwater Sustainability Agencies (GSAs) by local agencies to oversee designated groundwater
basins or subbasins. High and medium priority basins must develop Groundwater Sustainability
Plans (GSPs), with the Department of Water Resources providing regulations for evaluating these
plans and reviewing compliance every five years. The East Bay Plain Subbasin, which underlies the
project area is designated by California Department of Water Resources as Medium Priority. 34 The
East Bay Municipal Utilities District and City of Hayward are the water providers that lie atop the
East Bay Plain Subbasin and serve as the GSA for the subbasin.

Regional and Local Regulations

RWQCB Water Quality Control Plan (Basin Plan)
The Basin Plan, developed by the RWQCB, delineates beneficial uses of surface waters,
groundwaters, wetlands, and estuaries within the region, including drinking water supply, aquatic
life habitat, and recreational activities. To maintain these uses, the plan establishes specific water
quality objectives, which include limits on pollutants such as nutrients, heavy metals, and organic
chemicals, as well as physical parameters like temperature and turbidity. The Basin Plan integrates
TMDLs for various pollutants, addressing sources such as urban runoff, agricultural activities, and
industrial discharges. It also establishes implementation programs that include permitting
processes, enforcement mechanisms, and guidelines for monitoring and assessment to ensure
compliance with state and federal water quality standards. Additionally, the plan incorporates
strategies for managing non-point source pollution, controlling stormwater runoff, and restoring
impaired water bodies.
As designated in the Basin Plan, the existing beneficial uses for the Central San Francisco Bay are
industrial service supply (IND), industrial process supply (PROC), commercial and sport fishing
(COMM), shell fish harvesting (SHELL), estuarine habitat (EST), fish migration (MIGR), preservation
of rare and endangered species (RARE), fish spawning (SPWN), wildlife habitat (WILD), water
contract recreation (REC-1), non-contact water recreation (REC-2), and navigation (NAV). Beneficial
uses of Strawberry Creek include warm freshwater habitat (WARM), wildlife habitat (WILD), water
contract recreation (REC-1), non-contact water recreation (REC-2). The existing beneficial uses for
the East Bay Plain Subbasin are Municipal and domestic water supply (MUN), industrial service
supply (IND), industrial process supply (PROC), and agricultural water supply (AGR). 36
Water quality objectives for surface and ground waters relevant to the proposed project and project
area, which include the enclosed San Francisco Bay, include those listed in Table 3.8-1 and

Alameda Countywide Clean Water Program
The Alameda Countywide Clean Water Program (ACCWP) is a joint initiative of 17 local agencies—
including Alameda County, its 14 cities, the Alameda County Flood Control and Water Conservation
District, and Zone 7 Water Agency—working together to reduce stormwater pollution and protect
the region’s creeks, wetlands, and the San Francisco Bay. The program was established to support
compliance with the federal Clean Water Act and NPDES stormwater permit issued by the San
Francisco Bay Regional Water Quality Control Board. 39
ACCWP focuses on a range of activities including public education, pollution prevention, municipal
operations support, construction site oversight, and water quality monitoring. The program
promotes Low Impact Development (LID) strategies, supports green infrastructure planning, and
engages residents and businesses to prevent pollutants like trash, oil, pesticides, and heavy metals
from entering storm drains.

Regional Shoreline Adaptation Plan
The Regional Shoreline Adaptation Plan (RSAP) was prepared pursuant to Senate Bill 272 (SB 272),
which directed the San Francisco Bay Conservation and Development Commission (BCDC) to
develop guidelines for local governments to use in addressing the anticipated impacts of sea level
rise along the San Francisco Bay shoreline. The RSAP establishes a coordinated framework to guide
adaptation actions that support the long-term resilience of Bay Area communities, infrastructure,
and ecosystems in the face of rising sea levels. The RSAP was adopted by the BCDC Commission in
December 2024. 40

McAteer-Petris Act
The McAteer-Petris Act (Public Resources Code 66600 et seq.) is implemented by the San Francisco
Bay Conservation and Development Commission (BCDC). This act directs BCDC to exercise its
authority to issue or deny permit applications for placing fill, extracting minerals, or changing the
use of any land, water, or structure within the area of its jurisdiction (the Bay waters and a 100-foot-
wide shoreline band inland from the high tide line). The BCDC also carries out determinations of
consistency with the Federal Coastal Zone Protection Act for federally sponsored projects.

San Francisco Bay Region Municipal Regional Stormwater NPDES Permit
The San Francisco Bay Region Municipal Regional Stormwater NPDES Permit (Municipal Regional
Stormwater Permit; Order No. R2-2022-0018; NPDES No, CAS612008) is issued by the San Francisco
RWQCB for the San Francisco Bay Region. 41 Its purpose is to establish waste discharge requirements
and permit conditions for the discharge of stormwater runoff from municipal separate storm sewer
systems (MS4s) operated by various cities and counties in the San Francisco Bay region. The City of
Berkeley, in partnership with other municipal governments in Alameda County, is a participant in
the Alameda Countywide Clean Water Program, collectively referred to as the “Alameda
Permittees.” 42 The Alameda Permittees submitted a joint application to continue adhering to waste
discharge requirements under their NPDES permit to discharge from storm drains and watercourses
within the Alameda Permittee jurisdictions. The permit aims to regulate stormwater discharges to
protect water quality, comply with the Clean Water Act, and address pollutants such as mercury,
PCBs, pesticides, trash, and other contaminants that could harm the San Francisco Bay and
surrounding water bodies. 43
Provision C.3 of the Municipal Regional Stormwater NPDES Permit requires that new development
and significant redevelopment project include appropriate source control, site design, and
stormwater treatment measures to address stormwater runoff pollutant discharges and prevent
runoff flows from new development and redevelopment projects. LID methods are to be the
primary mechanism for achieving such aims.
Permit Provision C.3 b.ii designates that uncovered parking lots that create or replace 5,000 square
feet or more of impervious surface are a regulated project under the permit. Various exceptions
exist for certain practices, which include overlaying existing concrete or asphalt with new material
to a shallow depth, without expanding the area of coverage.

Municipal Regional Stormwater Permit Technical Guidance Manual
The Technical Guidance Manual for Alameda County provides detailed instructions and standards
for the implementation of stormwater management practices required to comply with the
Municipal Regional Stormwater NPDES Permit. The manual's primary purpose is to guide
municipalities, developers, engineers, and planners in designing, constructing, and maintaining
stormwater control measures that comply with the stringent water quality standards set by the

Municipal Regional Stormwater NPDES Permit. The manual covers design and sizing of LID features
like bioretention systems, permeable pavements, and green roofs, which are essential for
minimizing the volume and improving the quality of stormwater runoff. It also provides detailed
guidance on hydromodification management, which involves controlling the flow and volume of
runoff to prevent erosion and protect stream channels. The manual also serves as a key reference
for compliance documentation, helping municipalities and developers demonstrate that their
projects meet the regulatory requirements of the Municipal Regional Stormwater NPDES Permit.

2023 Manual for the San Francisco Bay Area Hydrology Model (BAHM)
The BAHM Manual provides a framework for simulating and managing stormwater runoff in urban
and suburban areas within the San Francisco Bay Area. This tool is designed to support compliance
with the Municipal Regional Permit by helping engineers, planners, and developers design
stormwater management systems that effectively mimic natural hydrology. The manual covers the
model's application for sizing detention and retention facilities, such as bioretention cells and
infiltration basins, to control peak flows and maintain pre-development hydrologic conditions. It
includes updated methodologies for hydrologic analysis, including rainfall-runoff modeling, flow
duration analysis, and the assessment of hydromodification impacts on local streams. The 2023
edition also incorporates new climate data and improved algorithms to enhance the accuracy of
predictions, addressing challenges such as increased storm intensity and variability due to climate
change.

San Francisco Bay Plan
The San Francisco Bay Plan is the guiding policy document for the BCDC codified by the McAteer-
Petris Act. The plan includes policies to ensure water quality in San Francisco Bay is maintained at
levels sufficient for the protection and beneficial use of San Francisco Bay. For additional
information about pertinent policies, please refer to Section 3.9, Land Use and Planning.

East Bay Plain Subbasin Groundwater Sustainability Plan
The East Bay Plain Subbasin GSP was prepared by the East Bay Municipal Utility District GSA and City
of Hayward GSA. The GSP is a comprehensive framework designed to ensure the long-term
sustainability of groundwater resources in the East Bay Plain Subbasin, which underlies portions of
Alameda and Contra Costa Counties. The GSP includes strategies to balance groundwater extraction
with natural recharge, prevent seawater intrusion, and protect water quality, adhering to the
requirements of the SGMA. The plan includes detailed hydrogeological assessments, water budget
analyses, and monitoring protocols to track groundwater levels, subsidence, and water quality. It
also identifies management actions, such as demand management, artificial recharge projects, and
regulatory measures, to mitigate overdraft and maintain a sustainable yield that supports both
current and future water demands while safeguarding the ecological and economic health of the
region. 44

boards, and commissions on land use changes, funding allocations, and development regulations.

priority issue areas. The Plan's policies apply to all properties within Berkeley's city limits, both

3.8.4      Impacts Analysis
Significance Criteria
The City of Berkeley utilizes the following 2025 CEQA Guidelines Appendix G significance criteria
questions related to hydrology and water quality.
Would the proposed project:
a) Violate any water quality standards or waste discharge requirements or otherwise substantially
   degrade surface or ground water quality?
b) Substantially decrease groundwater supplies or interfere substantially with groundwater
   recharge such that the project may impede sustainable groundwater management of the basin?
c) Substantially alter the existing drainage pattern of the site or area, including through the
   alteration of the course of a stream or river or through the addition of impervious surfaces, in a
   manner which would:
   i. result in a substantial erosion or siltation on- or off-site?
   ii. substantially increase the rate or amount of surface runoff in a manner which would result
        in flooding on- or offsite?
   iii. create or contribute runoff water which would exceed the capacity of existing or planned
        stormwater drainage systems or provide substantial additional sources of polluted runoff?
   iv. impede or redirect flood flows?

d) In flood hazard, tsunami, or seiche zones, risk release of pollutants due to project inundation?
e) Conflict with or obstruct implementation of a water quality control plan or sustainable
   groundwater management plan?

Approach to Analysis

Hydrology and Water Quality
Impacts related to hydrology and water quality were determined by comparing the activities and
future built conditions that would be facilitated by the proposed project to the existing (baseline)
environmental conditions for hydrology and water quality, as characterized above in Section 3.8.2,
Environmental Setting. Impact characterizations were informed through review of information
regarding regional and local surface water, groundwater, and flooding conditions contained in
available sources of information, including but not limited to the San Francisco Bay RWQCB Basin
Plan, East Bay Plain Subbasin Groundwater GSP, and FEMA FIRMs, as well as site-specific and plan-
specific features.



Draft Environmental Impact Report                                                               3.8-25
City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project

The impact evaluation focuses on effects on surface and groundwater quality, groundwater supply
and drainage (erosion, siltation, flooding, stormwater system exceedance, polluted runoff), and
flooding (flood flows and release of pollutants due to inundation). Water quality impacts were
assessed based on water quality standards, existing impairments, potential contaminants generated
by the project, and stormwater treatment requirements. Project impacts to hydrology and water
quality are evaluated based on the project’s adherence to local, state, and federal standards; the
nature of proposed soil disturbance, construction activities, and groundwater dewatering during
construction; the change in land use and proposed operational activities; changes in pre- and post-
project stormwater flows; changes in impervious surfaces, and proposed operational BMPs for
control of surface runoff and reduction of pollutants in stormwater runoff.
San Francisco Bay is impaired for chlordane, Dichloro-Diphenyl-Trichloroethane (DDT), dieldrin,
dioxin compounds, furan compounds, invasive species, mercury, PCBs, selenium, and trash and
Strawberry Creek is impaired for trash. Impacts related to invasive species are discussed in Section
3.3, Biological Resources, and is not discussed further in this section. The use of pesticides
containing chlordane, DDT, and dieldrin are banned in the United States. The proposed project
would not involve use of these chemicals, and testing of sediment in San Francisco Bay did not
detect these chemicals in high concentrations. 46 Therefore, the analysis focuses on the project’s
potential to contribute to the existing mercury, PCB, selenium, dioxins, furans, and trash
impairments.
Depth to groundwater and the need for groundwater extraction during construction and operation
was assessed to determine potential groundwater impacts. Inundation and flooding are assessed by
reviewing potential inundation zone maps and data relative to structures that would be constructed
as part of the proposed project.
Topics not covered in the following impact analysis include water supply availability and adequacy
of wastewater conveyance and treatment infrastructure, which are discussed in Section 3.14,
Utilities and Service Systems. In addition, impacts related to wetlands and waters of the United
States are discussed in Section 3.3, Biological Resources.

EIR Scoping Comments Consideration
This section addresses comments received in response to the EIR NOP related to various concerns
regarding hydrology and water quality.
Scoping comments included comments related to groundwater dynamics, water quality, sediment
control, flooding, stormwater catchment, and sea level rise. Water quality regulations including the

Specific Thresholds of Significance
For purposes of the following impact analysis, the following thresholds are used to evaluate the
significance of hydrology and water quality impacts resulting from implementation of the proposed
project.
   Violate any surface water or groundwater quality standards or waste discharge requirements, or
    conflict with the San Francisco Bay Basin Plan, in a way that would:
     Result in an exceedance of a water quality objective, specified in the Basin Plan and shown
        in Table 3.8-1 or Table 3.8-2, in a manner that would impair beneficial uses; or
     Discharge a pollutant that the water body (i.e., San Francisco Bay) is listed as impaired with
        on the 303(d) list (see Surface Water Quality subsection in Section 3.8.2, Environmental
        Setting).

   Interfere with implementation of the East Bay Plain Subbasin GSP, or deplete groundwater
    supplies or recharge, or conflict with the Subbasin GSP in a way that would obstruct sustainable
    management of groundwater.
   Alter an existing drainage pattern through alteration of the course of Strawberry Creek or
    increased impervious surfaces and resulting in on-site or off-site:
     Erosion;
     Siltation; or
     Flooding.

   Create or contribute new runoff water that would exceed the capacity of existing or planned
    stormwater management infrastructure.
   Interfere with floodplain management in a way that would reduce coastal resilience to flooding
    related to storm surge and/or sea level rise.
   Release pollutants due to project inundation associated with flood hazard, tsunami, or seiche.

Construction

LANDSIDE CONSTRUCTION SURFACE WATER QUALITY
Construction activities associated with the project — such as pavement removal, demolition,
grading and excavation, filling and compaction, and construction of project elements including



Draft Environmental Impact Report                                                                3.8-27
City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project

utility upgrades and parking lot or pathway modifications — have the potential to degrade water
quality by disturbing soil and increasing spill risk and trash generation. During periods of heavy rain
or high winds, disturbance of soils from excavation, grading, or other construction activities,
including those within designated staging areas, could elevate the risk of erosion and sediment
transport. Stormwater runoff or wind could convey exposed or eroded sediments into the storm
drain system or directly into San Francisco Bay. Sedimentation in receiving waters can impair water
quality by reducing light penetration, interfering with photosynthesis and oxygen exchange, and
disrupting the respiration, growth, and reproduction of aquatic organisms. Sediments may also
serve as a transport medium for other pollutants, including nutrients, trace metals, and
hydrocarbons, which could contribute to additional degradation of water quality. Trash generated
during construction could contribute to the existing trash impairments in San Francisco Bay and
Strawberry Creek. Impacts on Strawberry Creek culvert and outfall would be avoided to the extent
practicable, given that work in this area would be limited to the undergrounding of an electrical
conduit.
As discussed in Section 3.7, Hazards and Hazardous Materials, in the discussion labeled Soil
Contaminants at the Project Site, elevated concentrations of aerially-deposited lead may be present
along existing roadways, including those near the eastern portion of the project site, near I-80. Soil
along the eastern boundary of the project site may contain concentrations of lead exceeding state
regulatory thresholds, and any waste generated from the disturbance of soil in these locations may
be regulated as a non-hazardous or hazardous waste. Disturbance of these soils could transport lead
to receiving waters.
In addition to pollutant contributions from disturbed soils, the delivery, handling, and storage of
construction materials and wastes, as well as the operation of construction equipment, could
increase the potential for stormwater contamination. Spills or leaks from heavy equipment and
machinery could introduce oil and grease into surface runoff; hydrocarbon compounds associated
with such pollutants can be toxic to aquatic organisms at relatively low concentrations. Staging
areas and active construction sites could also generate pollutants from the use of paints, solvents,
cleaning agents, and metals. Excavated materials could contain hazardous substances that, if
exposed to stormwater, could be transported into the San Francisco Bay. Larger pollutants such as
trash, debris, and organic matter are also commonly associated with construction disturbance.
Furthermore, concrete used for structural work, footings, and paving could contribute to elevated
pH or other water quality issues if spilled or improperly managed. Therefore, landside construction
activities associated with the project could result in violations of water quality standards or waste
discharge requirements.
However, project construction would be subject to regulatory requirements intended to minimize
erosion and siltation and other construction-related pollutants. These include preparation of a
SWPPP and implementation of BMPs in accordance with the State Water Resources Control Board’s
Construction Stormwater General Permit. BMPs would include, but not be limited to, erosion
controls, sediment containment measures, stabilization of disturbed soils, trash management, and
spill prevention protocols. Compliance with the Construction Stormwater General Permit, as well as
implementation of the required SWPPP and construction BMPs would minimize pollutant discharge
in stormwater runoff. With compliance with existing regulations, project construction would not
violate water quality standards or waste discharge requirements or otherwise substantially degrade
surface water quality. Therefore, landside construction impacts related to surface water quality
would be less than significant.

LANDSIDE CONSTRUCTION GROUNDWATER QUALITY
Where groundwater dewatering is necessary, it would be limited to trench sumps and short-term
pumping to control localized groundwater intrusion. Project construction activities such as
excavation, grading, and utility installation involve temporary disturbance of soils and the use of
construction equipment, though most of the project area is paved and highly developed, with
limited connection to deeper regional aquifers.
Geotechnical investigations conducted for the project indicate that shallow perched groundwater
may be encountered at elevations several feet above high tide, particularly below elevation 6.5 feet,
and that perched water on clay within the fill materials should be anticipated during subsurface
utility construction. 47 Therefore, while dewatering of the deeper aquifer would not be required,
localized groundwater dewatering is anticipated during construction where perched groundwater or
tidally influenced shallow groundwater is encountered during excavation activities. Localized
pumping from sumps within trenches may be necessary to keep excavations dry.
If not properly managed, dewatering effluent could discharge to Strawberry Creek or San Francisco
Bay, carrying suspended sediments, turbidity, or residual contaminants. Such discharges could
temporarily degrade surface water quality by reducing light penetration, altering dissolved oxygen
levels, and impairing aquatic habitat. Dewatering flows would be subject to the Construction
Stormwater General Permit requirements and would require testing and treatment, if needed (such
as sediment filtration, settling tanks, or controlled discharge to designated facilities), to meet the
water quality limitations specified in the Construction Stormwater General Permit prior to discharge
to surface waters.
Without proper controls, accidental releases of fuels, oils, concrete wash water, or other
construction-related pollutants could infiltrate shallow soils and migrate into perched groundwater,
potentially affecting groundwater quality in violation of the objectives identified in Table 3.8-2.
Implementation of a project-specific SWPPP, adherence to the Construction Stormwater General
Permit, and spill prevention measures would minimize pollutant discharge and protect perched
groundwater quality. With compliance with existing regulations, project construction would not
substantially degrade groundwater quality. Therefore, landside construction impacts related to
groundwater quality would be less than significant.

WATERSIDE CONSTRUCTION SURFACE WATER QUALITY
Construction activities within surface waters have the greatest potential to affect water quality in
the San Francisco Bay. Impacts to the San Francisco Bay would be primarily due to construction-
related dredging, demolition of the existing pier, and construction of a new pier. In-water
construction activities, such as dredging, existing pile removal and new pile installation, and pier
deck demolition and construction, as well as any associated sediment disturbance, have the
potential to directly affect San Francisco Bay water quality. Some of the existing pier piles, if
wooden, could contain hazardous materials, such as creosote, that could be released during
demolition and removal activities. Dredging of debris, removal of existing pier infrastructure, and
pier installation could resuspend bottom sediments, increasing turbidity in the immediate project
vicinity. Elevated turbidity can reduce light penetration, affecting photosynthetic organisms and
potentially adversely affecting water quality. Sediment resuspension may also release adsorbed
contaminants such as metals, hydrocarbons, or legacy pollutants into the water column, where they
can be transported by currents and dispersed to adjacent areas.

DREDGING
Dredging activities have the potential to temporarily degrade water quality by resuspending bottom
sediments into the water column. As described previously, in 2025, sediment sampling and analysis
was conducted within five dredge units in the project vicinity and sediment samples were found to
contain metals, organochlorine pesticides, polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons, PCBs, and
dioxins/furans. Although contaminants were present, the concentrations of such contaminants
indicate that sediments are not likely to pose significant hazards if managed according to reuse site
requirements.
In-water sediment disturbance associated with the project would be limited in extent, localized, and
temporary, and would not result in substantial or persistent degradation of water quality. Studies
conducted in San Francisco Bay indicate that turbidity generated by dredging activities, typically
more intensive than pile installation or removal, diminishes to background levels within a radius of
approximately 600 feet within one tidal cycle for singular events. 48 Given that Bay waters are
naturally highly turbid and subject to pronounced fluctuations due to tidal action, wind-driven
waves, and regional sediment transport, project-related turbidity would not be expected to
measurably increase local or regional turbidity beyond baseline conditions and impacts would be
less than significant.

PIER AND PILE DEMOLITION AND REMOVAL AND CONSTRUCTION OF PIER AND BREAKWATER
Demolition of the closed pier is anticipated to be conducted using a crane positioned on a floating
crane barge and supporting tugboats, material barges, and various smaller support vessels.
Demolition of the closed pier would involve the removal of the existing concrete decking followed
by the removal of existing 20-inch octagonal piles. The 20-inch piles would be removed using either
a dead pull method or the use of a vibratory hammer. If full removal is not possible, the 20-inch pipe
piles may be cut at the mudline.
Accidental release of construction materials/debris, concrete slurry, or equipment fluids into the
San Francisco Bay could contribute to water quality degradation. Given the project site’s location
within tidal waters, such impacts could be rapidly conveyed beyond the immediate construction
zone. These activities could result in temporary exceedances of water quality standards, which could
impair beneficial uses. During construction, removed piles/deck slab and appurtenances will be
loaded onto a barge and piles will be transported to a staging area. The barge will be designed to
prohibit sediment or debris from falling back into the water. The work surface on the barge deck will
include a containment basin for creosote, piles, concrete, and any mud or sediment removed during
pulling. Upon removal from substrate, the piles will be moved expeditiously from the water into the
containment basin. Any sediment accumulated from the pile removal operations will be assumed to
contain creosote and will be contained and disposed offsite in an appropriate landfill.
Work surfaces on a barge deck or pier will include a containment basin for pile and any sediment
removed during pulling.
    Work surfaces on a barge deck will be cleaned by disposing of sediment or other residues along
     with cut off piling, if so employed.
    The containment basin will be removed and disposed in accordance with applicable federal and
     state regulations.

Operation

LANDSIDE OPERATION SURFACE WATER QUALITY
The existing project site includes approximately 280,000 square feet of impervious surface, and the
proposed project includes 248,000 square feet of impervious surface. The majority of the landside
portion of the project site is already covered by impervious surfaces, such as roadways, parking lots,
and paved pedestrian areas. Implementation of the proposed project would not increase the extent
of impervious surfaces and would result in a net decrease of approximately 32,000 square feet of
impervious area. Therefore, due to a decrease in impervious surfaces and implementation of
anticipated stormwater management BMPs to be physically included on site as part of the proposed
project, runoff amounts and runoff quality are anticipated to improve relative to existing conditions,
and additional pollutant loading of surface water runoff is not anticipated. In addition, the
Hydrologic and Hydraulic Technical Report prepared as part of the Design for this project indicates
that the project would provide a water quality benefit through reduced runoff peaks and volumes.
Through the construction of permeable parking, bioretention areas, and flow-through planters the
required 4 percent through the C.3 program will be exceeded. In addition, this project will not result
in new storm drain outfalls to the San Francisco Bay. Storm water and storm drain improvements
will tie into existing outfalls. 49
Existing uses at and adjacent to the project site, including commercial operations, marina activities,
and public parking areas, generate pollutants that could impair water quality if not properly
managed prior to discharge. Typical pollutants associated with such uses include suspended solids,
pathogens, nutrients, pesticides, organic compounds, trash and debris, oxygen-demanding
substances, and oil and grease, with heavy metals commonly associated with parking areas.

The existing Municipal Regional Stormwater Permit, which would be applicable to the project states
that all new development and redevelopment projects shall include LID BMPs and source control
measures to limit pollutant generation, discharge and runoff. 50 The project would include BMPs to
treat and manage stormwater prior to discharge. 51 University Avenue and the Seawall Drive Parking
Lot Improvement Plans would include permeable parking areas and bioretention facilities.
Permeable paving consists of a High-Density Polyethylene grid (or other permeable surface) filled
with gravel over a 3-foot-deep drain rock reservoir for stormwater infiltration. Subdrainage piping
and connections to existing outfalls would be developed. Collectively, these features would improve
water quality by filtering pollutants and reducing untreated runoff compared to existing conditions.
The project would also includes LID features — including site design measures, source control BMPs
and pollutant control BMPs—to reduce the operation-related discharge of pollutants to the
maximum extent practicable. LID features would also include the use of bioretention basins and
media, curb cuts, permeable pavements on non-ADA lots, and stormwater plantings designed to
retain and reduce from stormwater flows. 52 Implementation of these site-specific LID features and
pollutant control BMPs, consistent with the requirements of the City’s stormwater management
program, would provide treatment and filtration of potential pollutants from runoff prior to
discharge to San Francisco Bay. The primary water quality benefit of LID is reducing or eliminating
direct stormwater runoff to the storm drain system or receiving waters. The initial “first flush” of
stormwater during a rainfall event typically contains the highest concentration of pollutants; by
routing this runoff through LID features, pollutants can be removed through retention, infiltration
into engineered soil layers and/or native soils, and evapotranspiration before reaching the San
Francisco Bay.
Visitors to the Berkeley Waterfront and ferry customers have the potential to generate trash, which
could contribute to the existing trash impairments in the San Francisco Bay and Strawberry Creek.
However, trash cans would be placed throughout the project site, including on the pier, breakwater,
public plaza, and the proposed parking lot. In addition, the City would perform routine
maintenance, including emptying trash receptacles. Trash management would minimize the
potential for trash to be transported to surface waters.
With a decrease in net impervious area and implementation of operational BMPs, landside
operation of proposed project would not violate water quality standards or waste discharge
requirements. Therefore, landside operational impacts related to surface water quality would be
less than significant.

Furthermore, as discussed above, the project would overall reduce the amount of impervious
surfaces and the project would, therefore, not substantially change groundwater infiltration.
Therefore, landside operational impacts related to groundwater quality would be less than
significant.

WATERSIDE OPERATION SURFACE WATER QUALITY
The existing pier is an older structure, and deteriorating concrete piles or decking can leach fine
particulates, lime, and elevate pH into surrounding waters. Corroding steel reinforcement may
release trace metals such as iron or zinc into the Bay. Replacing the pier would reduce the existing
water quality issues associated with the existing deteriorating pier. As part of the proposed project,
pollutants such as primer, paint, paint chips, solvents, oils, fuels, sludges, detergents, and cleansers
would be generated during operation.
Projects in Berkeley are subject to CalOSHA regulations regarding management of certain hazardous
materials. Title 8 of the California Code of Regulations Section 5194, 5531-5608, and 5198 cover the
control and management of chemicals, including paints, solvents, fuels, detergents and sludges, and
lead. CalOSHA requires testing, monitoring, containment, and disposal of these materials, such that
exposure levels do not exceed CalOSHA standards. 53
Operation of the proposed ferry facilities, including gangways, boarding floats, guide piles, fenders,
and the Universal Charging Floats, would introduce new overwater structures and associated vessel
activity into San Francisco Bay that could affect water quality. Routine ferry operations would
generate propeller wash and wave action, which could cause localized turbidity and resuspension of
bottom sediments, particularly in the vicinity of guide piles and fenders. The project would minimize
propeller-wash–induced turbidity and sediment resuspension through a combination of design,
operations, and monitoring measures. The berth and maneuvering basin would be designed with
adequate depth and scour protection to dissipate jet energy, and vessels would follow a low-wake
approach with posted speed limits and captain training to limit throttle use.
Ferry operating procedures would require vessels to begin reducing speed approximately 0.33
nautical miles (about 2,000 feet) from the terminal to minimize wake effects and to transition to
neutral propulsion approximately 0.25 nautical miles (about 1,500 feet) from the berth to allow for
control transfer and docking preparations at the wing station. These operational guidelines may be
adjusted as needed to account for site-specific conditions such as weather, ambient wave climate,
and wake-sensitive areas. Approach distances may be further refined based on observed wake
propagation toward the shoreline, marina breakwater, and adjacent uses.
The Universal Charging Floats would contain specialized electrical charging systems and Echandia
LTO-chemistry lithium-ion batteries for rapid charging of electric ferry vessels. Although these
systems are designed for marine applications and incorporate multiple safety features—such as
battery management systems with real-time monitoring, ventilation and cooling systems, smoke-
tight compartments, multiple-tiered fire suppression systems, and monitoring—malfunction or
failure of components could result in the release of battery electrolytes, cooling fluids, or
firefighting agents into the San Francisco Bay. While the likelihood of such events is low given the
system’s engineered safeguards, any accidental discharge could degrade water quality through the
introduction of chemical contaminants. Standard operating procedures, such as routine inspection
and maintenance of battery and cooling systems, secondary containment and spill response
readiness on the charging floats, and emergency shutdown and reporting protocols in the event of
leaks or malfunctions, would reduce risk of contamination associated with these materials.
Other operational activities, such as maintenance of ancillary systems, washing of vessels, and the
use of hose bibs for cleaning and fire suppression, could also contribute pollutants to the
surrounding waters. Pollutants potentially associated with these activities include detergents,

Mitigation Measures

MITIGATION MEASURE HYD-1: INCLUDE AND IMPLEMENT ADDITIONAL BEST MANAGEMENT PRACTICES
IN THE SWPPP PRIOR TO AND DURING PIER DEMOLITION

In compliance with the requirements of the Construction Stormwater General Permit, prior to
construction the construction contractor shall prepare a Stormwater Pollution Prevention Plan
(SWPPP) and implement the SWPPP during construction. The SWPPP shall be submitted to the
Berkeley Public Works Department and the State Water Resources Control Board (via the
Stormwater Multiple Application and Report Tracking System [SMARTS]) for review and approval at
least 60 days prior to start of construction. In addition to standard Erosion Control, Sediment
Control, and Good Housekeeping Best Management Practices, the following Best Management
Practices shall be included in the SWPPP and implemented during pier demolition:
   Site washout areas shall be located at least 100 feet from a storm drain, open ditch or surface
    water and ensure that runoff flows from such activities do not enter receiving water bodies,
    unless otherwise approved by the RWQCB.
   All re-fueling, cleaning, and maintenance of equipment shall occur at least 100 feet from storm
    drain, open ditch or surface water and/or within secondary containment, unless otherwise
    approved by the RWQCB.
   Particular care shall be exercised to prevent foreign materials (e.g., construction scraps, wood
    preservatives, other chemicals and debris, etc.) from entering the San Francisco Bay during pier
    demolition.
     If wood preservatives must be applied to cut-wood surfaces, the materials, whenever
         feasible, shall be treated at an onshore location to preclude the possibility of spills into State
         waters.
     A containment boom shall be placed around all active portions of a construction site where
         wood scraps or other floatable debris could enter the water.
     The containment boom and net shall be cleared daily or as often as necessary to prevent
         accumulation of debris.
     Tarps and basins shall be used above deck to contain debris and materials.
     Dipnets shall be on-site and can be used to retrieve debris if it accidentally falls into the
         water.

Construction
Because perched and tidally influenced groundwater is present at shallow depths, localized
dewatering may alter shallow subsurface conditions during construction. Groundwater dewatering
of the deeper regional aquifer would not be required. However, localized trench pumping has the
potential to lower perched groundwater levels in the immediate work area. These effects would be
temporary and localized and would not conflict with the sustainable management of the
groundwater basin or groundwater subbasin. Therefore, construction impacts related to
groundwater supply/recharge and groundwater management plan consistency would be less than
significant.

Operation
The project site is located within the northwestern portion of the East Bay Plain Subbasin, where
groundwater is not a primary source of municipal supply and the depth to groundwater is
approximately 5 to 13.4 feet below the surface. 54 The landside portion of the site is already
predominantly covered by impervious surfaces, and the proposed project would result in a net
decrease of approximately 32,000 square feet of impervious area through the inclusion of
permeable paving, bioretention facilities, and other LID features. These measures would enhance
localized infiltration opportunities compared to existing conditions and would not reduce the
capacity for groundwater recharge. The project does not include groundwater extraction for
operational water supply, and no dewatering or pumping activities are proposed during operation
that would lower groundwater levels. For these reasons, operation of the proposed project would
not substantially decrease groundwater supplies or interfere with groundwater recharge such that
sustainable groundwater management of the East Bay Plain Subbasin or Santa Clara Valley

Construction

EROSION AND SILTATION
Construction of the proposed project would involve pavement removal, grading, excavation, filling,
parking areas, utilities, and pedestrian pathways. These activities would temporarily disturb soils
and alter drainage patterns and, during periods of heavy rainfall or high winds, could increase the
potential for erosion and transport of sediment from upland portions of the site into the storm drain
system or directly into San Francisco Bay. However, the project is required to comply with
regulatory requirements designed to minimize erosion and siltation, including preparation of a
SWPPP and implementation of BMPs in compliance with the Construction Stormwater General
Permit. As part of the implementation of the SWPPP, these BMPs could include erosion control
measures, sediment containment devices, stabilization of disturbed soils, and spill prevention
protocols. Therefore, construction impacts related to drainage pattern alteration specific to erosion
and siltation would be temporary, localized, and less than significant.

RUNOFF AND FLOODING
Construction could alter drainage patterns and change runoff patterns. Temporary construction
staging areas could generate localized runoff, but SWPPP BMPs for stormwater control and site
stabilization would ensure that construction activities would not substantially increase runoff in a
manner that causes flooding on- or off-site. Development and implementation of a SWPPP would be
required under the State Water Resources Control Board’s Construction General Permit and is
independent of the Water Quality Certification process. Compliance with these existing regulatory
requirements will address concerns related to water quality. Therefore, construction impacts
related to drainage pattern alteration specific to runoff and flooding would be less than significant.

DRAINAGE SYSTEM CAPACITY AND POLLUTED RUNOFF
Construction activities could produce pollutant-laden runoff (sediment, hydrocarbons, trash, debris,
or concrete wash water). Compliance with the Construction Stormwater General Permit requires
implementation of a SWPPP and stormwater BMPs, such as proper material storage, spill
containment, and waste management, to reduce discharges of polluted runoff. In addition, runoff
from the site would continue to be directed into existing storm drain infrastructure, which are
adequately sized to handle flows with BMP implementation. Construction would not generate flows
exceeding system capacity or provide substantial additional sources of polluted runoff. Therefore,
construction impacts related to drainage pattern alteration specific to drainage system capacity and
polluted runoff would be less than significant.

FLOOD FLOW IMPEDANCE
The proposed project does not involve modifications to any natural stream channel, river, or
designated floodway, nor does it alter the Strawberry Creek culvert or outfall, which would be
avoided to the extent feasible during construction. Construction staging and in-water work would
be managed to avoid creating barriers to overland flow. The Hydrologic and Hydraulic Technical
Report prepared as part of the Design for the project indicates that the project would provide
reduced runoff peaks and volumes, compared to existing conditions. 55The project would not impede
or redirect flood flows in a manner that increases flood risk. Therefore, construction impacts related
to drainage pattern alteration specific to flood flow impedance would be less than significant.

Operation

EROSION AND SILTATION
During operation, the project would not result in substantial erosion or siltation because the site
would be stabilized with new pavement, permeable paving, landscaped areas, and bioretention
facilities. Compared to existing conditions, the project would reduce the overall impervious areas
and increase vegetated and pervious areas, thereby reducing runoff velocity and promoting
infiltration. These features are designed to slow and detain stormwater prior to discharge, which
minimizes the potential for erosion and sediment transport both onsite and in downstream
conveyance systems. Operation of the project would also be subject to ongoing compliance with
applicable Municipal Regional Stormwater NPDES Permit requirements, which mandate routine
maintenance of drainage facilities, permeable surfaces, and LID features to preserve stormwater
function and reduce erosion. With implementation of these design elements and compliance with

regulatory requirements, operational impacts related to drainage pattern alteration specific to

RUNOFF AND FLOODING
Under existing conditions, the landside portion of the project site consists of approximately 280,000
square feet of impervious surface area, including roadways, parking lots, and paved pedestrian
areas. The proposed project would reduce total impervious surface area by approximately 32,000
square feet, primarily through the use of permeable paving and landscaped bioretention facilities in
the renovated Seawall Drive parking lot and along University Avenue. The net reduction in
impervious surfaces, combined with the infiltration capacity of permeable paving would reduce
runoff volumes and peak flows relative to existing conditions. Peak flows would also be managed by
bioretention basins to capture and control stormwater flows. These LID features are designed to
promote infiltration, slow runoff, and detain stormwater prior to discharge, thereby reducing both
runoff volumes and peak flow rates relative to existing conditions. As a result, the project would
improve stormwater retention and infiltration capacity compared to existing conditions and would
not contribute to increased flooding potential from site-generated runoff. Accordingly, the
proposed project would not substantially increase runoff in a manner that results in flooding on- or
off-site during operations. Therefore, operational impacts related to drainage pattern alteration
specific to runoff and flooding would be less than significant.

DRAINAGE SYSTEM CAPACITY AND POLLUTED RUNOFF
The proposed drainage improvements, including new subdrainage piping and outfalls would be
designed to convey stormwater to onsite treatment and detention areas prior to discharge to San
Francisco Bay. Permeable pavement systems would incorporate a High-Density Polyethylene grid (or
other permeable surface) filled with gravel over a 3-foot-deep drain rock reservoir to temporarily
store stormwater and promote infiltration. Bioretention facilities would capture and treat the “first
flush” of runoff, which typically contains the highest pollutant concentrations, before discharging at
controlled rates. These measures would lower pollutant loads in stormwater and maintain or reduce
peak discharge rates to the municipal storm drain system compared to existing conditions, ensuring
that the project would not generate flows that exceed the system’s capacity. Accordingly, the
proposed project would not create or contribute runoff that exceeds the capacity of the storm drain
system or provide substantial additional sources of polluted runoff. Therefore, operational impacts
related to drainage pattern alteration specific to drainage system capacity and polluted runoff
would be less than significant.

FLOOD FLOW IMPEDANCE
The proposed project does not involve modifications to any natural stream channel, river, or
designated floodway, nor does it alter the Strawberry Creek culvert or outfall, which would be
avoided to the extent feasible during construction. Grading and drainage improvements would
maintain existing surface flow directions and preserve existing conveyance pathways to San
Francisco Bay. Permeable pavement, bioretention, and subdrainage systems would improve onsite
infiltration and stormwater management without creating barriers to overland flow. In addition,
larger above-ground structures for the landside improvements, such as the restroom, would be
located outside of the 500-year floodplains. While the proposed breakwater and piles will be
located within Zone VE of the 100-year floodplain, the project is unlikely to change the water
elevation or exacerbate flooding due to the size and capacity of San Francisco Bay and relatively
small volume of the new in-water structures. In addition, because portions of the project area are

Construction
Construction of the new pier would occur within San Francisco Bay and along the Berkeley
Waterfront, where the work area is subject to tidal flooding, storm surge, and wind-driven wave
action. Portions of the in-water work zone are located within FEMA Zone VE, which is susceptible to
coastal flooding and wave run-up. Elevated water levels during construction, whether from extreme
tides, storm surge, or short-duration flood events could inundate active work areas, material staging
zones, or equipment platforms. Such inundation could mobilize construction-related pollutants,
including suspended sediments from pile installation or removal, dredging, and pier demolition;
concrete slurry; uncured grout; treated wood fragments; paints and coatings; petroleum-based
products such as hydraulic fluids, oils, and fuels; and debris generated during demolition.
Construction equipment operating in flooded or wave-affected zones may be at greater risk for
leaks or spills of fuel and lubricants, which could disperse rapidly in tidal waters. Pollutants
discharged to surface waters can temporarily degrade water quality and impair beneficial uses.
The Construction Stormwater General Permit requires that all qualifying construction projects
prepare and implement a SWPPP that identifies potential pollutant sources and prescribes BMPs to
minimize discharges of pollutants to receiving waters. As part of the SWPPP, contractors must
implement Good Housekeeping BMPs, which include proper storage, handling, and disposal of
construction materials, chemicals, and hazardous substances. On waterfront sites subject to tidal
action or potential seawater inundation, these measures include storing materials in designated
upland or covered areas, using secondary containment for fuels, oils, and solvents, and securing
containers to prevent displacement during high water or wave action. Collectively, these practices
help ensure that construction and hazardous materials are managed to minimize the risk of
