accidental release or mobilization, thereby protecting water quality and complying with permit
requirements. With compliance with permit conditions and implementation of BMPs, construction
would not release pollutants due to inundation Therefore, construction impacts related to risk of
pollutant release due to inundation would be less than significant.

Operation
Portions of the project site are located within Zone VE of the 100-year coastal floodplain, which is
subject to tidal flooding and storm-induced wave action, and within the mapped tsunami inundation
zone for the San Francisco Bay shoreline. Due to its location on the Berkeley Waterfront, the site
could also be affected by seiche events generated within the San Francisco Bay during seismic
activity. In the event of inundation from coastal flooding, tsunami, or seiche, potential pollutant
sources at the site would primarily be associated with overwater ferry infrastructure and small
quantities of maintenance materials stored landside. However, the project is designed to withstand
long-term sea level rise impacts and minimize pollutant release risks through incorporation of
multiple protective features, including enclosed and covered outdoor materials and waste storage
areas, storm drain inlet protection, spill prevention and response protocols. The Universal Charging
Float battery systems would be housed in smoke-tight, watertight compartments with real-time
monitoring, automated shutoff systems, and multiple redundant fire suppression systems,
substantially reducing the potential for pollutant release in the event of inundation.
The proposed project is designed to address projected sea level rise, consistent with the 2024
California Sea Level Rise Guidance. The project has been designed to last through 2075 and also
considers possible conditions through the year 2100. Based on sea level rise projections, the design
allows for about 1.6 feet of higher water levels by 2075. To address this, the breakwater, pier deck,
and plaza are all set at or above recommended heights to ensure they remain safe and functional
even with future higher tides and waves. These elevations also account for extreme wave conditions
and are intended to maintain operational functionality and public safety under projected mid-
century sea level rise. By integrating these climate-adaptive design features with operational BMPs,
the project would not present a substantial risk of pollutant release due to inundation from
flooding, tsunami, seiche, or sea level rise within its design life. Given these design features and
operational controls, the project would not present ongoing substantial risk of pollutant release due
to flooding, tsunami, or seiche events. Therefore, operational impacts related to risk of pollutant
release due to inundation would be less than significant.

Stormwater General Permit, including monitoring and treatment of dewatering discharge would
minimize these risks. Potential dewatering-related impacts to water quality would be controlled.
Therefore, construction impacts related to East Bay Subbasin Plan consistency would be less than
significant.

Surface Water Quality
Cumulative projects at the Berkeley Waterfront—including marina dredging, dock repairs, new

cumulative impact with respect to surface water quality.

Groundwater Supplies and Recharge and Groundwater Quality
Cumulative development in the project vicinity—including the maximum development potential in
the Draft Waterfront Specific Plan and residential infill—would add impervious surfaces that could

and recharge, as well as groundwater quality.

bioretention basins and vegetated swales. Therefore, cumulative projects in combination with
implementation of the proposed project would result in a less than significant cumulative impact
with respect to runoff and flooding impacts.

State Regulations

Public Trust Doctrine
The Public Trust Doctrine requires the State of California to hold certain lands in trust for the benefit
of the public. Historically, the doctrine protected public rights for navigation, commerce, and
fisheries, but landmark court decisions have expanded its scope to include recreation, ecological
preservation, and scenic and wildlife habitat protection. Under this doctrine, sovereign lands
became state property upon California’s admission to the Union in 1850 and are managed by the
California State Lands Commission or by local jurisdictions under legislative trust grants. Public Trust
lands cannot be sold and must be used for purposes that promote or protect trust values. 2
In Berkeley, portions of the shoreline and adjacent open water are sovereign marsh, tide, and
submerged lands granted to the City of Berkeley by the Legislature. The initial grant was enacted in
1913 and subsequently amended in 1961 to confirm and broaden allowable public-interest uses
with trust obligations. The City, as trustee, is responsible for managing these lands in accordance
with its granting statutes and the Public Trust Doctrine. Within the granted trust lands, allowable
uses are those that accommodate or improve navigation, water-dependent transportation, public
access, recreation, and environmental protection, and may include visitor-serving facilities when
they further statewide public trust purposes. Uses that inhibit public access, are not water-
dependent, or could be sited elsewhere are generally inconsistent with trust obligations. 3
Consistency with the Public Trust Doctrine is not required by CEQA because CEQA Guidelines Section
15125(d) only requires evaluation of adopted plans and policies that were established for the
purpose of avoiding or mitigating an environmental effect. The Public Trust Doctrine is a common
law principle, not an adopted land use or policy under CEQA. Therefore, it is provided here for
context but is not analyzed further in this EIR.

McAteer-Petris Act
The McAteer-Petris Act establishes BCDC with the authority to regulate land use and development
in the coastal areas of the San Francisco Bay area, including the Berkeley Waterfront area. The Act
aims to limit the unnecessary filling of the Bay, promote public access, and provide comprehensive
planning through the San Francisco Bay Plan. The Act also grants BCDC the power to issue permits
for projects within its jurisdiction, which includes the Bay open waters, marshes, mudflats, and a
100-foot shoreline band.

California Government Code Section 66605 establishes the conditions under which filling of the San
Francisco Bay and certain waterways is permitted. It states that such filling should only be

Regional and Local Regulations

BCDC San Francisco Bay Plan
In compliance with the McAteer-Petris Act, BCDC prepared the first San Francisco Bay Plan in 1968
which was transmitted to the California Legislature and the Governor in 1969. BCDC amends the Bay
Plan over time to address regional needs. The San Francisco Bay Plan includes policies to guide
future uses of the Bay and the shoreline. The Plan aims to protect the Bay from unnecessary filling,
promote public access, and ensure sustainable development. It designates priority use areas for
water-oriented activities, such as ports and recreational facilities, and establishes environmental
safeguards to preserve the Bay's natural resources. The Plan also includes specific policies for
shoreline protection, habitat restoration, and climate resilience, ensuring that land use and planning
decisions support ecological health and community needs. Pertinent policies are identified and
addressed in detail under Impact LU-2 within this EIR section.

ABAG/MTC Plan Bay Area 2050
The ABAG/MTC Plan Bay Area 2050, adopted in October 2021 and last updated in November 2024,
integrated transportation and land-use plan for the nine-county San Francisco Bay Area, including
Alameda County. Plan Bay Area 2050 meets all state and federal requirements for a Regional
Transportation Plan and Sustainable Communities Strategy, also referred to as the RTP/SCS. The
Plan describes where and how the region can accommodate the slightly fewer than 1.4 million new
households and 1.4 million new jobs projected in the Bay Area by 2050 and details the regional
transportation investment strategy over this period. The Plan identifies 35 strategies that focus on
improving housing, the economy, transportation, and the environment across the Bay Area over a
30-year period. The plan has identified four geographic areas to guide where future growth in
housing and jobs would be focused over the next 30 years: Priority Development Areas (PDA),
Priority Production Areas (PPA), Transit Rich Areas (TRA), and High-Resource Areas (HRA). ABAG and
MTC developed land use and transportation scenarios in Plan Bay Area 2050 that distribute the total
amount of anticipated growth across the region and measure how well each scenario measures
against the Plan goals. Based upon performance, the preferred scenario provides a regional pattern
of household and employment growth and a corresponding transportation investment strategy. The
following strategies are applicable to the Waterfront area, and are therefore applicable to the
proposed project:
   Strategy T3. Enable a Seamless Mobility Experience.
   Strategy T5. Implement a Per-Mile Tolling on Congested Freeways with Transit Alternatives.
   Strategy T8. Build a complete streets network.
   Strategy EN1. Adapt to Sea-Level Rise.
   Strategy EN8. Expand clean vehicle initiatives.

Pertinent policies are identified and addressed in detail under Impact LU-2 within this EIR section.

Bay Area Clean Air Plan
The Bay Area Air District Bay Area Clean Air Plan is a comprehensive regional strategy adopted in
2017 to address climate change and improve air quality across the nine counties under its
jurisdiction. This plan is discussed further in Section 3.2, Air Quality, of this EIR.

Berkeley Climate Action Plan
The City of Berkeley adopted a Climate Action Plan (CAP) in 2009 with the goal of reducing
communitywide GHG emissions by 80 percent below 2000 levels by 2050. The core
recommendation strategies and actions of the CAP cover the following topics: 4
    Sustainable Transportation and Land Use
    Building Energy Use
    Waste Reduction and Recycling
    Community Outreach and Empowerment
    Preparing for Climate Change Impacts

Berkeley General Plan
Adopted in 2002 and amended in 2023, the Berkeley General Plan is a long-range plan of policies for
the development and preservation of Berkeley. The General Plan identifies the following seven
major goals:
1. Preserve Berkeley’s unique character and quality of life;
2. Ensure that Berkeley has an adequate supply of decent housing, living wage jobs, and
   businesses providing basic goods and services;
3. Protect local and regional environmental quality;
4. Maximize and improve citizen participation in municipal decision-making;
5. Create a sustainable Berkeley;
6. Make Berkeley a disaster-resistant community, that can survive, recover from, and thrive after a
   disaster; and
7. Maintain Berkeley’s infrastructure, including streets, sidewalks, buildings, and facilities; storm
   drains and sanitary sewers; and open space, parks, pathways, and recreation facilities.

The General Plan’s goals are implemented through decisions and actions consistent with the
objectives policies and actions of each of the nine Elements: Land Use, Transportation, Housing,
Disaster Preparedness & Safety, Open Space & Recreation, Environmental Management, Economic
Development and Employment, Urban Design & Preservation and Citizen Participation. The General
Plan explicitly recognizes that given its broad scope, “inherent tensions exist between Plan
objectives and policies that must be balanced against one another through the decision-making
process on particular development and land use decisions.”

LAND USE ELEMENT
The Land Use Element of the Berkeley General Plan includes goals, policies and actions that support
context-sensitive infill development, historic preservation, transit-oriented development, mobility

OPEN SPACE AND RECREATION ELEMENT
The Open Space and Recreation Element of the Berkeley General Plan provides a regulated
framework for the maintenance and continuous improvement of the City’s open space and
recreational facilities, including open spaces, parks, playgrounds, recreation centers, swim centers,
public gardens, the Marina, public paths, landscaped medians, and sidewalks.

TRANSPORTATION ELEMENT
The Transportation Element of the Berkeley General Plan is closely related to the Land Use Element.
The Transportation Element contains policies that regulate the movement of vehicles, people, and
goods throughout Berkeley. It prioritizes maximizing the efficiency of existing systems serving the
area and includes several plans and studies of neighborhoods throughout Berkeley.

DISASTER PREPAREDNESS & SAFETY ELEMENT
The Disaster Preparedness and Safety Element of the Berkeley General Plan establishes and
maintains an effective emergency response program that anticipates the potential for disasters;
maintains continuity of life-support functions during an emergency; and institutes community-based
disaster response planning, including businesses, non-governmental organizations, and
neighborhoods. It is discussed in more detail in Chapter 3.7, Hazards and Hazardous Materials, of
this EIR.

URBAN DESIGN & PRESERVATION ELEMENT
The Urban Design & Preservation Element of the Berkeley General Plan discusses the regulation of
historic preservation, urban design, visual character, and Berkeley’s built environment as a whole.
Pertinent policies are identified and addressed in detail under Impact LU-2 within this EIR section.

Berkeley Municipal Code
The Berkeley Municipal Code (BMC) is a collection of the City of Berkeley local laws and policies,
including general provisions, building and construction, public health and safety, environmental
protection, and public services. Relevant BMC policies include:
   BMC Chapter 6.20. Regulations for the Berkeley Marina, including recreation activities, berth
    applications, rates, service charges, and grants authority to the Harbormaster for managing
    marina operations to ensure safe and efficient use of marina facilities.
   BMC Chapter 6.52. Regulations governing the removal, pruning, and planting of trees on public
    property. This regulation is discussed further in Section 3.3, Biological Resources, of this EIR.
   BMC Chapter 12.20. Includes requirements for mitigation and replacement of trees removed
    during construction. This ordinance is discussed further in Section 3.3, Biological Resources, of
    this EIR.
   BMC Chapter 13.40. Establishes noise thresholds and enforcement procedures relevant for
    evaluating land use compatibility with transportation-related noise. BMC Chapter 13.40 is
    discussed further in Section 3.10, Noise, of this EIR.

    BMC Chapter 23. Chapter 23 includes the City’s Zoning Ordinance which establishes regulations
     for development and land use by dividing the City into different zones with specific restrictions
     and requirements based on permitted uses. Berkeley’s Zoning Ordinance describes the
     requirements for different zones including unclassified, residential, commercial, manufacturing,
     and overlay districts that cover two or more districts.

A summary of the use permitting process, including the allowed uses for the zoning designation of
Unclassified (U) is provided below, pursuant to BMC Section 23.208.020 (Unclassified District):
    B. Allowed Uses
      All uses not prohibited by law are permitted in the U district.
      A Use Permit is required to establish any use, consistent with the procedures in this section.

    C. Use Permit Procedures. The City shall review and act on Use Permit applications in the U
     district as follows:
      1. Each application shall be first submitted to the Planning Commission with the Planning
         Commission making a report to the Zoning Adjustments Board (ZAB). If the Planning
         Commission fails to take an action on the report within 30 days after a Use Permit
         application is deemed complete, the ZAB will consider the application without a Planning
         Commission report.
      2. After Planning Commission review, the ZAB shall take an action to approve, conditionally
         approve, or deny the application. The ZAB’s decision is not effective until after action by the
         City Council. ZAB decisions may not be appealed.
      3. The ZAB will send a report of its decision, including findings and any conditions, together
         with the Planning Commission report, to the City Clerk within 14 days of final action.
      4. The City Council will review and act on the application within 30 days of the ZAB decision.
      5. The Council may affirm, reverse, or modify the ZAB decision.

    D. Development Standards. All development standards in the U District shall be set forth in the
     Use Permit, including lot size, density, building height, setbacks, building separation, lot
     coverage, floor area ratio (FAR), usable open space, and off-street parking.
    E. Use Permit Findings To approve a Use Permit in the U district, the ZAB, Planning Commission,
     and City Council must all make the findings in Section 23.406.030.F (Administrative Use
     Permits – Findings for Approval).

Berkeley Waterfront Specific Plan
The City of Berkeley Waterfront Specific Plan, adopted in 1986, establishes the waterfront as an
area primarily for recreational, open space, and environmental uses, with preservation and
enhancement of beaches, marshes, and other natural habitats. The Plan area consists of 170 acres
of land bounded by I-80 to the east, the Berkeley Marina on the west, and the Albany and
Emeryville City limits to the north and south. 5 The project site generally is not within the 170 acres
of land included in the 1986 City of Berkeley Waterfront Specific Plan, with the possible exception of
the underground conduit that would be installed along University Avenue and Frontage Road.

Berkeley Marina Master Plan
The Berkeley Marina Master Plan, adopted in 2003, establishes a long-term strategy for the
development and enhancement of the Berkeley Marina. It aims to maintain and preserve the
Marina as a recreational and open space resource. The Plan restricts new development to replacing
and remodeling existing commercial and non-profit facilities, with limited expansion allowed on a
case-by-case basis. It emphasizes the conservation of open spaces, enhancement of public access,
and expansion of recreational facilities. The Plan also identifies specific capital improvement
projects to be implemented over the next twenty years.
Guiding Principal 1. Protect, restore, enhance, and expand wildlife habitat, open space, natural
areas, and biological resources.

    Improve Signage.
    Enhance the existing Public Plaza.

Guiding Principal 3. Maintain and upgrade existing infrastructure.
    Improve restroom facilities.
    Improve parking lots.

Berkeley Local Hazard Mitigation Plan
The Berkeley Local Hazard Mitigation Plan addresses earthquake, wildland-urban interface, extreme

Section 3.7, Hazards and Hazardous Materials, of this EIR.

Significance Criteria

b) Cause a significant environmental impact due to a conflict with any land use plan, policy, or

Approach to Analysis

Land Use Planning
The evaluation of proposed project impacts related to land use planning is based on a comparison of
the proposed project to the applicable plans, policies, and regulations to determine if the proposed
project would conflict with a plan, policy, or regulation adopted for the purpose of avoiding or
mitigating an environmental effect. This section also analyzes whether the proposed project would
physically divide a community.
Project conflicts were assessed with regard to applicable regional land use plans and policies,
specifically in the BCDC San Francisco Bay Plan, ABAG/MTC Plan Bay Area 2050, and Bay Area Air
District Bay Area Clean Air Plan. In addition, project conflicts were assessed with regard to
applicable local land use plans and policies, specifically the Berkeley Municipal Code related to

2026).

recreation, trees, and noise, Berkeley General Plan related to land use, transportation, recreation,
hazards/safety, and visual character/urban design, Berkeley Climate Action Plan, Berkeley Marina
Master Plan, Berkeley Local Hazard Mitigation Plan, and Berkeley Measure L. A policy inconsistency
is considered a significant adverse impact only if the inconsistency would result in a significant
adverse physical impact based on the established significance criterion. The analysis below provides
a discussion of the most relevant policies from the various planning documents. However, the City’s

EIR Scoping Comments Consideration
This section addresses comments received in response to the EIR NOP related to various concerns
regarding land use impacts.
BCDC and others provided a comment requesting that the EIR consider consistency with BCDC
policies in the Bay Plan. Please refer to Table 3.9-1, which includes a discussion of consistency with
pertinent policies. This comment was also made by the organization Save the Bay.
Similarly, individuals provided comments requesting that the EIR consider consistency with Measure
L and the Draft Waterfront Specific Plan. Please refer to the subsection titled “Berkeley Measure L
Consistency” under Impact LU-2, below, which includes a discussion of consistency with Measure L.
Consistency with the Draft Waterfront Specific Plan is not discussed in this EIR, as CEQA does not
require analysis of plans or policies that are in draft form and have not yet been adopted by the lead
agency. CEQA Guidelines Section 15125(d) requires an EIR to evaluate consistency with “applicable
plans and policies adopted for the purpose of avoiding or mitigating an environmental effect.”
Because the Draft Waterfront Specific Plan has not been adopted, it is not considered an applicable
plan for purposes of CEQA review.
The City also received a comment regarding urban blight and urban decay. Although neither urban
blight nor urban decay are potential impacts identified in Appendix G of the CEQA Guidelines, this
section addresses a comment submitted by an individual that raises concerns regarding these
issues. The case law cited by the commenter (Bakersfield Citizens for Local Control v. City of
Bakersfield (2004) 124 Cal.App.4th 1184) is not applicable to the proposed project because the
proposed project would not draw business or recreators away from existing businesses or
recreation opportunities at the Waterfront. On the contrary, the construction of recreational and
ferry facilities proposed by the project would have positive economic and social effects on the
Berkeley Waterfront and surrounding areas by drawing new customers and recreators to the area.
Existing businesses and existing recreational uses would continue and could flourish from increased
activity at the Berkeley Waterfront.

Specific Thresholds of Significance
For purposes of this analysis, the following thresholds are used to evaluate the significance of land
use/planning impacts resulting from implementation of the proposed project.
   New or replacement land uses resulting in physically dividing a community area within Berkeley.
   New or replacement land uses conflicting with the policies, measures, and standards of the
    BCDC San Francisco Bay Plan, ABAG/MTC Plan Bay Area 2050, Bay Area Clean Air Plan, Berkeley
    General Plan, Berkeley Municipal Code, Berkeley Marina Master Plan, Berkeley Climate Action
    Plan, Berkeley Local Hazard Mitigation Plan, or Berkeley Measure L.

The consistency analysis describes existing regional and local plans and policies and is intended to
fulfill the requirements of CEQA Guidelines Section 15125(d). The emphasis of the analysis is on the
project’s inconsistency and potential conflicts between the project and existing applicable land use
plans adopted for the purpose of avoiding or mitigating an environmental effect, and whether
inconsistencies, if any, would result in significant environmental effects. The project is considered
consistent with the provisions of the identified regional and local plans if it meets the general intent
of the applicable plans and does not conflict with directly applicable policies. A given project need
not be in perfect conformity with each and every policy nor does state law require precise
conformity of a proposed project with every policy or land use designation. Courts have also
acknowledged that general and specific plans attempt to balance a range of competing interests,
and that it is nearly, if not absolutely, impossible for a project to be in perfect conformity with each
and every policy set forth in the applicable plan.

Impact Evaluation

Established Community Division

Significance Criterion a: Would the proposed project physically divide an established community?

Impact LU-1     THE PROPOSED PROJECT WOULD NOT PHYSICALLY DIVIDE AN ESTABLISHED COMMUNITY AND
NO IMPACT WOULD OCCUR.


Construction
Impacts related to physical division of an established community primarily occur from the
implementation of infrastructure that could physically divide a community, such as a roadway that
limits movement. Construction would include landside improvements, including to the public plaza,
improvements to University Avenue and Seawall Drive, renovation of the parking lot, construction
of a new Bay Trail Extension, and implementation of associated amenities and utilities. Waterside
construction would include construction of the new pier, breakwater, and associated amenities for
recreation and the ferry. Activities would include demolition, dredging, pile-installation, installation
of the deck, float, and gangway. To the extent that construction activities obstruct roads, it would
be temporary and would not constitute a division of an established community (the Berkeley Marina
in this case). Therefore, no impacts related to potential division of a community would occur due to
construction of the project.




Draft Environmental Impact Report                                                                 3.9-11
City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project

Operation
The project site has a Berkeley General Plan land use designation of Waterfront/Marina and a
zoning designation of Unclassified (U), with existing land uses within the project site including
recreation, restaurant, marina, and transportation uses (roadways and surface parking). The
proposed project would involve the operation of a new ferry, at the same location as the existing
closed pier, and would establish the following land uses: (1) new infrastructure to support zero-
emission ferry service and (2) expanded recreational access. As described in Section 3.9.3, all uses
not prohibited by law are allowed in an Unclassified District, and a Use Permit is required to
establish any use in an Unclassified District. As such project operation is not prohibited by existing
zoning designations.
The established community located near the project site includes the people who reside on the live-
aboard boats within the Berkeley Marina. No new or altered operations would occur within the
Berkeley Marina Basin, and no permanent infrastructure would be established that would divide this
community. Existing and improved roadways would not be permanently blocked, access to the
community would not be limited, and movement within the community would not be limited.
Therefore, no operational impact related to the potential division of an established community
would occur.

Mitigation Measures
No mitigation would be required.

Significance After Mitigation
No Impact

 Policy 1. A proposed fill project should increase public access to the Bay to the maximum extent feasible, in accordance with the policies for                        Consistent. The proposed project would increase public access opportunities with the installation of a pier and breakwater, the development of
 Public Access to the Bay.                                                                                                                                             pedestrian and bicycle facilities connecting to the Bay Trail, and roadway safety improvements at the nearby public transit stops.
 Policy 2. In addition to the public access to the Bay provided by waterfront parks, beaches, marinas, and fishing piers, maximum feasible access                      Consistent. As described under Consistency with Public Access Policy 1, public access would be provided as part of the project design.
 to and along the waterfront and on any permitted fills should be provided in and through every new development in the Bay or on the shoreline,
 whether it be for housing, industry, port, airport, public facility, wildlife area, or other use, except in cases where public access would be clearly
 inconsistent with the project because of public safety considerations or significant use conflicts, including unavoidable, significant adverse
 effects on Bay natural resources. In these cases, in lieu access at another location, preferably near the project should be provided. If in lieu
 public access is required and cannot be provided near the project site, the required access should be located preferably near identified
 vulnerable or disadvantaged communities lacking well-maintained and convenient public access in order to foster more equitable public access
 around the Bay Area.
 Policy 4. Public access should be sited, designed and managed to prevent significant adverse effects on wildlife. To the extent necessary to                          Consistent.  understand the potential effects of public access on wildlife, information on the species and habitats of a proposed project site should be                           the pier would not result in significant impacts on wildlife.
 provided, and the likely human use of the access area analyzed. In determining the potential for significant adverse effects (such as impacts on
 endangered species, impacts on breeding and foraging areas, or fragmentation of wildlife corridors), site specific information provided by the
 project applicant, the best available scientific evidence, and expert advice should be used. In addition, the determination of significant adverse
 effects may also be considered within a regional context. Siting, design and management strategies should be employed to avoid or minimize
 adverse effects on wildlife, informed by the advisory principles in the Public Access Design Guidelines. If significant adverse effects cannot be
 avoided or reduced to a level below significance through siting, design and management strategies, then in lieu public access should be
 provided, consistent with the project and providing public access benefits equivalent to those that would have been achieved from on-site
 access. Where appropriate, effects of public access on wildlife should be monitored over time to determine whether revisions of management
 strategies are needed.

 l. The project would be planned to minimize the need for filling. (For example, all automobile parking should, wherever possible, be provided
    on nearby land or in multilevel structures rather than in extensive parking lots.)
 m. The proposed project would result in permanent public rights to use specific areas set aside for public access and recreation; these areas
    would be improved at least to finished grade and by installation of necessary basic utilities, at little or no cost to the public.
 n. The proposed project would, to the maximum extent feasible, establish a permanent shoreline in a particular area of the Bay, through
    dedication of lands and other permanent restrictions on all privately-owned and publicly-owned property bayward of the area approved for
    piers.
 o. The proposed project would provide, to the maximum extent feasible, for enhancement of fish and wildlife and other natural resources in
    the area of the development, and in no event would result in net damage to these values.

BERKELEY MUNICIPAL CODE CONSISTENCY
The project would comply with the Berkeley Zoning Ordinance, as the project uses would only be
allowed with a Use Permit under existing zoning and land designations. The project would also
comply with BMC Chapter 6.20, which governs the use of Marina facilities, as operation of the
project would be confined to the end of the municipal pier and out into the open water, which
would not interfere with the Marina. Consistency with Berkeley Municipal Code Chapter 6.52 and
Chapter 12.20, which regulate the removal and replacement of trees, is analyzed in Section 3.3,
Biological Resources, of this EIR (see Impact BIO-5). Therefore, the project would not conflict with
these Sections of the Berkeley Municipal Code, and related operational impacts would be less than
significant regarding consistency with these sections of the Code.
The City considered consistency with the noise thresholds established in Berkeley Municipal Code
Section 13.40. As described in detail under Impact NOI-1, construction noise impacts would exceed
the threshold established in the Code even after implementation of Mitigation Measure NOI-1 and
impacts were found to be significant and unavoidable.
Therefore, impacts related to Berkeley Municipal Code consistency would be significant and
unavoidable.

BERKELEY WATERFRONT MASTER PLAN CONSISTENCY
The Berkeley Waterfront Master Plan has a geographic scope that spans 170 acres of privately held
lands bounded by the Interstate 80 freeway on the east, the Berkeley Marina on the west, and the
Albany and Emeryville City limits on the north and south. The project site is not within the 170 acres
of privately held land that define the Plan’s geographic scope.
The Berkeley Waterfront Master Plan establishes a long-term vision for preserving and enhancing
the Waterfront as a recreational and open space resource while maintaining environmental quality
and public access. Although it is not within the geographic scope of the Plan, if these objectives
were applied to the project, it would be consistent with these objectives because it would reopen
the closed Berkeley Pier, provide new recreational opportunities, and improve shoreline access
through a public plaza and Bay Trail extension. The proposed project incorporates bicycle and
pedestrian improvements as well as water-dependent transportation, which aligns with policies to
reduce automobile dependence and enhance multimodal access. The proposed project would meet
or exceed applicable standards established by the Berkeley Waterfront Master Plan.

BERKELEY MARINA MASTER PLAN CONSISTENCY
The Berkeley Marina Master Plan provides a long-term vision for enhancing one of the City’s most
valued Waterfront assets. A key objective of the plan is to maintain and improve recreational,
environmental, and boating facilities while preserving the Marina’s open space and natural habitat.
The plan includes policies and capital improvements that support sustainable development of low-
impact and non-profit uses that will expand public access while complementing the Marina’s unique
character and ecological setting. Table 3.9-4, below, contains several of the Marina Master Plan
policies that are relevant to the project.

BERKELEY MEASURE L CONSISTENCY
As discussed above, Measure L provides that “no public parks” or “public open space... owned or
controlled or leased by the City or agency thereof, shall be used for any other purpose than public
parks and open space” without prior authorization from the voters (BMC Section 6.42.010). The
project is consistent with Measure L. None of the proposed project would take place within a public
park, with the exception of the installation of a new wayfinding sign in Shorebird Park. The
installation of this sign would not change the purpose or alter the use of Shorebird Park but rather is
consistent with its park use.
The other landside improvements would not take place on public parks or open space as defined by
Measure L. For example, the parking lot improvements would consist of renovations of an existing
parking lot; the cycle track improvements and bus facilities would be built in the public right of way;
the public plaza would replace an existing paved plaza area; and the Bay Trail Extension would be
built on an area currently occupied by parking stalls and a narrow dilapidated pathway. Even if the
improvements were located on public parks or open space as defined by Measure L, they would be
Measure L compliant because they do not change the use or purpose of these areas but rather
maintain their recreational nature and in fact enhance recreational opportunities there.
The waterside improvements include building a new pier in the same location as the existing,
deteriorated pier. The pier would not be built in a public park or in public open space as defined by
Measure L (see BMC 6.42.030). Even if the areas upon which the pier is built were subject to
Measure L, these improvements are Measure L compliant. This is because the new pier would not
change the purpose or alter the use of these areas because it is replacing the existing pier and
because it would maintain the recreational use of the area. In fact, the new pier would expand
recreational use because the current pier is inaccessible to the public.
In addition, the waterside improvements include installation of a ferry facility, ferry charging
infrastructure, and a breakwater in open water. None of these improvements would take place in
public parks or public open space as defined by Measure L. Even if these areas were subject to
Measure L, these waterside improvements do not change the use or purpose of these areas because
they will facilitate recreation by bringing recreators to the Waterfront and by providing recreational
opportunities. Therefore, the project would not conflict with Measure L, and related construction
and operational impacts would be less than significant.

3.10           Noise
3.10.1 Introduction
This section describes the existing conditions related to noise and vibration within the project site
and adjacent areas as well as the regulatory framework. This section also evaluates the possible
impacts related to noise and vibration that could result from construction and operation of the
proposed project. Information included in this section is based on the Berkeley General Plan, as well
as transportation volume data provided by Kittelson & Associates, Inc., which is included as
Appendix E to this EIR.

3.10.2 Environmental Setting
Characteristics of Noise
Sound is a vibratory disturbance created by a moving or vibrating source, which is capable of being
detected by the hearing organs. Noise is defined as sound that is loud, unpleasant, unexpected, or
undesired and may therefore be classified as a more specific group of sounds. The effects of noise
on people can include general annoyance, interference with speech communication, sleep
disturbance, and, in the extreme, hearing impairment. 1 Noise levels are commonly measured in
decibels (dB) using the A-weighted sound pressure level (dBA). The A-weighting scale is an
adjustment to the actual sound pressure levels so that they are consistent with the human hearing
response, which is most sensitive to frequencies around 4,000 Hertz (Hz) and less sensitive to
frequencies around and below 100 Hz. Decibels are measured on a logarithmic scale that quantifies
sound intensity in a manner similar to the Richter scale used to measure earthquake magnitudes. A
doubling of the energy of a noise source, such as doubling of roadway vehicle volume, would
increase the noise level by 3 dBA; reducing the energy in half would result in a 3 dBA decrease. 2
Table 3.10-1 shows some representative noise sources and their corresponding noise levels in dBA.




1 California Department of Transportation (Caltrans). 2013. Technical Noise Supplement to the Traffic Noise Analysis Protocol. (CT-

HWANP-RT-13-069.25.2) September. http://www.dot.ca.gov/hq/env/noise/pub/TeNS_Sept_2013B.pdf (accessed June 2025).
2 Crocker, Malcom J, Editor. 2007. Handbook of Noise and Vibration Control Book, ISBN: 978-0-471-39599-7, Wiley-VCH, October.

Human perception of noise has no simple correlation with sound energy: the perception of sound is
not linear in terms of dBA or in terms of sound energy. Two sources do not “sound twice as loud” as
one source. It is widely accepted that the average healthy ear can barely perceive changes of 3 dBA,
increase or decrease (i.e., twice the sound energy); that a change of 5 dBA is readily perceptible;
and that an increase (or decrease) of 10 dBA sounds twice (or half) as loud.
Sound changes in both level and frequency spectrum as it travels from the source to the receptor.
The most obvious change is the decrease in level as the distance from the source increases. The
manner in which noise reduces with distance depends on factors such as the type of sources (e.g.,
point or line, the path the sound will travel, site conditions, and obstructions). Noise levels from a
point source typically attenuate, or drop off, at a rate of 6 dBA per doubling of distance (e.g.,
construction, industrial machinery, ventilation units). Noise from a line source (e.g., roadway,
pipeline, railroad) typically attenuates at about 3 dBA per doubling of distance. The propagation of
noise is also affected by the intervening ground, known as ground absorption. A hard site, such as a
parking lot or smooth body of water, receives no additional ground attenuation and the changes in
noise levels with distance (drop-off rate) result from simply the geometric spreading of the source.
An additional ground attenuation value of 1.5 dBA per doubling of distance applies to a soft site
(e.g., soft dirt, grass, or scattered bushes and trees). Noise levels may also be reduced by
intervening structures. The amount of attenuation provided by this “shielding” depends on the size
of the object and the frequencies of the noise levels. Natural terrain features such as hills and dense
woods, and man-made features such as buildings and walls, can substantially alter noise levels.
Generally, any large structure blocking the line of sight will provide at least a 5-dBA reduction in
source noise levels at the receptor. 3 Structures can substantially reduce exposure to noise as well.
The Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) guidelines indicate that modern building construction
generally provides an exterior-to-interior noise level reduction of 20 to 35 dBA with closed windows.


3 FHWA. 2011. Highway Traffic Noise: Analysis and Abatement Guidance. December 2011.

https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/environment/noise/regulations_and_guidance/analysis_and_abatement_guidance/revguidance.pdf (accessed
June 2025).



3.10-2
                                                                                              Environmental Impact Analysis
                                                                                                                    Noise

The impact of noise is not a function of loudness alone. The time of day when noise occurs and the
duration of the noise are also important factors to consider when evaluating project noise impacts.
Most noise that lasts for more than a few seconds is variable in its intensity. Consequently, a variety
of noise descriptors have been developed. One of the most frequently used noise metrics is the
equivalent noise level (Leq), which considers both duration and sound power level. The Leq is defined
as the single steady A-weighted level equivalent to the same amount of energy as that contained in
the actual fluctuating levels over time. Typically, Leq is summed over a one-hour period. Lmax is the
highest root mean squared (RMS) sound pressure level within the sampling period, and Lmin is the
lowest RMS sound pressure level within the sampling period.
Noise that occurs at night tends to be more disturbing than that which occurs during the day.
Community noise is usually measured using Day-Night Average Level (Ldn), which is the 24-hour
average noise level with a +10 dBA penalty for noise occurring during nighttime (10:00 p.m. to
7:00 a.m.) hours; it is also measured using Community Noise Equivalent Level (CNEL), which is the
24-hour average noise level with a +5 dBA penalty for noise occurring from 7:00 p.m. to 10:00 p.m.
and a +10 dBA penalty for noise occurring from 10:00 p.m. to 7:00 a.m. Noise levels described by Ldn
and CNEL usually differ by about 1 dBA or less. The relationship between the peak-hour Leq value
and the Ldn/CNEL depends on the distribution of roadway noise during the day, evening, and night.
Quiet suburban areas typically have CNEL noise levels in the range of 40 to 50 dBA, while areas near
arterial streets are in the 50 to 60-plus CNEL range. Normal conversational levels are in the 60 to 65-
dBA Leq range; ambient noise levels greater than 65 dBA Leq can interrupt conversations. 4
Table 3.10-2 briefly defines measurement descriptors and other sound terminology used in this
section.

Characteristics of Vibration
Groundborne vibration of concern in environmental analysis consists of the oscillatory waves that
move from a source through the ground to adjacent structures. The number of cycles per second of
oscillation makes up the vibration frequency, described in terms of Hz. The frequency of a vibrating
object describes how rapidly it oscillates. The normal frequency range of most groundborne
vibration that can be felt by the human body is from a low of less than 1 Hz up to a high of about
200 Hz.2 Typically, groundborne vibration generated by human activities attenuates rapidly with
distance from the source of the vibration.
While people have varying sensitivities to vibrations at different frequencies, in general they are
most sensitive to low-frequency vibration. Vibration in buildings, such as from nearby construction
activities, may cause windows, items on shelves, and pictures on walls to rattle. Vibration of building
components can also take the form of an audible low-frequency rumbling noise, referred to as
groundborne noise. Groundborne noise is usually only a problem when the originating vibration
spectrum is dominated by frequencies in the upper end of the range (60 to 200 Hz), or when
foundations or utilities, such as sewer and water pipes, physically connect the structure and the
vibration source.4
Vibration energy spreads out as it travels through the ground, causing the vibration level to diminish
with distance away from the source. High-frequency vibrations diminish much more rapidly than
low frequencies, so low frequencies tend to dominate the spectrum at large distances from the



3.10-4
                                                                                               Environmental Impact Analysis
                                                                                                                     Noise

source. Discontinuities in the soil strata can also cause diffractions or channeling effects that affect
the propagation of vibration over long distances. 5 When a building is impacted by vibration, a
ground-to-foundation coupling loss will usually reduce the overall vibration level. However, under
rare circumstances, the ground-to-foundation coupling may amplify the vibration level due to
structural resonances of the floors and walls.
Vibration amplitudes are usually expressed in peak particle velocity (PPV). The PPV is normally
described in inches per second (in/sec). PPV is defined as the maximum instantaneous positive or
negative peak of a vibration signal. PPV is often used in monitoring of blasting vibration and other
construction activity because it is related to the stresses that are experienced by buildings.5

Noise-Sensitive Land Uses
Noise exposure goals for various types of land uses reflect the varying noise sensitivities associated
with those uses. The Environmental Management Element of the Berkeley General Plan identifies
residences, child-care centers, hospitals, nursing homes, and outdoor activity areas (such as those
associated with residences, schools, or parks) as noise-sensitive areas within the City. 6 Other noise-
sensitive land uses typically include libraries, schools, churches, and transient lodging (hotels and
motels). Sensitive land uses generally should not be subjected to noise levels that would be
considered intrusive in character or that would adversely affect their intended uses.

3.10.3 Regulatory Framework
Federal Regulations

Occupational Health and Safety Administration
The federal government regulates occupational noise exposure common in the workplace through
the Occupational Health and Safety Administration (OSHA). Noise limitations would apply to the
operation of construction equipment and could also apply to any proposed industrial land uses.
Noise exposure of this type is dependent on work conditions and is addressed through a facility’s
Health and Safety Plan, as required under OSHA, and is not addressed further in this analysis.

State Regulations

California General Plan Guidelines
State law requires general plans to include a Noise Element under Government Code Section
65302(f). The California General Plan Guidelines, published by the Governor’s Office of Planning and
Research, indicate acceptable, specific land use types in areas with specific noise exposure. The
guidelines also offer adjustment factors that may be used to arrive at noise acceptability standards
that reflect the noise control goals of the community, the community’s sensitivity to noise, and the
community’s assessment of the relative importance of noise pollution. These guidelines are
advisory, and local jurisdictions have the authority to set specific noise standards based on local
conditions.

Regional and Local Regulations

Berkeley General Plan 8
The Berkeley General Plan Environmental Management Element “…establishes policies for the
management and conservation of the city’s natural resources and the protection of the community
from hazards, pollution, and excessive noise”6. The following policies and actions from the
Environmental Management Element are applicable to the project:

Policy EM-43 Noise Reduction
Reduce significant noise levels and minimize new sources of noise. Actions:
A. Increase enforcement of the Noise Ordinance to reduce noise impacts.

Policy EM-44 Noise Prevention and Elimination
Protect public health and welfare by eliminating existing noise problems where feasible and by
preventing significant future degradation of the acoustic environment. Actions:
A. Incorporate noise considerations into land use planning decisions.
B. Ensure the effective enforcement of City, State, and Federal noise levels by appropriate City
   departments.

8 Berkeley, City of. 2002. Berkeley General Plan Environmental Management Element. Available:

https://berkeleyca.gov/sites/default/files/documents/11_Environmental%20Management%20Element-FINAL.pdf (accessed February
2026).

C. Coordinate with the California Occupational Safety and Health Administration (Cal-OSHA) to
   provide information on and enforcement of occupational noise requirements within the City of

Policy EM-46 Noise Mitigation
Require operational limitations and all feasible noise buffering for new uses that generate significant
noise impacts near residential, institutional, and recreational uses. Actions:
B. Mitigate significant noise impacts on parks and public open space, whenever feasible.

Policy EM-47 Land Use Compatibility
Ensure that noise-sensitive uses, including, but not limited to, residences, child-care centers,
hospitals, and nursing homes, are protected from detrimental noise levels. Action:
A. Noise-sensitive development proposals should be reviewed with respect to the Land Use
   Compatibility Guidelines below.
          If the noise level is within the “normally acceptable” level, noise exposure would be
          acceptable for the intended land use. Development may occur without requiring an
          evaluation of the noise environment unless the use could generate noise impacts on
          adjacent uses.
          If the noise level is within the “conditionally acceptable” level, noise exposure would be
          conditionally acceptable; a specified land use may be permitted only after detailed analysis
          of the noise environment and the project characteristics to determine whether noise
          insulation or protection features are required. Such noise insulation features may include
          measures to protect noise-sensitive outdoor activity areas (e.g., at residences, schools, or
          parks) or may include building sound insulation treatments such as sound-rated windows to
          protect interior spaces in sensitive receptors.
          If the noise level is within the “normally unacceptable” level, analysis and mitigation are
          required. Development should generally not be undertaken unless adequate noise
          mitigation options have been analyzed and appropriate mitigations incorporated into the
          project to reduce the exposure of people to unacceptable noise levels.
          If the noise level is within the “clearly unacceptable” level, new construction or
          development should not be undertaken unless all feasible noise mitigation options have
          been analyzed and appropriate mitigations incorporated into the project to reduce
          exposure of people to unacceptable noise levels.

3.10.4 Impacts Analysis
Significance Criteria
The City of Berkeley utilizes the following 2025 CEQA Guidelines Appendix G significance criteria
questions related to Noise. Would the proposed project:
a) Generate a substantial temporary or permanent increase in ambient noise levels in the vicinity
   of the project in excess of standards established in the local general plan or noise ordinance, or
   applicable standards of other agencies?
b) Generate excessive groundborne vibration or groundborne noise levels?




3.10-12
                                                                                                Environmental Impact Analysis
                                                                                                                      Noise

c) If located within the vicinity of a private airstrip or an airport land use plan or, where such a plan
   has not been adopted, within two miles of a public airport or public use airport, expose people
   residing or working in the project area to excessive noise levels?

Approach to Analysis
Please refer to Section 3.3, Biological Resources for a discussion of hydroacoustic effects on marine
mammals and fish.

Construction Noise
Construction noise was estimated using the FHWA Roadway Construction Noise Model (RCNM). 9
RCNM predicts construction noise levels for a variety of construction operations based on empirical
data and the application of acoustical propagation formulas. Using RCNM, construction noise levels
were estimated at sensitive receptors 10 near the project footprint based on the equipment list
expected to be used for the proposed project. RCNM provides reference noise levels for standard
construction equipment and applies noise attenuation at a rate of 6 dBA per doubling of distance
from the equipment.
Construction activity would result in temporary noise in the project area, exposing surrounding
sensitive receptors to increased noise levels. Construction of the project would involve both water
and land work. Construction phases involved with water work would include demolition, dredging,
pile installation, deck, float, and gangway construction, and amenities construction. Construction
phases involved with land work would include demolition, site preparation, grading, building
construction, paving, landscaping, and amenities construction. Construction equipment would
continually move around the project site over the course of a typical workday. Due to the complex
and mobile nature of construction activity within a project site, the FTA Transit Noise and Vibration
Impact Assessment Manual document recommends evaluating construction noise impacts from the
center of the construction site, stating that the distance variable in its recommended construction
noise calculation “assumes that all equipment operates at the center of the project.”4 Therefore,
construction noise impacts were evaluated from the approximate center of each work area where
construction activities are assumed to primarily occur during each phase. The three loudest pieces
of equipment were conservatively assumed to be operating at the same location at any given time.
Noise levels for various equipment types expected to be used during construction of the project are
based on reference noise levels from RCNM, shown in Table 3.10-8.

Stationary Operational Noise
The primary stationary noise (i.e., on-site operational noise) sources associated with the proposed
project would include operation of the new public plaza, recreational use of the extended pier and
new breakwater, and mechanical equipment associated with the Universal Charging Float. The
public plaza may be used for special events such as small concerts, fishing derbies, and pop-up-style
events. It is anticipated that special events would be limited to approximately five days per year
between the hours of 10:00 a.m. and 8:00 p.m. Amplified sound would only occur during special
events. The primary sources of noise-generating mechanical equipment associated with the
Universal Charging Floats are expected to consist of cooling equipment; however, the exact
equipment specifications are not known at the time of this analysis. Therefore, this analysis assumes
the use of a Carrier 30WG packaged chiller and heat pump for marine applications (or similar


3.10-14
                                                                                                   Environmental Impact Analysis
                                                                                                                         Noise

equipment). 11 Based on technical specifications for this product, this unit has a sound power level of
up to 78 dBA (depending on specific configurations and sizes), which equates to a sound pressure
level of 67 dBA at three feet away (see Appendix E for manufacturer's specifications). To determine
compliance with the City’s noise limits, this noise level/distance relationship was used to calculate
the expected noise level at the nearest sensitive receptors based on the proposed locations of the
Universal Charging Floats. It is assumed that this equipment operates as a point source of noise,
which has a characteristic noise attenuation of 6 dBA per doubling of distance away from the
source.

Mobile Operational Noise
The following approach was used for noise impacts from the operation of ferry vessels. Noise
measurement data for various electric and hybrid ferry vessels completed as part of the Silent@Sea
project 12 demonstrate that ferry vessels operating in electric propulsion mode generate noise levels
up to 73 dBA at a distance of 10 meters (32.8 feet). Use of this reference noise level represents a
conservative analysis, as it is based on noise measurement data of much larger vessels (i.e., vessels
111 meters in length); therefore, noise levels generated by the Berkeley WTPF ferry vessels would
likely be even lower. To determine compliance with the City’s noise limits, this noise level/distance
relationship was used to calculate the expected noise level at the nearest sensitive receptors based
on the proposed location of the ferry vessels and the nearest distance ferry vessels may operate
relative to nearby sensitive receptors.
In addition to operation of the ferry, the project would generate mobile operational noise in the
form of additional vehicles on nearby roadways (i.e., primarily on University Avenue) due to visitors
traveling to and from the project site. Existing roadway vehicles volumes were compared with
project-generated roadway vehicles volumes to determine the relative roadway vehicles noise
increase. Existing and project-generated roadway vehicles volumes used in this analysis are based
on roadway vehicles data provided by Kittelson & Associates, Inc. 13, presented in Table 3.10-9.

EIR Scoping Comments Consideration
This section addresses comments submitted by individuals and organizations in response to the EIR
NOP related to various concerns regarding noise impacts.
Organizations and individuals provided comments related to noise impacts from ferry operations.
These comments are discussed in the impact analysis below in Impact NOI-1. Scoping comments
related to noise impacts on biological resources, or underwater noise are addressed in Section 3.4,
Biological Resources.

Specific Thresholds of Significance
For purposes of this analysis, the following thresholds of significance are used to evaluate the
significance of noise and vibration resulting from implementation of the proposed project.

Construction Noise
The proposed project could have a significant impact if construction were to occur outside of the
allowable hours established in Berkeley Municipal Code Section 13.40.070(B)(7) (between 7:00 a.m.
and 7:00 p.m. on weekdays or between 9:00 a.m. and 8:00 p.m. on weekends or holidays). In
addition, construction noise impacts associated with the proposed project would be considered
significant if construction noise levels generated during allowable hours were to exceed the City’s
construction noise standards in Section 13.40.070(B)(7) (presented in Table 3.10-6 and Table 3.10-7
above).
While not zoned as residential uses, the live-aboard boats within the Marina were conservatively
evaluated using the City’s construction noise limits for low-density, multi-family residential land
uses. The multi-family residential threshold was chosen due to the quantity and density of live-
aboard boats in the Marina as well as the fact that the surrounding noise environment and nearby
land uses are more similar to that of a typical multi-family residential area compared to that of a
typical low-density residential area. Therefore, construction noise impacts upon live-aboard boats
were evaluated using the City’s construction noise threshold of 65 dBA for multi-family residential
land uses. The construction noise modeling in Impact NOI-1 uses the closest potential distance that


Draft Environmental Impact Report                                                                                          3.10-17
City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project

a live-aboard boat could be to construction, in order to provide a conservative analysis of the
loudest noise that could occur. Live-aboard boats within the Marina are located as close as
approximately 140 feet north of the project footprint. Thirteen houseboats within the Marina
located at the H and I docks as close as approximately 260 feet northwest of the project footprint.
Given that houseboats would be located further away than the closest live-aboard, the analysis
included in Impact NOI-1 would also apply for the houseboats.
The City does not define construction noise thresholds for parks or similar outdoor recreation
spaces (such as Shorebird Park); however, these uses are considered to be noise-sensitive receptors
pursuant to Berkeley General Plan Environmental Management Element Policy EM-47. 14 Therefore,
the City’s daytime construction noise threshold for similar noise-sensitive uses (i.e., low-density
residential land uses) of 60 dBA was used.

Stationary Operational Noise
Stationary operational noise impacts from mechanical equipment were analyzed using the Berkeley
Municipal Code maximum noise standards for multi-family residential as shown in Table 3.10-5
above. As explained above in the Construction Noise subsection, the multi-family residential land
use was used for the live-aboard boats, to provide a conservative analysis.
Pursuant to Berkeley Municipal Code Section 13.40.100, special event noise from the public plaza
would be significant if amplified sound increases the ambient noise level by more than 15 dBA 50
feet from the sound amplifying equipment. As discussed in the Existing Noise Conditions and
Sources section, the existing ambient noise level at ST-4 near the proposed plaza was measured to
be 51.6 dBA Leq during the day. Therefore, noise from special events would be significant if it
exceeds 66.6 dBA Leq at 50 feet from the sound amplifying equipment.

Mobile Operational Noise
A project normally has a significant effect on the environment related to noise if it substantially
increases the ambient noise levels in adjoining areas. Most people of average hearing ability can
detect changes in sound levels of approximately 3 dBA under normal, quiet conditions. Changes of 1
to 3 dBA are detectable under quiet, controlled conditions. Changes of less than 1 dBA are usually
not discernible. A change of 5 dBA is readily discernible to most people in an exterior environment.
Based on this, the following thresholds of significance, which are similar to those recommended by
the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) 15 were used to assess mobile off-site operational noise
impacts (i.e., roadway vehicle noise impacts) at sensitive receptors:
    Greater than 1.5 dBA Ldn/CNEL increase for ambient noise environments of 65 dBA Ldn/CNEL and
     higher
    Greater than 3 dBA Ldn/CNEL increase for ambient noise environments of 60-64 Ldn/CNEL
    Greater than 5 dBA Ldn/CNEL increase for ambient noise environments of less than 60 dBA
     Ldn/CNEL

As discussed in the Existing Noise Conditions and Sources section, the existing ambient noise level at
the project site was measured between approximately 49 and 57 dBA CNEL. Therefore, roadway
vehicle noise impacts would be considered significant if project-generated roadway vehicles were to
increase noise levels by 5 dBA CNEL or more.

Vibration
The City has not adopted a significance threshold to assess vibration impacts during construction
and operation. Therefore, vibration criteria recommended by the FTA (shown in Table 3.10-10) were
used to evaluate potential construction vibration impacts. Vibration impacts associated with
construction of the project would be significant if vibration levels exceed the FTA criteria shown in
Table 3.10-10 above at the nearest building structures. Based on these limits, vibration impacts
would be considered significant if levels were to exceed 0.3 in/sec PPV at any of the three
commercial structures near the project site. The nearest live-aboard boats and houseboats are
located on the water (and not on the ground surface where construction equipment would primarily
be operating). Due to the difference in mechanical impedance between the ground and water
surface, groundborne vibration levels resulting from use of construction equipment on land would
not effectively transmit to the water, as there would be substantial vibration energy loss at the
interface between land and water. Vibration levels at the nearest live-aboard boats and houseboats
would be negligible and are not evaluated further.

are conservatively assumed to be operating simultaneously. Noise levels associated with use of the

CONSTRUCTION ACTIVITIES

Landside
Construction of landside components would be limited to between 7:00 a.m. and 7:00 p.m. on
weekdays and between 9:00 a.m. and 8:00 p.m. on weekends or holidays, consistent with Section
13.40.070(B)(7) of the City’s Municipal Code. Landside improvements would include the public
plaza, improvements on University Avenue and Seawall Drive, the renovated parking lot, the new
Bay Trail Extension, and all associated amenities and utilities. Construction of landside components



3.10-20
                                                                                                  Environmental Impact Analysis
                                                                                                                        Noise

would include demolition; site preparation; geotechnical solutions, such as deep soil mixing and/or
retaining walls at the proposed plaza; grading; construction of proposed project components;
paving; landscaping; and placement of amenities.
Landside construction activities would occur in various locations within the project area.
Construction noise levels were conservatively calculated based on the closest distance between
each primary work area and the nearest sensitive receptor. Due to the mobile nature of
construction equipment over the course of a workday, construction noise levels at nearby sensitive
receptors were calculated from the approximate center of the various work areas, as this is more
representative of average noise levels over the course of a day. Estimated unmitigated landside
construction noise levels are presented at nearby sensitive receptors by construction phase in
Table 3.10-13. As shown in Table 3.10-13, unmitigated construction noise levels associated with
most phases of construction (i.e., site preparation, grading, geotechnical solutions, building
construction, paving, landscaping, and amenities installation) would exceed the City’s daytime noise
limits at the respective nearby sensitive receptors. Noise impacts associated with landside
construction activities would be potentially significant.
Implementation of Mitigation Measure NOI-1, including the use of temporary noise barriers, would
reduce landside construction noise levels by up to 20 dBA. 16,17 A comparison of landside
construction noise levels at nearby sensitive receptors with and without implementation of
Mitigation Measure NOI-1 is presented by phase in Table 3.10-14. As shown in Table 3.10-14,
implementation of Mitigation Measure NOI-1 would reduce construction noise levels associated
with each phase of landside construction to below the City’s respective limits at nearby sensitive
receptors. Therefore, landside construction noise impacts would be less than significant with
mitigation.

Waterside
Like landside project components, construction of waterside components would be limited to
between 7:00 a.m. and 7:00 p.m. on weekdays and between 9:00 a.m. and 8:00 p.m. on weekends
or holidays, consistent with Section 13.40.070(B)(7) of the City’s Municipal Code. However,
construction of waterside components may also require nighttime work to complete pile driving.
Noise impacts associated with nighttime construction work is discussed in the following section.
Waterside improvements would include improvements for the new pier, breakwater, and
associated amenities for recreation and the ferry. Construction of waterside components would
include demolition, dredging, pile installation, installation of the deck, float, and gangway, and
placement of amenities.
Waterside construction activities would primarily occur near the pier entrance, which represents
the location of waterside construction activities occurring to the nearest sensitive receptor (i.e.,
Shorebird Park to the east). Construction noise levels for all waterside activities were conservatively
calculated assuming that all construction equipment for each phase would be operating
simultaneously in this area. Estimated waterside construction noise levels are presented by
construction phase in Table 3.10-15. As shown in Table 3.10-15, construction noise levels associated
with most phases of waterside activities would exceed the City’s applicable noise threshold at the
nearest sensitive receptors (i.e., Shorebird Park to the east, Skates on the Bay Restaurant to the
north, and live-aboard boats to the northeast). Noise impacts associated with waterside
construction activities would be potentially significant.
Implementation of Mitigation Measure NOI-1, including the use of temporary noise barriers, would
reduce construction noise levels by up to 20 dBA for demolition, dredging, and construction of
waterside infrastructure and amenities (excluding pile driving). 18,19 Shrouding of pile driving
equipment would attenuate noise levels by 10 dBA or more. A comparison of waterside construction
noise levels at nearby sensitive receptors with and without implementation of Mitigation Measure
NOI-1 is presented in Table 3.10-16. As shown in Table 3.10-16, implementation of Mitigation
Measure NOI-1 would result in mitigated daytime construction noise levels of up to 70 dBA at
Shorebird Park, up to 67 dBA at the Skates on the Bay Restaurant, and up to 57 dBA at the nearest
live-aboard boats. Mitigated general construction noise levels at the Skates on the Bay Restaurant
and the nearest live-aboard boats would not exceed the City’s daytime noise thresholds of 70 and
65 dBA for commercial and multi-family residential uses, respectively. However, mitigated pile
driving noise levels (during the demolition and pile installation phases) at Shorebird Park would still
exceed the City’s daytime construction noise threshold of 60 dBA for low-density residential (or
similar noise-sensitive uses). Therefore, waterside construction noise impacts associated with pile
driving would be significant and unavoidable.

Nighttime Construction Work
Construction of waterside components may require nighttime construction work, which would
consist of pile driving to install piles for the pier. Nighttime pile driving is assumed to utilize the
same equipment as that during the daytime pile installation phase, which would be an impact pile
driver, crane, and a compressor. Simultaneous operation of these equipment types would produce a
combined noise level of 89 dBA Leq at a reference distance of 50 feet. During the initial periods of
pile installation, pile driving would occur at the pier entrance as close as 150 feet from Shorebird
Park and as close as 670 feet from the nearest potential live-aboard boat. At these distances, pile
driving activity would generate noise levels up to 79 and 66 dBA Leq at Shorebird Park and the
nearest live-aboard boat, respectively, which would exceed the respective City’s nighttime noise
limits of 45 dBA at R-1 and R-2 zoning districts and 55 dBA at R-3 zoning districts. 20 Therefore, noise
impacts associated with nighttime construction work would be potentially significant.
Implementation of Mitigation Measure NOI-1 would include measures to reduce noise impacts
associated with nighttime pile driving, which would reduce nighttime construction noise impacts by
up to 10 dBA or more. A comparison of nighttime construction noise levels with and without
implementation of Mitigation Measure NOI-1 is presented in Table 3.10-17. As shown in
Table 3.10-17, mitigated nighttime pile driving noise levels at Shorebird Park would be reduced from
79 dBA to 69 dBA, which would exceed the City’s nighttime noise threshold of 45 dBA for R-1 and R-
2 (i.e., low-density residential) zones. Mitigated nighttime construction noise levels at the nearest
live-aboard boat would be reduced from 66 dBA to 56 dBA, which would exceed the City’s nighttime
noise threshold of 55 dBA at R-3 (i.e., “Multi-family Residential”) zones. Therefore, noise impacts
associated with nighttime construction work would be significant and unavoidable.

   The zoning for the Marina area is “Unclassified” according to City’s Official Zoning Map (June 2022). However, based on the noise

this sensitive receptor. Based on the number of live-aboard boats within the Marina, it is assumed that the R-3 zoning (i.e., “Multiple-
family Residential”) is most applicable to these sensitive receptors.
