4          Other CEQA Required Discussions

This chapter discusses growth-inducing impacts and irreversible environmental impacts that would
be caused by the proposed project.

4.1        Significant Environmental Effects that Cannot be
           Avoided
Section 15126.2(b) of the CEQA Guidelines requires that an EIR describe any significant impacts that
cannot be avoided, even with the implementation of feasible mitigation measures. Implementation
of the proposed project would result in significant and unavoidable project-level and cumulative
impacts related to the following:
   Project-level Impacts
     Project-level waterside construction noise associated with pile driving and nighttime
        construction work noise (see Section 3.10, Noise);
     Project-level impacts related to the construction of new recreational facilities due to
        construction noise;
     Project-level impacts related to consistency with a regulation adopted for the purpose of
        avoiding or mitigating an environmental effect due to construction noise impacts (see
        Section 3.9, Land Use and Planning).
   Cumulative Impacts
     Cumulative waterside construction noise associated with pile driving and nighttime
        construction (see Section 3.10, Noise);
     Cumulative operational mobile (i.e., roadway vehicle) noise (see Section 3.10, Noise);
     Cumulative impacts related to the construction of new recreational facilities due to
        construction noise and cumulative operational noise impacts (see Section 3.11, Recreation);
     Cumulative impacts related to consistency with a regulation adopted for the purpose of
        avoiding or mitigating an environmental effect due to construction and operational noise
        impacts (see Section 3.9, Land Use and Planning).

4.2        Growth Inducing Impacts
There are two types of growth-inducing impacts that a project may have: direct and indirect. To
assess the potential for growth-inducing impacts, the proposed project’s characteristics that may
encourage and facilitate activities that individually or cumulatively may affect the environment must
be evaluated. CEQA Guidelines Section 15126.2(d) requires a discussion of a proposed project’s
potential to foster economic or population growth, including ways in which a project could remove
an obstacle to growth. Growth does not necessarily create significant physical changes to the
environment. However, depending upon the type, magnitude, and location of growth, it can result
in significant adverse environmental effects. The CEQA Guidelines, as interpreted by the City, state
that a significant growth-inducing impact may result if the proposed project would:




Draft Environmental Impact Report                                                                 4-1
City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project

     Induce substantial population growth in an area (for example, by proposing or facilitating new
      residences or employment-generating uses beyond the land use density/intensity envisioned in
      the general plan or other regional planning documents, such as Plan Bay Area 2050+);
     Substantially alter the planned location, distribution, density, or growth rate of the population
      of an area; or
     Include extensions of roads or other infrastructure not assumed in the general plan or adopted
      capital improvements project list when such infrastructure exceeds the needs of a project and
      could accommodate unplanned future development.

Direct growth-inducing impacts occur when the implementation of a project imposes new burdens
on a community by directly inducing population growth, or by leading to the construction of
additional developments in the same area. Also included in this category are projects that remove
physical obstacles to population growth (such as a new road into an undeveloped area or a
wastewater treatment plant with excess capacity that could allow additional development in the
service area). The proposed project would not entail housing or employment-generating office or
commercial uses, and would not alter the planned location, distribution, or growth rate of Berkeley
population.
Construction of transportation and recreational infrastructure, such as the proposed project, have
the potential to facilitate and serve growth. Projects that physically remove obstacles to growth, or
projects that indirectly induce growth, may provide a catalyst for future unrelated development in
an area such as a new residential community that requires additional public and transportation
services to support residents. While the proposed project would entail additional public transit
infrastructure in the form of ferry service, a raised cycle track, and improved bus stops, the
proposed additional transit service provided via the proposed project would serve existing
transportation demands and provide an alternative mode of transportation in lieu of single-
occupancy vehicle Transbay trips from the East Bay to San Francisco. For these reasons,
implementation of the proposed project would not result in direct or indirect growth-inducing
impacts.

4.2.1        Population and Employment Growth
The proposed project would not directly generate population or employment growth, because it
would not include the development of residential, commercial, or industrial uses. The proposed
project would entail the implementation of new ferry service between Berkeley and San Francisco.
The following discussion is focused on the potential for the new ferry service to result in unplanned
population and employment growth.
The implementation of new ferry service would allow individuals to commute from Berkeley to San
Francisco via ferry vessels. The proposed project may induce population growth if the new ferry
service results in land use changes that would support unplanned intensified development.
However, this is not expected to occur given the current planning for the project site and adjacent
area. Specifically, as discussed in Section 3.15, Effects Found Not to be Significant (see Section
3.15.3, Population and Housing), Plan Bay Area 2050 identifies that the area around the project site
has been identified as an area where growth is planned, including a planned ferry terminal;




4-2
                                                                                        Other CEQA Required Discussions



therefore, growth that occurs in the future as a result of the new ferry service would be considered
planned. 1
Furthermore, as shown in Section 3.9, Land Use and Planning, the project is overall consistent with
the policies in local plans, including the Berkeley General Plan. Future growth in the area near the
project site would require approvals from the City of Berkeley, and the City is currently in the
process of updating its Waterfront Specific Plan that would facilitate additional development in the
area. As shown in Table 3-1, the Draft Waterfront Specific Plan is considered as part of the
cumulative scenario for this EIR. Overall, the proposed ferry service would be beneficial and
complementary to land use and future growth plans. For these reasons, implementation of the
proposed project would not lead to direct or indirect growth impacts beyond what is anticipated
and planned for the region.

4.2.2         Removal of Obstacles to Growth
The proposed project is located in an area that is well served by existing utility and roadway
infrastructure. As described in Chapter 2, Project Description, the project would include utility
infrastructure extensions that would connect to existing utility infrastructure, including electrical,
water, wastewater, and telecommunication connections. Because these utility extensions and
connections would be sized to serve the proposed project, they would not result in the removal of
an obstacle for growth. The proposed project would also include roadway improvements,
specifically the repaving and restriping of University Avenue (between Marina Boulevard and
Seawall Drive) and Seawall Drive. However, these roadway improvements would not present a
significant change to existing roadway circulation and would be intended to accommodate expected
roadway vehicle volumes and project site access needs. No new roads would be required. The
project would not require the extension of new utility or roadway infrastructure through
undeveloped areas.
Furthermore, since the proposed project would not extend utility or roadway services into
undeveloped areas, propose new housing or businesses, or create infrastructure that would attract
additional population growth, it would not induce substantial unplanned population growth, either
directly or indirectly. Therefore, project operation would not conflict with land use policies of Plan
Bay Area 2050. For these reasons, project implementation would not remove an obstacle to growth.

4.3           Irreversible Environmental Effects
CEQA Guidelines Section 15126(c) requires that EIRs contain a discussion of significant irreversible
environmental changes and analyze the extent to which a project’s primary and secondary effects
would affect the environment and commit nonrenewable resources to uses that future generations
would not be able to reverse. “Significant irreversible environmental changes” include the use of
nonrenewable natural resources during implementation of the project, should this use result in the
unavailability of these resources in the future. Also, irreversible damage can result from
environmental accidents associated with the project. Irretrievable commitments of these resources
are required to be evaluated in an EIR to ensure that such consumption is justified.




1 Metropolitan Transportation Commission and Association of Bay Area Governments. 2021. Plan Bay Area 2050.

https://planbayarea.org/sites/default/files/documents/2021-05/Draft_Plan_Bay_Area_2050_May2021_0.pdf. (accessed June 2025).



Draft Environmental Impact Report                                                                                             4-3
City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project

CEQA also requires decision-makers to balance the benefits of a proposed project against its
unavoidable environmental risks in determining whether to approve a project. This discussion
addresses the use of non-renewable resources and irreversible impacts associated with the
construction and operation of the proposed project.
Construction of the proposed project would include the use of building materials and energy, some
of which would be non-renewable resources. Consumption of these resources would occur with any
development in the Bay Area region and are not unique to the Berkeley Waterfront area or the
proposed project. However, as discussed in Section 3.6, Greenhouse Gas Emissions and Energy, use
of such resources is not unusual compared to common construction projects and would not
substantially affect the availability of such resources.
The project would require an irreversible operational commitment of City services, including
electricity, water supply, and wastewater treatment. As discussed in Section 3.15, Effects Found Not
to be Significant (see Section 3.15.4, Public Services) and Section 3.14. Utilities and Service Systems,
impacts to public services and utilities would be less than significant. While the project would result
in an irreversible commitment of City services, the project would also offer emergency services,
such as the emergency movement of survivors, first responders, and disaster service workers
following a major disaster.
Because the proposed project would implement electric ferry service, operation of ferry service
would not increase local demand for non-renewable energy resources such as petroleum fuel and
natural gas. The proposed project would, however, increase the demand for electricity to power the
ferry vessels and the associated infrastructure on the project site (i.e., lighting, restroom). As
described in Section 3.6, Greenhouse Gas Emissions and Energy, electricity includes both renewable
and non-renewable sources, with sources becoming increasingly more renewable to comply with SB
100 requirements. The project’s consumption of electricity would constitute, in part, an irreversible
consumption of some non-renewable sources.
While there would be no new population and housing growth and associated roadway vehicle trips
resulting from implementation of the proposed project, additional roadway vehicle trips to access
the project site to utilize project ferry and recreational services would increase petroleum fuel use
by such vehicles. However, as discussed in Section 3.12, Transportation, on balance the project
would result in an overall reduction in vehicle miles traveled or VMT. Therefore, the project would
replace existing roadway vehicle trips that use petroleum fuel for the entirety of travel from the East
Bay to San Francico with shorter roadway vehicle trips to access the project site and then use the
electric ferry to traverse to San Francisco. Therefore, the irreversible environmental effect from
roadway vehicle petroleum use and associated generated criteria pollutants, toxic air contaminants,
and greenhouse gas emissions would be less than compared to existing conditions. Furthermore,
the project would provide new electric roadway vehicle charging parking spaces that could
encourage roadway vehicle users to opt for use of electric-run rather than petroleum-run vehicles.
As discussed in Section 3.15, Effects Found Not to Be Significant, and above in Section 4.2, Growth
Inducing Impacts, the proposed project would not extend services to unplanned development,
propose new housing or businesses, or create infrastructure that would attract additional
population growth. Therefore, the proposed project would not induce substantial unplanned
population growth, either directly or indirectly, that would result in the commitment of
nonrenewable resources needed to support unplanned population growth.

4.4        Mandatory Findings of Significance
Pursuant to CEQA Guidelines Appendix G Section XVIII, the following mandatory findings of
significance analysis is provided.

a. Does the proposed plan have the potential to substantially degrade the quality of the
   environment, substantially reduce the habitat of a fish or wildlife species, cause a fish or wildlife
   population to drop below self-sustaining levels, threaten to eliminate a plant or animal
   community, substantially reduce the number or restrict the range of a rare or endangered plant
   or animal or eliminate important examples of the major periods of California history or
   prehistory?
The proposed project would not eliminate or threaten wildlife habitats. As discussed in more detail
in Section 3.3, Biological Resources, implementation of the proposed project could result in
construction and operational impacts related to wildlife, fish, and plant species. However, with
implementation of identified mitigation measures, biological resources impacts would be less than
significant with mitigation. The proposed project would also not eliminate important examples of
the major periods of California history or prehistory. As discussed in more detail in Section 3.4,
Cultural Resources, and Section 3.13, Tribal Cultural Resources, implementation of the proposed
project could result in construction impacts related to historic, archaeological, and tribal resources.
However, with implementation of identified mitigation measures, cultural and tribal cultural
resources impacts would be less than significant with mitigation.

b. Does the proposed plan have impacts that are individually limited, but cumulatively
   considerable? (“Cumulatively considerable” means that the incremental effects of a project are
   considerable when viewed in connection with the effects of past projects, the effects of other
   current projects, and the effects of probable future projects)?
Cumulative impacts are discussed throughout this EIR, in the individual environmental resource
topic sections of Chapter 3. Section 3.10, Noise, identifies that it is possible that construction of the
proposed project and other cumulative projects could occur at the same time. This section also
identifies that even with implementation of project mitigation and the cumulative project adhering
to City construction noise thresholds, it is possible that construction noise levels may still exceed the
City thresholds due to the quantity of cumulative projects and their close proximities to one
another. As such, this EIR concludes that the proposed project’s contribution to a potentially
significant construction-related cumulative noise impact could be significant and unavoidable (if
construction of cumulative projects occur at the same time as the Project).
In addition, while the proposed project would not individually result in a significant roadway vehicle
operational noise impact, when other cumulative projects are considered (namely the maximum
potential development associated with the Draft Waterfront Specific Plan) in conjunction with the
proposed project, the proposed project would have a significant and unavoidable contribution to a
cumulative roadway vehicle operational noise impact. Because of this cumulative impact, the
proposed project would also result in cumulative impacts related to environmental effects from the
implementation of new recreational facilities, as well as consistency with a regulation (Berkeley
Municipal Code) adopted for the purpose of avoiding or mitigating an environmental effect.

c. Does the proposed plan have environmental effects which will cause substantial adverse effects
   on human beings, either directly or indirectly?
The proposed project would result in adverse effects on human beings. As discussed in more detail
in Section 3.2, Air Quality, and Section 3.10, Noise, implementation of the proposed project could
result in temporary construction impacts related to air quality and noise that could, in turn, affect
human beings. With implementation of identified mitigation measures, temporary construction
impacts associated with air quality (criteria air pollutants and toxic air contaminants) and some of
the temporary construction impacts associated with noise would be less than significant or less than
significant with mitigation. However, there remains potential for significant and unavoidable
adverse impacts to human beings due to noise generated during waterside construction and
nighttime construction work. In addition, the project’s contribution to the cumulative operational
mobile (i.e., roadway vehicle) noise impact would be significant and unavoidable.

5          Alternatives

5.1        Introduction
Pursuant to California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) Guidelines Section 15126.6, this chapter
contains a comparative impact assessment of alternatives to the proposed project. The primary
purpose of an alternatives analysis under CEQA is to provide decision-makers and the public with a
reasonable range of feasible alternatives to the proposed project that could attain most of the basic
project’s objectives, while avoiding or reducing any of the project’s significant adverse
environmental effects.
Analysis of three alternatives to the proposed project is provided for informational purposes and to
allow decision-makers to consider the proposed project in light of hypothetical alternatives, thereby
promoting CEQA’s purpose as an information disclosure statute. This analysis is guided by the
following considerations set forth under CEQA Guidelines Section 15126.6:
   An EIR need not consider every conceivable alternative to a project;
   An EIR should identify alternatives that were considered by the lead agency, but rejected as
    infeasible during the scoping process;
   Reasons for rejecting an alternative include:
     Failure to meet most of the basic project objectives;
     Infeasibility; or
     Inability to avoid significant environmental effects.

5.2        Significant Impacts
The implementation of the proposed project was analyzed for potentially significant impacts related
to each of the environmental issues discussed in Sections 3.1 through 3.14. The results of the
analysis indicate that the proposed project would result in the following significant and unavoidable
impacts:
   Land Use and Planning (inconsistency with noise standards established by the Berkeley
    Municipal Code)
   Noise (waterside construction noise impacts associated with pile driving and nighttime
    construction noise)
   Recreation (construction noise impacts related to the construction of a recreational resource)

In addition, the results of the analysis indicate that the proposed project would result in the
following significant impacts that would be reduced to a less-than-significant level with mitigation:
   Aesthetics (construction impacts related to nighttime lighting)
   Air Quality (construction impacts related to criteria air pollutants and Toxic Air Contaminants)
   Biological Resources (construction impacts on special-status species, sensitive marine habitats,
    jurisdictional waters, and consistency with local policies protecting biological resources; and
    operation impacts on special-status species, jurisdictional waters, wildlife movement, and
    consistency with local policies protecting biological resources)

     Cultural Resources (construction impacts related to unanticipated archaeological resources)
     Geology and Soils (construction impacts related to unique paleontological resource or geologic
      feature)
     Hydrology and Water Quality (waterside construction impacts related to water quality)

5.3          Project Objectives
As described in Chapter 2, Project Description, the City’s project objectives are as follows:
     Enhance public access and recreational opportunities at the Berkeley Waterfront that:
       Develop or enhance public pier facilities at the City of Berkeley Waterfront.
       Provide sufficient public access and recreational opportunities at the Berkeley Waterfront
         that meet regional needs, consistent with BCDC Bay Plan Policies maximizing access to the
         Bay.
       Minimize environmental impacts by considering existing infrastructure and sea level rise
         projections.
       Encourage the use of public transit, bicycle, and other forms of active transportation and
         sustainable travel to access the site.

     Provide efficient and environmentally friendly zero emission public ferry service between
      Berkeley and San Francisco that:
       Improves regional connectivity and resiliency with enhanced public transportation choices
          for East Bay residents, including for accessing jobs in San Francisco and other locations along
          the Bay for commerce and recreational purposes, and to address existing deficiencies in the
          Transbay transportation network.
       Reduces the use of single-occupancy vehicles for Transbay trips, thereby reducing
          greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and air quality emissions and decreasing congestion on the
          regional roadway system, consistent with regional and Statewide goals.
       Provides travel times and costs that are competitive with other Transbay modes of travel.
       Provides public transit facilities that are compatible with operations and recreational
          activities at the Berkeley Waterfront.
       Provides navigable conditions for safe and efficient operation of ferry vessels.
       Provides options for emergency response and transportation services in case of an
          emergency, such as natural or human-caused event that disables roads, other transit,
          bridges, and/or tunnels.

For the purposes of this alternatives analysis, the City considers the two top bullets as the basic
project objectives. In other words, for an alternative to meet the basic project objectives, they
would need to meet of the following basic objectives: (1) enhance public access and recreational
opportunities at the Berkeley Waterfront and (2) provide efficient and environmentally friendly zero
emission public ferry service between Berkeley and San Francisco.

5.5             Alternative 1: No Project Alternative
5.5.1           Description
CEQA Guidelines Section 15126.6(e)(2) requires that the alternatives discussion include an analysis
of a “No Project” Alternative. Pursuant to CEQA, the “No Project” Alternative refers to the analysis
of existing conditions and what would reasonably be expected to occur in the foreseeable future if
the proposed project was not approved. This is based on current plans and consistent with available
infrastructure information. Pursuant to CEQA Guidelines 15126.6(e)(3)(a,b), the “No Project”
Alternative typically will proceed along one of two lines: (1) when a project is a revision of an
existing regulatory plan or policy, the “No Project” Alternative will be continuation of the existing
plan or policy; or (2) if a project is something other than a land use regulatory plan, such as a
development project on identifiable property, the “No Project” Alternative is the circumstance



Draft Environmental Impact Report                                                                             5-3
City of Berkeley
Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project

under which a project does not proceed. Thus, in the case of this EIR for a project and not a plan,
the “No Project” Alternative would entail the circumstance under which a project does not proceed.
Under the No Project Alternative, none of the improvements associated with the project and the
current uses would remain. Below is a summary of the No Project Alternative.
     The pier, breakwater, and associated infrastructure for the ferry vessels would not be installed,
      and the pier would continue to deteriorate and remain closed to the public.
     No new ferry service from Berkeley would be established and vehicle trips across the Bay would
      continue at their current rate.
     No new public plaza would be installed.
     None of the improvements along University Avenue or Seawall Drive would be installed,
      including no new cycle track, no upgraded bus facilities, and no Bay Trail Extension. Vehicles,
      buses, pedestrians, and bicyclists would continue to use the existing facilities.
     The Seawall Drive East Parking lot would remain in its current condition.
     None of the construction associated with the project would occur.

5.5.2        Impact Analysis
Aesthetics
Under Alternative 1, the site would remain in its current condition, with no ferry infrastructure,
public plaza, recreation, or transportation improvements implemented. Existing facilities such as the
deteriorating pier and Seawall Drive East Parking lot would remain unchanged, and vehicle trips
across the Bay would continue at their current rate. The Waterfront would not undergo any
aesthetic improvements that would otherwise be facilitated by the proposed project. Furthermore,
residents would have limited opportunities to access the scenic quality of the Waterfront, as under
Alternative 1, the pier would remain closed and the Waterfront would continue to deteriorate.
However, there would be no adverse construction-related impacts to aesthetics. Therefore,
Alternative 1 impacts to aesthetics would be less than significant.
The proposed project’s impacts related to aesthetics would be less than significant with mitigation
(see Section 3.1, Aesthetics). Alternative 1 would have a greater level of aesthetics impacts
compared to the proposed project, but not to the extent of increasing the impact significance level.
This greater level of impact would be due to the lack of an update in the design, lighting standards,
and Waterfront improvements that the proposed project would provide. While Alternative 1 would
not require Mitigation Measure AES-1, since it would not require nighttime construction, these
would be temporary impacts, while the overall lack of updating the project site would be a
permanent effect. For that reason, Alternative 1 would have a greater impact than the proposed
project.

Air Quality
Under Alternative 1, the site would remain in its current condition, with no ferry infrastructure,
public plaza, recreation, or transportation improvements implemented. Existing facilities such as the
deteriorating pier and Seawall Drive East Parking lot would remain unchanged, and vehicle trips
across the Bay would continue at their current rate. There would not be any temporary
construction-related impacts on air quality. However, in the long term, there would be fewer
reductions in criteria pollutants, as Bay Area residents would continue to utilize single-occupancy



5-4
                                                                                          Alternatives



vehicles for transbay transportation. Alternative 1 impacts on air quality would be less than
significant.
The proposed project’s impacts related to air quality would be less than significant with mitigation
(see Section 3.2, Air Quality). Alternative 1 would not result in the construction-related emissions
associated with the proposed project. However, Alternative 1 would result in greater levels of
criteria pollutant and toxic air contaminant emission due to the continued projected growth in the
region. Without the implementation of zero-emissions transportation infrastructure, Alternative 1
would have greater Air Quality emissions impacts compared to the proposed project.

Biological Resources
Under Alternative 1, the site would remain in its current condition, with no ferry infrastructure,
public plaza, recreation, or transportation improvements implemented. Existing facilities such as the
deteriorating pier and Seawall Drive East Parking lot would remain unchanged, and vehicle trips
across the Bay would continue at their current rate. Alternative 1 would not adversely affect
terrestrial or marine wildlife or habitats, as Alternative 1 would not involve any ground disturbance,
construction, or operation of ferry service. Therefore, Alternative 1 would have no impact on
biological resources.
The proposed project’s impacts related to biological resources would be less than significant with
mitigation (see Section 3.3, Biological Resources). Alternative 1 would result in reduced impacts on
biological resources, as there would be no project construction. Therefore, the impact significance
level would be reduced, and no mitigation would be required.

Cultural Resources
Under Alternative 1, the site would remain in its current condition, with no ferry infrastructure,
public plaza, recreation, or transportation improvements implemented. Existing facilities such as the
deteriorating pier and Seawall Drive East Parking lot would remain unchanged. No construction-
related ground disturbance would occur, and therefore, Alternative 1 would not pose any potential
risk of altering cultural resources. Therefore, Alternative 1 would have no impact on cultural
resources.
The proposed project’s impacts related to cultural resources would be less than significant with
mitigation (see Section 3.4, Cultural Resources). Alternative 1 would result in reduced impacts, as
the alternative would not facilitate any construction or excavation. Therefore, the impact
significance level would be reduced, and no mitigation would be required.

Geology and Soils
Under Alternative 1, the site would remain in its current condition, with no ferry infrastructure,
public plaza, recreation, or transportation improvements implemented. Existing facilities such as the
deteriorating pier and Seawall Drive East Parking lot would remain unchanged. Given that no
dredging, site excavation, or other ground disturbing activities would occur, Alternative 1 would not
pose a risk to paleontological resources or unique geologic features. Therefore, Alternative 1 would
have no impact on geology and soils.
The proposed project’s impacts related to geology and soils would be less than significant with
mitigation (see Section 3.5, Geology and Soils). Alternative 1 would have a lesser impact level
compared to the proposed project due to the lack of ground disturbing activities that would

otherwise occur with development of the proposed project. The impact significance level would be

Greenhouse Gas Emissions and Energy
Under Alternative 1, the site would remain in its current condition, with no ferry infrastructure,
public plaza, recreation, or transportation improvements implemented. Existing facilities such as the
deteriorating pier and Seawall Drive East Parking lot would remain unchanged, and vehicle trips
across the Bay would continue at their current rate. Projected regional growth would continue
without the development of zero-emissions transbay transportation opportunities, and vehicle

there would be no construction-related GHG emissions impacts, and there would be no energy

energy use reductions associated with regional VMT reductions under Alternative 1 than would
occur under the proposed project. Therefore, Alternative 1 impacts related to GHG emissions and
energy would be greater than the proposed project.

Hazards and Hazardous Materials
Under Alternative 1, the site would remain in its current condition, with no ferry infrastructure,
public plaza, recreation, or transportation improvements implemented. Existing facilities such as the
deteriorating pier and Seawall Drive East Parking lot would remain unchanged. Less construction
would occur in what is characterized by the City of Berkeley as an Environmental Management Area,

There would also be no hazards related to the storage or maintenance of lithium batteries that
would be required to support operation of the ferry service. Additionally, while there would be
fewer visitors to the Waterfront, an area with strained emergency evacuation capabilities, there
would be no implementation of the additional emergency evacuation capabilities that the proposed
project would provide. Therefore, Alternative 1 impacts to hazards and hazardous materials would
be less than significant.
The proposed project’s impacts related to hazards and hazardous materials would be less than
significant (see Section 3.7, Hazardous Materials). Alternative 1 would have a similar impact level
compared to the proposed project. While construction of Alternative 1 would not require
excavation in areas that are potentially contaminated, Alternative 1 would also not remove
potential contaminants from the project site (i.e., potential creosote in pier pilings). In addition,
under the No Project Alternative, there would not be the added benefit of having emergency
evacuation capabilities from the ferry vessels.

construction activities that could potentially affect water quality from sedimentation or accidental

The proposed project’s impacts related to utilities and service systems would be less than significant

there would be no increased demand compared to existing conditions, as there would be no
construction or operation requiring water, wastewater, solid waste, telecommunication, or
electricity services beyond what is already available at the Berkeley Waterfront. Therefore,
Alternative 1 would have a reduced utilities and service systems impact significance level compared
to the proposed project.

5.5.3      Conclusion
In summary, because Alternative 1 (the No Project Alternative) would not require construction, it
would avoid the environmental impacts associated with biological resources, cultural resources,
geology and soils, recreation, tribal cultural resources, and utilities and service systems. In addition,
Alternative 1 would reduce impacts related to hydrology, water quality and noise. It would also
result in greater impacts to aesthetics, as it would enable the Waterfront facilities to continue
deteriorating without aesthetic improvements, however, impacts to aesthetics would remain at a
similar significance level. Impacts on air quality, GHG emissions, land use and planning, and
transportation are also expected to be greater than the proposed project, because Alternative 1
would not provide the same reductions in VMT, criteria air pollutants, and GHG emissions,
compared with the proposed project.
This Alternative would not meet the basic project objectives. This Alternative would not enhance
public access and recreational opportunities at the Berkeley Waterfront and would not provide
efficient and environmentally friendly zero emission public ferry service between Berkeley and San
Francisco.

this Alternative would depend on future engineering to identify the shortened length that would

5.6.3      Conclusion
In summary, because Alternative 2 (Shortened Breakwater Alternative) would result in less
construction due to a shortened breakwater, Alternative 2 would have slightly reduced
construction-related impacts to air quality, biological resources, GHG emissions, hydrology and
water quality, and noise. While these impacts would be slightly reduced, the overall significant
conclusion would remain the same, the same mitigation measures would apply, and impacts to
noise, recreation, and land use and planning would remain significant and unavoidable.
The primary purpose of the breakwater is to provide a safe harbor for the ferry vessels that would
dock next to the pier. The shortened breakwater under this Alternative would meet the primary
purpose of the breakwater. This Alternative would provide ferry service, as well as enhanced public
access and recreational opportunities and would, therefore, meet most of the basic project
objectives. However, because the shortened breakwater under this Alternative would provide
slightly less public access and recreational opportunities, it would meet the project objectives to a
slightly lesser extent than the proposed project.

5.7.3       Conclusion
In summary, because Alternative 3 (Shortened Pier Alternative) would result in less construction due
to a shortened pier, Alternative 3 would have slightly reduced construction-related impacts to air
quality, biological resources, GHG emissions, hydrology and water quality, and noise. While these
impacts would be slightly reduced, the overall significant conclusion would remain the same, the
same mitigation measures would apply, and impacts to noise, recreation, and land use and planning
would remain significant and unavoidable.
The primary purpose of the pier beyond the breakwater is to provide enhanced public access and
recreational opportunities. Unlike the breakwater that has a dual purpose of providing a safe harbor
for ferry vessels and providing public access/recreational opportunities; or the portion of the pier
from the public plaza to the breakwater, which has the dual purpose of providing access to ferry
vessels and public access/recreational opportunities; the portion of the pier beyond the
breakwater’s sole purpose is provide public access/recreational opportunities.
While this Alternative would meet most of the basic project objectives by providing ferry service and
some enhanced public access and recreational opportunities, it would meet the project objectives
to a lesser extent than the proposed project, since it would reduce the amount of public
access/recreational opportunities by approximately 405 feet.

5.8         Alternative 4: Reduced Landside Facilities
            Alternative
5.8.1       Description
The Reduced Landside Facilities Alternative (Alternative 4) would implement the proposed project
as planned, with a few key differences. Under Alternative 4, the facilities located on the water,
including the pier, breakwater, and associated infrastructure for the ferry vessels would be
implemented in the same way as the proposed project; however, on the land side, the number of
facilities would be reduced. Specifically, under this alternative, utilities would still be installed on the
land side to connect to the proposed new infrastructure on the proposed new pier; however, the
following facilities would not be implemented: cycle track; renovations to University Avenue and
Seawall Drive; bus facilities; public plaza; Bay Trail Extension; and renovated parking lot off Seawall
Drive, including no installation of EV charging for parking stalls. Some landside construction is
required for Alternative 4, in order to complete the Pier, due to the elevation of the Pier
(approximately 6 feet above existing plaza elevation) and the need for emergency vehicle access
onto the Pier. At a minimum this would include the Pier Abutment itself (including deep soil mixing
to create a seismically stable landing for the abutment) and retaining wall and fill in the area to
create vehicle and accessible connections between the existing sidewalk/Seawall Drive and the new
pier.

Berkeley Water Transportation Pier Ferry Project


5.8.2      Impact Analysis
Aesthetics
Under Alternative 4, all waterside components of the proposed project would remain, and landside
improvements would be scaled back. Landside elements such as the cycle track, public plaza, Bay
Trail Extension, and bus facilities would be omitted, but essential utilities connecting to the pier and
infrastructure (i.e., pier abutment and retaining wall) needed for the pier would still be installed.
The omission of landside features would result in fewer visual changes to the existing waterfront
setting; however, the omitted improvements-the cycle track, public plaza, Bay Trail Extension, and
bus facilities are all surface level improvements that are not noticeable in themselves. Construction
activities would still be needed for utilities and pier connections, although the area of disturbance
would be smaller for Alternative 4. The type of construction equipment that would be used for
Alternative 4 would be similar to what would be used for the proposed project. Like the proposed
project, Alternative 4 would require nighttime construction and would, therefore, require the
implementation of Mitigation Measure AES-1. Alternative 4 impacts would be less than significant
with mitigation.
The proposed project’s impacts related to aesthetics would be less than significant with mitigation
(see Section 3.1, Aesthetics). Alternative 4 would have a similar level of aesthetics impact during
construction of the pier and operation; however, its reduced landside development would
substantially lessen changes to visual character of the waterfront and shorten the duration and
extent of temporary construction-related visual impacts, however not to the extent of changing the
significance level.

Air Quality
Under Alternative 4, all waterside components of the proposed project would remain, and landside
improvements would be scaled back. Landside elements such as the cycle track, public plaza, Bay
Trail Extension, and bus facilities would be omitted, but essential utilities connecting to the pier
would still be installed. Similar construction-related air quality emissions mitigation would be
implemented. The reduction in landside development would shorten the overall construction
schedule and decrease the amount of heavy-duty equipment used compared to the proposed
project. Operational emissions would remain similar, as waterside infrastructure would be
unchanged. While the lack of land side development may result in a fewer number of visitors to the
Berkeley Waterfront, there would also be fewer opportunities for active transportation. Therefore,
Alternative 4 impacts on air quality would be less than significant with mitigation.
The proposed project’s impacts related to air quality would be less than significant with mitigation
(see Section 3.2, Air Quality). Alternative 4 would have reduced construction-related impacts.
However, impacts from operation of Alternative 4 may be greater than the proposed project
because Alternative 4 would not install EV chargers and because the lack of facilities under
Alternative 4 might attract fewer people to use the ferry service, thereby potentially resulting in
more VMT by single-occupancy vehicles driving over the Bay Bridge, and therefore more air quality
emissions, compared to the proposed project.

Biological Resources
Under Alternative 4, all waterside components of the proposed project would remain, and landside
improvements would be scaled back. Landside elements such as the cycle track, public plaza, Bay

Trail Extension, and bus facilities would be omitted, but essential utilities connecting to the pier
would still be installed. The reduction of landside features would decrease disturbance to terrestrial
habitats and wildlife compared to the proposed project. All federal, State, and local regulations and
mitigation measures would still apply to avoid impacts on marine biological resources. Therefore,
Alternative 4 impacts to biological resources would be less than significant with mitigation.
The proposed project’s impacts related to biological resources would be less than significant with

on aquatic resources and require the same mitigation measures as the proposed project (MMs BIO-

Cultural Resources
Under Alternative 4, all waterside components of the proposed project would remain, and landside
improvements would be scaled back. Landside elements such as the cycle track, public plaza, Bay
Trail Extension, and bus facilities would be omitted, but essential utilities connecting to the pier
would still be installed. The reduced landside construction would reduce construction activities and
overall landside ground disturbance, which reduces the likelihood of discovering archaeological
resources. However, mitigation measures related to inadvertent discovery of cultural resources
would still be required during construction. Therefore, Alternative 4 impacts on cultural resources
would be less than significant with mitigation.
The proposed project’s impacts related to cultural resources would be less than significant with
mitigation (see Section 3.4, Cultural Resources). Alternative 4 would have similar impacts on cultural
resources and require the same mitigation (Mitigation Measure CR-1) as the proposed project, but
impacts would be reduced due to the smaller landside footprint.

Geology and Soils
Under Alternative 4, all waterside components of the proposed project would remain, and landside
improvements would be scaled back. Landside elements such as the cycle track, public plaza, Bay
Trail Extension, and bus facilities would be omitted, but essential utilities connecting to the pier
would still be installed. Landside construction would be reduced, which would decrease ground
disturbance and associated risks with geologic and soil resources. Mitigation measures for
paleontological resources would still be required during construction. Therefore, Alternative 4
impacts on geology and soils would be less than significant with mitigation.
The proposed project’s impacts related to geological and soil resources would be less than
significant with mitigation (see Section 3.5, Geology and Soils). Alternative 4 would have a similar
level of impact on geological and soil resources and would require the same mitigation measures
(Mitigation Measures GEO-1 and GEO-2), but impacts would be reduced due to the smaller landside
footprint.

Under Alternative 4, all waterside components of the proposed project would remain, and landside

Trail Extension, and bus facilities would be omitted, but essential utilities connecting to the pier
would still be installed. This reduction would shorten the overall construction schedule and
decrease the amount of heavy-duty equipment used, resulting in a reduction in construction-related

GHG emissions and energy consumption compared to the proposed project. Operational emissions
would remain similar because ferry service and associated waterside infrastructure would remain

The proposed project’s impacts related to GHG emissions and energy would be less than significant

Hazards and Hazardous Materials
Under Alternative 4, all waterside components of the proposed project would remain, and landside
improvements would be scaled back. Landside elements such as the cycle track, public plaza, Bay
Trail Extension, and bus facilities would be omitted, but essential utilities connecting to the pier
would still be installed. This reduction would shorten the overall construction schedule and
decrease the amount of hazardous materials used, transported, and disposed of during landside
activities. Operational conditions would remain the same, as ferry service and associated
infrastructure under Alternative 4 would be the same as the proposed project. Therefore,
Alternative 4 impacts to hazards and hazardous materials would be less than significant.
The proposed project’s impacts related to hazards and hazardous materials would be less than
significant (see Section 3.7, Hazards and Hazardous Materials). Alternative 4 would have a similar
level of operational impact but reduced construction-related hazards due to the omission of
landside development.

Hydrology and Water Quality
Under Alternative 4, all waterside components of the proposed project would remain, and landside
improvements would be scaled back. Landside elements such as the cycle track, public plaza, Bay
Trail Extension, and bus facilities would be omitted, but essential utilities connecting to the pier
would still be installed. The reduction in landside construction would decrease the amount of
ground disturbance and new impervious surface area on land, slightly reducing potential effects on
drainage patterns and stormwater runoff compared to the proposed project. Alternative 4 would
adhere to applicable hydrology and water quality standards and remain subject to the same
mitigation measures related to construction in the water. Therefore, Alternative 4 impacts to
hydrology and water quality would be less than significant with mitigation.
The proposed project’s impacts related to hydrology and water quality would be less than significant
with mitigation (see Section 3.8, Hydrology and Water Quality). Alternative 4 would have similar
impacts during construction and operation but slightly reduced landside effects due to the smaller
footprint.

Land Use and Planning
Under Alternative 4, all waterside components of the proposed project would remain, and landside
improvements would be scaled back. Landside elements such as the cycle track, public plaza, Bay



5-22
                                                                                          Alternatives



Trail Extension, and bus facilities would be omitted, but essential utilities connecting to the pier
would still be installed. The reduction in landside development would decrease the overall footprint
of development and would not introduce new inconsistencies with applicable land use plans or
policies. Nonetheless, like the proposed project, this Alternative would be inconsistent with policies
related to construction noise and because of this, impacts would be significant and unavoidable.
Therefore, Alternative 4 impacts to land use and planning would be significant and unavoidable.
The proposed project’s impacts related to land use and planning would be significant and

identified in local plans as a means of providing different opportunities for people to move in the
City of Berkeley. Without these features, Alternative 4 would create greater inconsistencies with
local plans.

Noise
Under Alternative 4, all waterside components of the proposed project would remain, and landside
improvements would be scaled back. Landside elements such as the cycle track, public plaza, Bay
Trail Extension, and bus facilities would be omitted, but essential utilities connecting to the pier
would still be installed. Landside construction would be reduced, overall reducing construction noise
on land. However, nighttime pile driving and marine construction activities would still occur.
Therefore, Alternative 4 impacts to noise would remain significant and unavoidable.
The proposed project’s impacts related to noise would be significant and unavoidable during
construction (see Section 3.10, Noise). Alternative 4 would have a slightly reduced impact compared
to the proposed project due to the reduced landside construction noise, but not to the extent of
reducing the impact level or eliminating the need for mitigation (Mitigation Measure NOI-1).

Recreation
Under Alternative 4, all waterside components of the proposed project would remain, and landside
improvements would be scaled back. Landside elements such as the cycle track, public plaza, Bay
Trail Extension, and bus facilities would be omitted, but essential utilities connecting to the pier
would still be installed. Alternative 4 would decrease construction-related disturbance on land but
would also limit the enhancement of recreational opportunities. Nonetheless, under this
Alternative, construction of the pier and breakwater would remain. As with the proposed project,
these would be considered recreational facilities and the impacts associated with the construction
of these facilities under Alternative 4 would be significant and unavoidable (due to construction
noise)
The proposed project’s impacts related to recreation would be significant and unavoidable due to
construction-related noise (see Section 3.11, Recreation). Alternative 4 would have reduced
construction-related impacts on recreation due to the construction of less recreational facilities.

Transportation
Under Alternative 4, all waterside components of the proposed project would remain, and landside
improvements would be scaled back. Landside elements such as the cycle track, public plaza, Bay
Trail Extension, and bus facilities would be omitted, but essential utilities connecting to the pier
would still be installed. Alternative 4 would not include improvements to circulation and pedestrian

safety on University Avenue but would provide a zero-emission Transbay transportation option to
reduce single-occupancy vehicle usage and VMT. Therefore, Alternative 4 impacts to transportation
would be less than significant, similar to the proposed project.
The proposed project’s impacts related to transportation would be less than significant (see
Section 3.12, Transportation). Alternative 4 would have a greater impact compared to the proposed

Tribal Cultural Resources
Under Alternative 4, all waterside components of the proposed project would remain, and landside
improvements would be scaled back. Landside elements such as the cycle track, public plaza, Bay
Trail Extension, and bus facilities would be omitted, but essential utilities connecting to the pier
would still be installed. The omission of landside development would reduce construction activities
and overall landside ground disturbance, which reduces the likelihood of discovering tribal cultural
resources compared to the proposed project. However, mitigation measures related to inadvertent
discovery of tribal cultural resources would still be required during construction. Therefore,
Alternative 4 impacts to tribal cultural resources would be less than significant with mitigation.
The proposed project’s impacts related to tribal cultural resources would be less than significant
with mitigation (see Section 3.13, Tribal Cultural Resources). Alternative 4 would have similar
impacts on tribal cultural resources and require the same mitigation (Mitigation Measures TCR-1
through TCR-5) as the proposed project, but impacts would be reduced due to the smaller landside
footprint.

Utilities and Service Systems
Under Alternative 4, all waterside components of the proposed project would remain, and landside
improvements would be scaled back. Landside elements such as the cycle track, public plaza, Bay
Trail Extension, and bus facilities would be omitted, but essential utilities connecting to the pier
would still be installed. Overall, utility connections would remain similar to the proposed project.
For example, water connections would be needed for both the pier and the restroom; sewer
connections would be needed for the restroom; telecommunication connections would be needed
for the ferry infrastructure; and electricity connections would be needed to charge ferry vessels but
might be reduced given there would no longer be a need for EV chargers. Alternative 4 would
require implementation of the same mitigation as the proposed project, to reduce impacts related
to construction of utilities, and impacts would be less than significant with mitigation.
The proposed project’s impacts related to utilities and service systems would be less than significant
with mitigation (see Section 3.14, Utilities and Service Systems). Alternative 4 would have similar
operational utilities and service systems impacts, as there would still be a substantial energy
demand to support operation of the ferry vessels. However the overall demand would decrease
compared to the proposed project, as there would be fewer landside amenities requiring water,
wastewater, electricity, and solid waste services under Alternative 4.

5.8.3          Conclusion
In summary, because Alternative 4 (Reduced Landside Facilities Alternative) would result in less
construction and excavation due to the implementation of less landside facilities, Alternative 4
would have slightly reduced construction-related impacts on aesthetics, biological resources,
cultural resources, geology and soils, hazards and hazardous materials, hydrology and water quality,
noise, recreation, tribal cultural resources, and utilities and service systems. While these impacts
would be slightly reduced, the overall significant conclusion would remain the same, the same
mitigation measures would apply, and impacts on noise, recreation, and land use and planning
would remain significant and unavoidable. Furthermore, under this alternative there could be
slightly greater impacts on air quality, GHG emissions, land use and planning, and transportation,
due to the potential for the site to be used by less visitors compared to the proposed project, due to
its reduced attractiveness with less amenities.
Alternative 4 would achieve most of the basic project objectives, however to a much lesser extent
than the proposed project. While the proposed project would provide efficient and environmentally
friendly zero emission public ferry service between Berkeley and San Francisco and while the
proposed project would enhance public access and recreational opportunities at the Berkeley
Waterfront, the public access and recreational opportunities would be greatly reduced under this
alternative compared to the proposed project. Under this Alternative, people using the Berkeley
Waterfront would not be able to use a cycle track to access the project site; would not be able to
congregate in a public plaza; would not be able to use the Bay Trail Extension off Seawall Drive; and
overall, would not be able to enjoy the Bay as much as under the proposed project.

5.9            Alternatives Considered but Rejected
The following summarizes alternatives considered, but ultimately rejected for inclusion in the
analysis, because they would not meet most of the project objectives, would not substantially
reduce impacts compared to the proposed project, or were determined to be infeasible.
    The City considered alternative locations; however, the City ultimately rejected these
     alternative locations. Below is a summary of the various alternative locations that were
     considered but rejected:
      Berkeley Marina Basin. Under this potential alternative, ferry vessels would dock within the
         Berkeley Marina Basin. This alternative location is one that was studied previously as part of
         a Draft EIS/EIR from 2008. 1 As part of this analysis, it was found that implementation of a
         ferry terminal in the Marina would require removal of docks within the Marina. This
         alternative would not meet the basic project objectives to: (1) enhance public access and
         recreational opportunities at the Berkeley Waterfront and (2) provide efficient and
         environmentally friendly zero emission public ferry service between Berkeley and San
         Francisco. In order for an alternative to meet the basic project objectives, it must meet both
         of the objectives identified above. This Alternative would not meet the objective of
         enhancing public access and recreational opportunities at the Berkeley Waterfront. Under
         this alternative, the pier would remain closed and would continue to deteriorate. Patrons
         under this alternative would access the Berkeley Waterfront; however, there wouldn’t be
         enhanced public access and recreational opportunities. Given the location of this
         alternative, there would be no need for a new pier, no public plaza for the pier, no cycle

           track to connect to the public plaza, and no Bay Trail Extension along Seawall Drive.
           Furthermore, removing docks within the Marina would reduce recreational opportunities at
           the Waterfront. Next, this alternative would not meet the basic project objective of
           providing efficient and environmentally friendly zero emission public ferry service between
           Berkeley and San Francisco, because this alternative would not be considered efficient. This
           alternative would compromise ferry travel times and overall operational performance.
           Inside the marina, the ferry vessels would face additional maneuvering constraints,

           factors would extend the overall travel times, reduce service reliability and diminish the
           competitiveness of the Berkeley- San Francisco Ferry Route, compared to other Transbay
           modes of travel. 2 Because this alternative is not considered operationally feasible and does
           not meet the basic project objectives, this alternative has been considered but rejected.
          Foot of Gilman Street. The City received scoping comments about considering locating the
           project at the foot of Gilman Street as a potential alternative. This alternative location is one
           that was studied previously as part of a Draft EIS/EIR from 2008. 3 This alternative would be
           located at the western end of Gilman street, next to the Berkeley Waterfront. This
           alternative has been rejected from further consideration because it would increase
           environmental impacts. This alternative would locate the ferry terminal within Eastshore
           State Park in an area that is more ecologically sensitive than the proposed project site. The
           2008 Draft EIS/EIR documented that this alternative could affect eelgrass habitat. 4 This
           alternative is expected to result in greater impacts on biological resources and similar other
           impacts than the proposed project (i.e., similar construction-related impacts on noise and
           air quality, given its proximity to Tom Bates Regional Complex). Because this alternative
           would increase environmental impacts and not reduce significant environmental impacts,
           this alternative has been considered but rejected.
          HS Lordship Site. The 2008 Berkeley/Albany Ferry Terminal Study Draft EIS/EIR identified
           the HS Lordship Site Alternative, which would be located in the cove behind the former HS
           Lordship Restaurant. This potential alternative was rejected in the past given constraints
           related to additional dredging, slower operating speeds, conflicts with BCDC Bay Plan
           policies, and lack of public support. 5 Due to its location, this alternative is expected to
           increase environmental impacts and not reduce significant environmental impacts. This
           includes the following potentially increased impacts: potential land use inconsistencies and
           additional impacts from additional dredging For this reason, this alternative has been
           considered but rejected.
          Locations outside of the City of Berkeley. The City received scoping comments about

           locations are outside of the City’s jurisdiction. Golden Gate Fields is within the City of Albany
           and the Emeryville Marina is within the City of Emeryville. Because the City of Berkeley has
           no jurisdiction over these areas, these alternatives would not be considered potentially
           feasible. In addition, because these alternatives are not located within the Berkeley
           Waterfront, they would not meet the basic project objective of the project, to enhance
           public access and recreational opportunities at the Berkeley Waterfront. Because these

    Smaller scale ferry service. Under this potential alternative, smaller ferry vessels or a reduced
     ferry vessel schedule would be used. A smaller ferry or reduced ferry vessel schedule would still
     result in additional ferry vessels and would not reduce a significant environmental impact.
     Regarding biological resources, in general, fish and marine mammals potentially near the
     Berkeley waterfront are adapted to the high activity level of an active marina and would avoid
     ferry boats as they now avoid commercial and recreational boaters. An alternative that would
     introduce a smaller scale ferry service would still have the same potential impact. Therefore,
     this alternative would not reduce any environmental impacts. Because this alternative would
     not reduce significant environmental impacts, this alternative has been considered but rejected.
    No ferry service with new pier Alternative. Under this potential alternative, the proposed pier
     could be implemented similar to the proposed project (1,080 feet), but no ferry service would
     be installed. This project would be overall similar to the proposed project but would not include
     the infrastructure associated with the ferry vessels (no breakwater, gangways, floats, etc.). This
     alternative would not meet the two basic project objectives to: (1) enhance public access and
     recreational opportunities at the Berkeley Waterfront and (2) provide efficient and
     environmentally friendly zero emission public ferry service between Berkeley and San Francisco.
     In order for an alternative to meet the basic project objectives, it must meet both of the
     objectives identified above. While this alternative would meet the first objective to enhance
     public access and recreational opportunities at the Berkeley Waterfront, it would not provide
     efficient and environmentally friendly zero emission public ferry service between Berkeley and
     San Francisco. In addition, this alternative is not feasible. WETA would only provide project
     funding if the ferry is included, and since Berkeley requires funding to restore the closed pier, it
     is only with WETA support that the pier can be rebuilt. WETA can only fund and implement ferry
     projects. Because this alternative is not considered feasible and does not meet the basic project
     objectives, this alternative has been considered but rejected.
    Repair the Existing Pier Alternative. This potential alternative would entail repairing the
     existing pier. This Alternative is not considered feasible due to the current condition of the pier.
     Based on review from qualified engineers, there is widespread spalling 6 of concrete that is
     exposing the layers of reinforcing materials, which are severely corroded and have resulted in
     portions of the pier collapsing. This deterioration is due to the age of the structure and the high
     level of chlorine in the concrete, which causes the reinforcing to rust and leads to spalling and
     more corrosion. There is no way to extract the chlorine from the concrete and thus the pier has
     reached its end of service life. 7 Because this alternative is not considered feasible, this
     alternative has been considered but rejected.
    Monopile Alternative. This potential alternative entails using a single-row of piles rather than a
     double-row of piles in the water. In order to meet the seismic demands for the pier, the area of
     the monopile would need to be greater than the combined area of the dual row of proposed
     piles. 8 Since a monopile would result in more fill due to its larger area, it would not reduce any
     environmental impacts. Because this alternative would not reduce significant environmental
     impacts, this alternative has been considered but rejected.

6 Spalling refers to the breaking, flaking, or chipping away of concrete, often caused by corrosion of embedded reinforcing steel.

    Increasing Bay Area Rapid Transit (BART) capacity. The City received a scoping comment to
     consider improving BART capacity. The City of Berkeley has no jurisdiction over BART and would
     not be able to make any changes associated with the capacity. Since the City would not be able
     to make any changes to BART capacity, this potential alternative is considered infeasible and has
     been considered but rejected.
    Improving access to BART within Berkeley. The City received a scoping comment to consider
     improving BART access. While the City could feasibly make improvements that would increase
     access to BART, this alternative would not meet the basic project objectives. The project has
     two basic objectives: (1) enhance public access and recreational opportunities at the Berkeley
     Waterfront and (2) provide efficient and environmentally friendly zero emission public ferry
     service between Berkeley and San Francisco. This potential alternative would not meet these
     basic project objectives and has therefore been considered but rejected.
    Feasibility Alternatives. As part of the Feasibility Study, the City considered four different
     potential configurations for the pier. 9 These configurations were known as Sword, Dog Leg, Fish
     Hook, and Circle. The City conducted community outreach to determine the community’s
     preference, which ended up being the Sword Configuration. The Sword Configuration design is
     included as part of the proposed project design. Because the community has provided their
     preference, the City is not considering a potential alternative pier configuration for the project.
     Furthermore, these potential alternative configurations are not expected to result in reduced
     environmental impacts. These alternatives would still require fill and work in the Bay, and the
     environmental impacts associated with the different configurations are expected to be the same
     as the proposed project. The operational impacts would remain the same. Because these
     alternatives would not reduce significant environmental impacts, these alternatives have been
     considered but rejected.

5.10            Environmentally Superior Alternative
CEQA Guidelines Section 15126(e)(2) requires identification of an environmentally superior
alternative. If the “No Project” Alternative is environmentally superior, CEQA requires selection of
the “environmentally superior alternative other than the No Project Alternative” from among the
proposed project and the alternatives evaluated.

Alternative 1 Comparison to Proposed Project Summary
The No Project Alternative would generally result in greater impacts compared to the proposed
project (see Table 5-2). By not implementing ferry service, Alternative 1 would result in greater
impacts related to air quality, GHG emissions, land use and planning, and transportation, because
Alternative 1 would not provide the same reductions in VMT, criteria air pollutants, and GHG
emissions, as the proposed project. Alternative 1 would avoid certain temporary environmental
impacts associated with construction for the following resources: with biological resources, cultural
resources, geology and soils, hydrology and water quality noise, recreation, tribal cultural resources,
and utilities and service systems. In addition, the proposed project would avoid the operational
impacts associated with potential whale strikes and public plaza noise, both of which were found to
be less than significant with mitigation for the proposed project. Alternative 1 would not meet the
plan’s objectives, as it would not enhance public access and recreational opportunities at the
Berkeley Waterfront and would not provide efficient and environmentally friendly zero emission
public ferry service between Berkeley and San Francisco.
